Arnold Palmer (drink):
{{Short description|Drink made of iced tea and lemonade}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=July 2024}}
{{Infobox beverage|ingredients=[[Iced tea]] and [[lemonade]]| type=[[Non-alcoholic mixed drink]]||image=My new obsession the arnold palmer!!! (5184944881).jpg}}

The '''Arnold Palmer''', also known as the '''half and half''', is a [[non-alcoholic mixed drink]] that combines [[iced tea]] and [[lemonade]]. The name refers to the professional American golfer [[Arnold Palmer]], who was known to often request and drink this beverage combination; some attribute the invention of the beverage to the golfer.<ref>{{cite book|title=This Golfing Life|publisher=Atlantic Monthly Press|pages=[https://archive.org/details/thisgolfinglife00mich/page/181 181]–182|author=Bamberger, Michael|url=https://archive.org/details/thisgolfinglife00mich|url-access=registration|isbn=9780871139283|date=2005-11-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The NFL Gameday Cookbook|author1=Lampe, Ray |author2=Beisch, Leigh |name-list-style=amp |page=230}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Cooking the Cowboy Way|author=Spears, Grady|page=177|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F_e02lAmY74C&pg=PA177|isbn=9780740773921|date=2009-10-20|publisher=Andrews McMeel |display-authors=etal}}</ref>

There are two alcoholic cocktail versions, one is the [[John Daly (cocktail)|John Daly]] which has [[vodka]] and the other is the [[Lee Trevino]] or Juan Daly which has [[tequila]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Kelley|first=Brent|publisher=[[About.com]]|title=The John Daly Drink: Recipes, and Why the Cocktail Is Named for the Golfer|url=http://golf.about.com/od/golfentertainment/a/john-daly-drink.htm|access-date=5 June 2015|archive-date=7 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150407010827/http://golf.about.com/od/golfentertainment/a/john-daly-drink.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Savage | first=Amanda | title=Thirsty Thursday: The Lee Trevino Phoenix Public Market Cafe Nightlife | website=Nightlife | date=August 8, 2013 |url=https://www.arizonafoothillsmagazine.com/aznightlife/thirsty-thursday-the-lee-trevino-from-phoenix-public-market-cafe/ | access-date=November 19, 2025}}</ref> [[MillerCoors]] began marketing and distributing a commercially available malt-based version of the beverage under the Arnold Palmer Spiked name in early 2018.<ref>{{cite news|title=Behind the Beer: Arnold Palmer Spiked Show Promise Amid Early Growth|url=https://www.millercoorsblog.com/news/arnold-palmer-spiked-shows-promise-amid-early-growth/|access-date=July 30, 2018|archive-date=July 31, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180731213216/https://www.millercoorsblog.com/news/arnold-palmer-spiked-shows-promise-amid-early-growth/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==History==
In 2012, an ESPN ''[[30 for 30#30 for 30 Shorts|30 for 30 Shorts]]'' documentary was produced on the drink, featuring Palmer, beverage experts, a group of [[Professional Golfers' Association of America|PGA]] golfers and comedian [[Will Arnett]] discussing the drink's history and popularity.<ref name=30for30>{{cite web|title=30 for 30 Shorts: The Arnold Palmer|url=http://www.grantland.com/story/_/id/8683633/the-latest-offering-new-30-30-documentary-series|publisher=Grantland.com|access-date=July 14, 2013|date=November 28, 2012}}</ref> In the film, Palmer attributes the spreading of the drink's name to an incident in which a woman copied his ordering the drink at lunch after a long day of designing a golf course in [[Palm Springs, California]] during the late 1960s, saying "I'll have that Arnold Palmer drink, too."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.arnoldpalmer.com/beverages|title=Arnold Palmer|website=www.arnoldpalmer.com}}</ref> Palmer preferred three parts unsweetened tea, to one part lemonade, but when mixed equal parts tea and lemonade, the drink is sometimes called a ''Half & Half''.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Arnold Palmer Drink|url=http://golf.about.com/od/arnoldpalmer/fl/Arnold-Palmer-Drink.htm|publisher=golf.about.com|access-date=September 25, 2016|archive-date=November 11, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161111025632/http://golf.about.com/od/arnoldpalmer/fl/Arnold-Palmer-Drink.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Sidewalk chefs serve up taste of Pimlico|url=http://www.baltimoresun.com/news/maryland/bs-md-preakness-neighborhood-food-20130516,0,6503062.story|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|access-date=July 29, 2014|date=May 17, 2013|archive-date=July 29, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140729183633/http://www.baltimoresun.com/news/maryland/bs-md-preakness-neighborhood-food-20130516,0,6503062.story|url-status=dead}}</ref>

According to a waitress at [[Augusta National Golf Club]], Palmer ordered his namesake beverage by saying, "I'll have a Mr. Palmer."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Politi |first1=Steve |title=Masters 2013: How does Arnold Palmer order an Arnold Palmer? |url=https://www.nj.com/golf/index.ssf/2013/04/masters_2013_how_does_arnold_p.html |access-date=2018-04-01 |work=NJ.com |date=2013-04-09}}</ref> When Palmer visited the [[Latrobe Country Club]] in his hometown, the staff at the snack shack served the beverage to him or his wife, Kit, without prompting. "Mr. Palmer should never have to order the drink named after him," wrote a former snack shack employee about the club's rules.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/arnold-palmer-the-humble-king-of-latrobe-1474936494|title=Arnold Palmer, the Humble King of Latrobe|last=Schwartzel|first=Erich|date=2016-09-27|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|issn=0099-9660|access-date=2016-09-27}}</ref>

The first mention of the beverage nationally was in the ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' 1997 "Hot Issue". Screenwriter [[Scott Alexander and Larry Karaszewski|Scott Alexander]] said it was the new "hot drink" and called it the "Half-and-Half." Alexander wrote, "It's half-iced tea and half-lemonade. At any Hollywood lunch, everyone orders it."<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Hot in Hollywood |magazine=Rolling Stone |date=August 21, 1997 |issue=767 |page=76}}</ref>

== Mass-produced versions ==
The drink has been sold under the Arnold Palmer trademark via a licensing arrangement with Innovative Flavors since 2001. [[Arizona Beverage Company]] began marketing and selling the beverage with Palmer's picture and signature on the bottle in 2002 and has handled distribution ever since.<ref name="tee">{{cite web|last=Byrd|first=Chris|title=Tea for Tee|url=http://www.arnoldpalmer.com/BRANDS/KINGDOM/ARCHIVE/2010/03/tea_for_tee.aspx|publisher=Kingdom Magazine|access-date=11 June 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121113082349/http://www.arnoldpalmer.com/BRANDS/KINGDOM/ARCHIVE/2010/03/tea_for_tee.aspx|archive-date=13 November 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> The line has expanded to include various flavors including Green Tea, Southern Style Sweet Tea and Pink Lemonade, Zero Calorie, Strawberry, Peach, Mango and Natural Energy. Lemonade combined with iced tea is also sold without the Arnold Palmer trademark by other companies, such as [[Nestea]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.shortys.ca/3002-large_default/20794115.jpg|title=Nestea half and half|access-date=2018-02-10|archive-date=2018-02-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180211071758/https://www.shortys.ca/3002-large_default/20794115.jpg|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Lipton Brisk]], [[Honest Tea]] (as Half and Half), [[Nantucket Nectars]] (as Half and Half), [[Country Time]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.myfoodandfamily.com/|title=My Food and Family Recipes|website=My Food and Family}}</ref> [[Sweet Leaf Tea Company|Sweet Leaf]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://purityorganic.com/|title=Purity Organic & Sweet Leaf Tea|website=Purity Organic|access-date=2020-10-30|archive-date=2020-11-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101014817/https://purityorganic.com/|url-status=dead}}</ref> XINGtea,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.xingicedtea.com/products/16oz-bottles/|title=XINGtea Half & Half|access-date=29 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160410084450/http://www.xingicedtea.com/products/16oz-bottles/|archive-date=10 April 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Snapple]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.snapple.com/products/snapple-original-half-n-half-tea|title=Half 'n Half|website=Snapple}}</ref> and [[Peace Iced Tea]] (as Caddyshack). It has 23 mg of caffeine per 23 oz drink.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.coca-cola.com/us/en/brands/peace-tea#accordion-ea070d0097-item-3bae7e345b | title=Products | publisher=Coca Cola US | accessdate=5 April 2024}}</ref> In 2021, Chick-fil-A began selling its own version marketed as "Sunjoy."<ref>{{cite web |last=Blumberg |first=Perri Ormont |date=April 23, 2021 |title=Welcome, Sunjoy! Popular Off-Menu Beverage of Sweet Tea and Lemonade Joins Chick-fil-A's Official Menu |url=https://www.southernliving.com/food/drinks/chick-fil-a-adds-sunjoy-to-menu |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240808033857/https://www.southernliving.com/food/drinks/chick-fil-a-adds-sunjoy-to-menu |archive-date=August 8, 2024 |website=Southern Living |access-date=November 7, 2025}}</ref>

== Arnold Palmer variations ==
The drink has many variations, with and without alcohol.  Non-alcoholic variations include the Winnie Palmer<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cheers to June |url=https://yellowstonevalleywoman.com/cheers-to-june |access-date=2026-01-05 |website=yellowstonevalleywoman.com |language=en-US}}</ref> (made with sweet tea and lemonade), the Jennie Wong (made with lemonade and Coke)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Reddit - The heart of the internet |url=https://www.reddit.com/r/stopdrinking/comments/1pksxfv/comment/nxh9iuo/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=web3x&utm_name=web3xcss&utm_term=1&utm_content=share_button |access-date=2026-01-05 |website=www.reddit.com}}</ref>, and the Green Tea Arnold Palmer<ref>{{Cite web |last=link |first=Get |last2=Facebook |last3=X |last4=Pinterest |last5=Apps |first5=Other |title=Arnold Palmer Recipes: 11 Delicious Variations on the Original |url=https://www.golfcompendium.com/2018/10/arnold-palmer-drink-recipes-variations.html |access-date=2026-01-05}}</ref> (made with frozen lemonade concentrate).

Cannabis tea:
{{short description|Cannabis-infused drink}}
[[File:Té de marihuana.jpg|thumb|Cannabis tea with [[cinnamon]] and a spoonful of [[agave honey]]]]
{{Cannabis sidebar}}
[[File:Cannabis sativa (7864534966).jpg|thumb|Male flower tops]]
'''Cannabis tea''' (also known as weed tea, [[Marijuana (word)|pot tea]],  a cannabis [[decoction]]) is a [[Cannabis edible#Drink|cannabis-infused drink]] prepared by steeping various parts of the [[cannabis (drug)|cannabis]] plant in hot or cold water. Cannabis tea is commonly recognized as an alternative form of preparation and consumption of the [[Cannabis|cannabis plant]], more popularly known as [[marijuana]], pot, or [[weed]]. This plant has long been recognized as an [[Herbalism|herbal medicine]]<ref>{{Cite book|title=Cannabis and Cannabinoids: Pharmacology, Toxicology, and Therapeutic Potential|last=Russo|first=Ethan|publisher=Routledge|year=2013|pages=37–51}}</ref> employed by health professionals worldwide to ease symptoms of disease,<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Use of traditional complementary and alternative medicine for HIV patients in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa|journal = BMC Public Health|volume = 8|pages = 255|last=Peltzer|first=Karl|date=Summer 2008|doi=10.1186/1471-2458-8-255|pmid = 18652666|pmc = 2503977 | doi-access=free }}</ref> as well as a [[psychoactive drug]] used recreationally<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Cannabis use and mental health in young people: cohort study|last=Patton|first=George|date=2002|journal=The BMJ|volume=325|issue=7374|pages=1195–1198|doi=10.1136/bmj.325.7374.1195|pmid=12446533|pmc=135489}}</ref> and in spiritual traditions. Though less commonly practiced than popular methods like [[smoking]] or consuming [[Cannabis edible|edible]]s''',''' drinking cannabis tea can produce comparable physical and mental [[therapeutic effect]]s. Such effects are largely attributed to the [[Thc|THC]] and [[Cannabidiol|CBD]] content of the tea, levels of which are drastically dependent on individual preparation techniques involving volume, amount of cannabis, and boiling time.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Hazekamp|first=Arno|date=Spring 2017|title=Cannabis tea revisited: A systematic evaluation of the cannabinoid composition of cannabis tea|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|volume=113|issue=1|pages=85–90|doi=10.1016/j.jep.2007.05.019|pmid=17604926|s2cid=13800834 }}</ref> Also in common with these administration forms of cannabis is the heating component performed before usage. Due to the rather uncommon nature of this particular practice of cannabis consumption in modern times (in contrast to historical use) as well as the legality of cannabis throughout the world, the research available on the composition of cannabis tea is limited and based broadly around what is known of cannabis as it exists [[botanically]].

== Composition ==
According to a 2007 study published in the ''[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]]'', the composition of cannabis tea is affected by criteria including, but not limited to, the duration of time over which the cannabis is steeped, the volume of tea prepared, and the period of time for which the tea is stored before consumption.<ref name=":0" /> The study mentions the ways in which levels of THC and [[Tetrahydrocannabinolic acid synthase|THCA]] impact variability of composition by changing the bioactivity of the beverage. Therefore, cannabis teas that include less bioactive cannabinoids, "based on HPLC peak area"<ref name=":0" /> will demonstrate varying compositions.

== Preparation ==
According to a recent study on cannabinoid concentration and [[Chemical stability#Outside chemistry|stability]] in preparations of [[Hash oil|cannabis oil]] and tea, a boiling period of fifteen minutes was found to be sufficient in order to reach the highest concentrations of cannabinoids in tea solutions.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Pacifici|first=R|date=August 2017|title=Evaluation of cannabinoids concentration and stability in standardized preparations of cannabis tea and cannabis oil by ultra-high performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry.|journal=Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine|volume=55|issue=10|pages=1555–1563|pmid=28207408|doi=10.1515/cclm-2016-1060|s2cid=21424914}}</ref> However, preparation of cannabis oil in the study was found to ensure a higher stability of cannabinoids than that which was found in preparation of cannabis tea.<ref name=":3" />

To produce psychoactive effects, cannabis used in tea must first be [[Decarboxylation|decarboxylated]]. As with regular tea, spices are often added. Typically, the tea is allowed to simmer for 5–10 minutes.<ref name="CBDzine">{{cite web |title=Types of Drinks |url=https://cbdzine.com/edibles/types-of-drinks/ |website=CBDzine |publisher=WordPress |access-date=6 May 2021 |archive-date=6 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506205832/https://cbdzine.com/edibles/types-of-drinks/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Folk medicine ==
Cannabis tea was used for centuries in folk medicine as it was thought to be a treatment for rheumatism, cystitis, and various urinary diseases.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kabelik|first=J.|date=1960|title=Cannabis as a medicament|url=https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/bulletin/bulletin_1960-01-01_3_page003.html|journal=Die Pharmazie}}</ref>

In an article in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', it is projected that cannabis has been used medicinally for nearly 12,000 years. The oldest confirmed reference to medicinal cannabis is ~2700 BC, in Ancient China. There is ~190AD evidence that a Chinese physician, Hua T'o, used an emulsion of tea and wine to anesthetize a patient for surgery. {{Citation needed|date=January 2025}}

According to a short communication published in the [[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]], based on the research of Zias et al. regarding cannabis use in ancient childbirth, cannabis is said to have been used to assist women during childbirth. The communication is regarding an anthropological find of a birthing mother, dated to the 4th century AD., "We assume that the ashes found in the tomb were cannabis, burned in a vessel and administered to the young girl as an inhalant to facilitate the birth process."<ref name=":2" />  Cannabis tea has been traditionally used by Jamaican women as a remedy for morning sickness associated with pregnancy. {{Citation needed|date=January 2025}} There is no evidence that cannabis is an abortive medicine."

== Legal status ==
Cannabis tea is controlled as a derivative of cannabis in most countries as is required of countries whose governments are party to the [[United Nations]]' [[Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.unodc.org/documents/commissions/CND/Int_Drug_Control_Conventions/Ebook/The_International_Drug_Control_Conventions_E.pdf|title=The International Drug Control Conventions|last=United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime|date=1988|publisher=www.unodc.org}}</ref> However, similar to the regulation surrounding [[Alcohol by volume|alcohol content]] of [[kombucha]], there are some forms of cannabis tea with cannabis levels considered to be highly undetectable. These variations of the drink do not contain the psychoactive cannabinoid known as THC ([[Tetrahydrocannabinol|delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol]]) and, instead, contain the non-psychoactive cannabinoids [[cannabidiol]] (CBD) or [[cannabinol]] (CBN)—both of which tend to go undetected in cannabis use/intoxication [[drug test]]s.<ref name=":0" /> As such, the legal status of cannabis tea is largely dependent on its composition and preparation.

=== United States ===
Cannabis tea is [[Controlled Substances Act#Schedules of controlled substances|scheduled]] at the [[Federal government of the United States|federal level]] in the [[United States]] by nature of being a derivative of ''[[Cannabis sativa]]'', and it is therefore illegal to possess, buy, and sell.<ref name="PART 1308 — SCHEDULES OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES - 1308.11 Schedule I">{{Cite web |url=http://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/21cfr/cfr/1308/1308_11.htm |title=§1308.11 Schedule I. |access-date=2015-01-04 |archive-date=2009-08-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090827043725/http://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/21cfr/cfr/1308/1308_11.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> Due to variances in statewide laws, and the reluctance of the federal government to overrule the states, however, the federal legislation has little impact on nationwide use, and is "generally applied only against persons who possess, cultivate, or distribute large quantities of cannabis".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.safeaccessnow.org/federal_marijuana_law|title=Federal Marijuana Law}}</ref> As such, regulation of recreational and/or medicinal growth and use on an individual level is not the responsibility of the federal government.

==== Colorado law ====
In [[Colorado]], for [[medical cannabis|medical purposes]], cannabis tea is a "Medical Marijuana Infused Product" which is "a product infused with medical marijuana that is intended for use or consumption other than by [[smoking]], including edible products, [[ointment]]s, and [[Tincture of cannabis|tincture]]s. These products, when manufactured or sold by a licensed medical marijuana center or a medical marijuana-infused product manufacturer, shall not be considered a [[food]] or [[drug]] for the purposes of the "[[Colorado Food and Drug Act]]", part 4 of article 5 of title 25, C.R.S."<ref name=CO_MED>{{cite web|title=Colorado Medical Marijuana Code|url=http://www.colorado.gov/cs/Satellite?blobcol=urldata&blobheadername1=Content-Disposition&blobheadername2=Content-Type&blobheadervalue1=inline%3B+filename%3D%22Medical+Marijuana+Code.pdf%22&blobheadervalue2=application%2Fpdf&blobkey=id&blobtable=MungoBlobs&blobwhere=1251781475604&ssbinary=true|publisher=Colorado.gov|access-date=Jan 4, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150104235325/http://www.colorado.gov/cs/Satellite?blobcol=urldata&blobheadername1=Content-Disposition&blobheadername2=Content-Type&blobheadervalue1=inline%3B+filename%3D%22Medical+Marijuana+Code.pdf%22&blobheadervalue2=application%2Fpdf&blobkey=id&blobtable=MungoBlobs&blobwhere=1251781475604&ssbinary=true|archive-date=January 4, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> Colorado currently stands as one of 33 states that have laws legalizing marijuana<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.governing.com/gov-data/safety-justice/state-marijuana-laws-map-medical-recreational.html|title=State Marijuana Laws in 2018 Map|date=7 November 2012 |publisher=www.governing.com|language=en|access-date=2018-12-10}}</ref> as of 2018.

== Adverse effects ==
Although not as widely published as the beneficial, therapeutic effects of cannabis tea, adverse effects of consumption have been found to exist, in addition to the known adverse effects of cannabis use in general.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hall|first=Wayne|date=January 2015|title=What has research over the past two decades revealed about the adverse health effects of recreational cannabis use?|journal=Addiction|volume=110|issue=1|pages=19–35|doi=10.1111/add.12703|issn=1360-0443|pmid=25287883|url=http://espace.library.uq.edu.au/view/UQ:346328/Hall_2014_20ycann_OA_post.pdf}}</ref> Based upon the findings of select studies,<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Merzouki|first=A|s2cid=6358400|date=Summer 2000|title=Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) and abortion|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|volume=73|issue=3|pages=501–503|doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(00)00323-8|pmid=11091005}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Mims|first=Robert|date=July 1977|title=Adverse Effects of Intravenous Cannabis Tea|journal=Journal of the National Medical Association|volume=69|issue=7|pages=491–495|pmc=2536936|pmid=875075}}</ref> it appears as though such effects occur mainly as a result of unconventional methods or dosage used when interacting with the decoction.

'''''Bandung''''', '''''sirap bandung''''', '''''air bandung''''', '''''iced bandung''''' or '''''rose syrup drink''''' is a drink popular in [[Maritime Southeast Asia]], notably in [[Brunei]], Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. It consists of [[evaporated milk]] or [[condensed milk]] flavoured with [[Rose water|rose syrup]] ([[Rose water|rose]] [[Squash (drink)|cordial]]), giving it a pink colour.<ref name="BandungSG"/>

==Regional names==
The term ''bandung'' means "pairs",<ref>{{citation|chapter-url=http://search.cari.com.my/dictionary/dic_malay.php?db_table=mdict&words=fix1&keyword=bandung|chapter=Bandung|title=Online Dictionary|publisher=[[Cari Internet|Cari.com.my]]|access-date=29 March 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722230943/http://search.cari.com.my/dictionary/dic_malay.php?db_table=mdict&words=fix1&keyword=bandung|archive-date=22 July 2011}}</ref> while ''sirap'' means "syrup"<ref>{{citation|chapter-url=http://search.cari.com.my/dictionary/dic.php?db_table=edict&words=fix1&keyword=syrup|chapter=Syrup|title=Online Dictionary|publisher=Cari.com.my|access-date=29 March 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722231022/http://search.cari.com.my/dictionary/dic.php?db_table=edict&words=fix1&keyword=syrup|archive-date=22 July 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> and ''air'' means "water".<ref>{{citation|chapter-url=http://search.cari.com.my/dictionary/dic.php?db_table=edict&words=fix1&keyword=water|chapter=Water|title=Online Dictionary|publisher=Cari.com.my|access-date=29 March 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722231103/http://search.cari.com.my/dictionary/dic.php?db_table=edict&words=fix1&keyword=water|archive-date=22 July 2011}}</ref> in the [[Malay language|Malay]] and [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]] languages, and the sirap refers to the rose-flavoured base syrup. More broadly, ''bandung'' refers to anything that is mixed from other ingredients or comes in pairs, such as the term ''rumah berbandung'' to refer to a [[semi-detached]] house, or "[[mee bandung Muar|mee bandung]]" which refers to a noodle dish.<ref>{{citation|url=https://prpm.dbp.gov.my/Cari1?keyword=bandung|title=Online Keyword Search: Bandung|work=Pusat Rujukan Persuratan Melayu|publisher=[[Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka]]|language=ms|year=2017|access-date=6 April 2021}}</ref> The name has no connection to the city of [[Bandung]] in Indonesia, but a variant of the drink can be found there as "[[soda gembira]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nlb.gov.sg/sure/bandung-in-bandung/|publisher=National Library Board, Singapore|last=Yinghong|first=Cai|year=2014|access-date=26 December 2016|title=Bandung in Bandung|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170422080502/http://www.nlb.gov.sg/sure/bandung-in-bandung/|archive-date=22 April 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.mahfudztejani.com/2014/07/di-malaysia-bandung-mempunyai-arti.html|title=Di Malaysia : Bandung Mempunyai Arti Berbeda|language=id|date=5 July 2014|publisher=Mahfudz Tejani: Memaparkan Apa Yang Patut Di Paparkan|location=Jakarta Indonesia|access-date=6 April 2021|archive-date=5 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230405101636/http://www.mahfudztejani.com/2014/07/di-malaysia-bandung-mempunyai-arti.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Details==
Originating out of Singapore in the early 20th century during its time as an important British colonial ''[[entrepôt]]'',<ref name="BandungSG"/> ''Bandung'' is a favourite beverage especially among the [[Singaporean Malay]] community and subsequently the [[Malays (ethnic group)|Malay]] communities of Southeast Asia. It is usually served during [[Iftar]] in [[Ramadan]] month or wedding receptions with other foods such as ''[[biryani|nasi beriani]]'' or ''[[rendang]]''. Modern innovations include adding [[grass jelly]] or [[soda water]] and are served as [[street food]] especially at night markets.

==Variations==
The soda water variant may be more commonly known as ''[[Soda gembira]]'' by Indonesians, although it has a distinct taste to ''Bandung'' due to the addition of a carbonated soft drink, such as [[Fanta]]. It may be bought pre-mixed or made at home.<ref>{{citation|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=obcTAAAAIBAJ&sjid=C5ADAAAAIBAJ&pg=3306,4140842&dq=bandung+rose+drink&hl=en|periodical=New Straits Times|title=Air bandung drink now in packets|date=31 December 1992|access-date=29 March 2010}}{{Dead link|date=March 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> In Malaysia, the drink is usually served with grass jelly (''bandung cincau'') which is sometimes mixed with [[lychee]] puree (''bandung cincau laici'') or [[basil seed]]/[[chia seed]] (''bandung selasih'').<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.utusan.com.my/seri/2024/03/sirap-bandung-cincau-selasih/|title=Sirap bandung cincau selasih|trans-title=Grass jelly bandung syrup with basil/chia seed|last=Md Said|first=Rosalinda|language=ms|work=Utusan Malaysia|date=30 March 2024|access-date=17 November 2024|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Catering to local tastes and culinary traditions, Singapore's [[McDonald's]] occasionally releases desserts inspired by the drink's taste in the country, including Bandung-flavoured [[McFlurry]], [[sundae]], and [[soft serve]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Qua |first1=Mei Rei |title=McDonald's S'pore Has Bandung Flavoured Soft Serve Available in Dessert Kiosks |url=https://singaporefoodie.com/mcdonalds-spore-has-bandung-flavoured-soft-serve-available-in-dessert-kiosks/ |website=Singapore Foodie |access-date=25 July 2023 |date=4 January 2021}}</ref>

A '''Baby Guinness''' is a [[Mixed drink shooters and drink shots|shooter]], a style of [[cocktail]], or mixed alcoholic beverage, intended to be consumed in one shot. A Baby Guinness does not contain [[Guinness]] stout. Its name is derived from the fact that it is made in such a way as to look like a tiny glass of [[stout]] containing Irish cream and coffee liqueur.

==Preparation==
In a [[shot glass]] a portion of [[coffee liqueur]] is topped by a layer of [[Irish cream]] which is poured over the back of a spoon so that it sits on the coffee liqueur. The ratio of coffee liqueur to Irish cream varies but is generally around 3-to-1. The resulting drink resembles a miniature pint of Guinness stout, with the coffee liqueur serving as the beer and the Irish cream as the head. It is normally served in a [[shot glass]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.bostonherald.com/entertainment/food_dining/food/view/2009_05_27_Baby_Guinness/|title=Baby Guinness|date=May 27, 2009|work=Food and Recipes|publisher=Boston Herald|accessdate=2009-06-24}}</ref>

Some recipes call for the Irish cream to be whipped then spooned on top of the coffee liqueur in order to look more like the head on a pint of Guinness.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.recipezaar.com/Baby-Guinness-243991|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120907083753/http://www.recipezaar.com/Baby-Guinness-243991|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 7, 2012|title=Baby Guinness|date=August 2, 2007|publisher=RecipeZaar|accessdate=2009-06-24}}</ref> Over time, the Baby Guinness became a widely recognized shooter in Irish pubs and beyond, known for its visual resemblance to a miniature Guinness pint.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://metro.co.uk/2025/07/04/baby-guinness-origin-story-reveals-youve-doing-shots-wrong-21162790/ |title=The origin story of Baby Guinness reveals you’ve been doing the shots all wrong |publisher=Metro News |date=2025-07-04 |accessdate=2025-08-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/baby-guinness-shot-cocktail-recipe-history/ |title=The Rise of the Baby Guinness |publisher=PUNCH |date=2025-03-17 |accessdate=2025-08-07}}</ref>

===Variations===
In some places, a Baby Guinness is served with black [[Sambuca]] instead of coffee liqueur<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.drmixology.com/baby_guinness.cfm|title=Baby Guinness|publisher=Dr. Mixology|accessdate=2009-06-24|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090505220816/http://www.drmixology.com/baby_guinness.cfm|archivedate=2009-05-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theoxfordretreat.com/menus/Bar.pdf|title=The Oxford Retreat's Bar Menu|publisher=[The Oxford Retreat Pub]|accessdate=2009-06-24}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref> creating a drink similar to a [[Slippery Nipple]].

'''Bandrek''' is a traditional hot, sweet and spicy beverage native to [[Sundanese people|Sundanese]] of [[West Java]], [[Indonesia]].<ref name="JPost1">{{cite web|title=Bandung a haven for snack-lovers and shoppers |author=Yuli Tri Suwarni |date=April 22, 2005 |url=http://m.thejakartapost.com/news/2005/04/22/bandung-haven-snacklovers-and-shoppers.html |publisher=The Jakarta Post |access-date=August 20, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140821134717/http://m.thejakartapost.com/news/2005/04/22/bandung-haven-snacklovers-and-shoppers.html |archive-date=August 21, 2014 }}</ref> The Sundanese people who live in the cool, highlands consume bandrek to warm themselves at night and during cold weather.

This hot beverage is made of a mixture of ginger water, palm sugar and cinnamon.<ref name="JPost1"/> Other ingredients such as, [[star anise]], [[cloves]], [[coriander]] seeds, [[cardamom]] pods, [[lemongrass]], and a small amount of [[black pepper]] are sometimes added.<ref name="Kompas">{{cite web | title=Torehan Sejarah dalam Segelas Bandrek | author=M Yusuf Zain | date=February 7, 2014 | url=http://travel.kompas.com/read/2014/02/07/1315009/Torehan.Sejarah.dalam.Segelas.Bandrek | publisher=Kompas.com | language=id | access-date=August 20, 2014}}</ref> Milk can also be added to the mix, depending on one's taste. [[condensed milk|Sweetened condensed milk]] or [[coconut milk]] is commonly used for this purpose.

It is believed that ''bandrek'' has a healing effect on minor health problems, such as sore throat.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

==Variations==
Sometimes pieces of young coconut flesh are added as well. The latest variant includes pieces of [[durian]] placed into the bandrek.<ref name="Kompas"/>

Batini (drink):
{{Notability|date=September 2020}}
A '''Batini''' is a [[vodka]]-based [[cocktail]] that is the official drink of the [[Austin Bat Fest]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Alarcón|first=Claudia|date=September 22, 2006|title=Batini III|url=https://www.austinchronicle.com/food/2006-09-22/404231/|access-date=2021-10-18|website=www.austinchronicle.com|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2019-05-22|title=What to drink at renowned The Driskill Bar in Austin, Texas.|url=https://thirstymag.com/drink-driskill-bar-austin/|access-date=2021-10-18|website=thirsty.|language=en-US}}</ref> The drink was created by bartenders from the Four Seasons Hotel Austin.

== History ==
In August 2004, The Austin Convention and Visitor's Bureau hosted a contest to designate the official drink of Austin.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=16 August 2004|title=Batini named Austin's "official drink"|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/austin/stories/2004/08/16/daily49.html|access-date=2021-10-18|website=www.bizjournals.com}}</ref> Five Austin-area hotels submitted recipes to become the official Batini for the city.<ref name=":0" /> The Four Seasons Austin recipe won the contest and was on the menu at the Lobby Lounge.<ref name=":0" />

In 2006, the Four Seasons won the Batini contest again with their "Batini Black" entrant.<ref name=":1" /> The Batini black was similar to the original, including Tito's Vodka, and Blue Curacao but added in a splash of simple syrup, grapefruit juice, champagne and fresh blackberries.<ref name=":1" />

A Batini contest is an annual event for local bartenders at the Austin Bat Fest.<ref name=":2" />

== Ingredients and preparation ==
The ingredients needed for the Batini are:<ref name=":0" />

* [[Tito's Vodka]] 
* [[Chambord (liqueur)|Chambord]] 
* [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Blue Curacao]]
* [[Sangria]]
* [[Red wine]]
* Cherry garnish

All of the ingredients are shaken together and served with a cherry garnish.<ref name=":0" />

== Variations ==

=== Batini Black ===
Ingredients in a Batini Black are:<ref name=":1" /> 

* [[Tito's Vodka]]
* [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Blue Curacao]]
* Splash of [[simple syrup]]
* [[Grapefruit juice]]
* Fresh blackberries
* Topped with [[champagne]]

Shake together Tito's, Blue Curacao, splash of simple syrup, grapefruit juice, and fresh blackberries. Strain into a cocktail glass and top off with champagne.<ref name=":1" />

'''Bajigur''' is a hot and sweet beverage native to the [[Sundanese people]] of [[West Java]], [[Indonesia]]. The main ingredients are [[coconut milk]] and [[Arenga pinnata|Aren]] [[palm sugar|sugar]];<ref name=insight-guide>{{cite book |author1=Insight Guides |title=Insight Guides Indonesia (Travel Guide eBook) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=egEbDAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Bajigur%22&pg=PT169 |publisher=Apa Publications (UK) Limited |access-date=25 January 2023 |language=en |date=3 May 2016|isbn=9781786710314 }}</ref> usually to add taste, a small amount of [[ginger]] and a small pinch of [[salt]]. Traditionally fragrant [[pandanus amaryllifolius|pandan]] leaves were added, but now often artificial [[vanilla]] powder is used. It can also include ''kopi tubruk'', finely pounded coffee.

This beverage is served hot and is sold through vendor carts traveling in villages and residential areas. The carts are equipped with portable stoves to keep the beverage hot. Bajigur is considered suitable to be consumed in cool highlands, or during cold nights or rainy days to warm oneself. The beverage is usually accompanied with traditional snacks such as steamed [[banana]], boiled [[sweet potato]] or boiled [[peanut]]s.

In [[Javanese language]], the term "''bajigur''" was used as a [[minced oath]] for the swear word "''bajingan''" or "''bajirut''".

Chapman (drink):

[[File:Chapman in a punch bowl.jpg|thumb|Chapman served in a punch bowl]]
'''Chapman''' is a [[non-alcoholic drink]] originated from [[Nigeria]]. Often referred to as a non-alcoholic punch, it is traditionally made with a mix of Fanta, Sprite, Cucumber, Lemon, [[Grenadine]] and [[Angostura bitters]] and is traditionally served in a large mug with ice and a few slices of cucumber.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Iwalaiye |first=Temi |date=2021-05-13 |title=How-Tos: Making traditional Chapman at home |url=https://www.pulse.ng/lifestyle/fashion/how-to-make-traditional-chapman-at-home/5njxkfp |access-date=2022-07-02 |newspaper=[[Pulse Nigeria]]|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=inyese |first=amaka |date=2015-06-22 |title=Nigerian chapman |url=https://www.pulse.ng/lifestyle/food-travel/perfectly-refreshing-punch-nigerian-chapman/wgn4z1d |access-date=2022-07-02 |newspaper=[[Pulse Nigeria]]}}</ref> It is often described as Nigeria's favourite drink and though predominantly served without alcohol, it can also be served with a hint of vodka or rum.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2017-08-18 |title=Simplest Way To Make Chapman |url=https://guardian.ng/life/food/how-to-make-chapman/ |location=Lagos, Nigeria|access-date=2022-07-02 |newspaper=[[The Guardian (Nigeria)|The Guardian]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

== History ==
It is believed that the cocktail originated at a local bar in [[Ikoyi Club]], Lagos, Nigeria.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dvees.com/drinks/|title=Our Drinks|website=DVees|language=en-GB|access-date=2018-10-28}}</ref> The drink was created by Samuel Alamutu, a [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]] bartender  at the country club who was asked to make something special for his favourite customer named Chapman.

== Ingredients and variations ==
Chapman is probably Nigeria's most famous and favourite drink and it is served in many bars, clubs, restaurants and special occasions in the country and is increasing in popularity across West Africa.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2019-11-10 |title=Learn How To Make Chapman With A PhD |url=https://guardian.ng/life/learn-how-to-make-chapman-with-a-phd/ |location=Lagos, Nigeria|access-date=2022-07-02 |newspaper=[[The Guardian (Nigeria)|The Guardian]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Other ingredients ===
Chapman stands out as a [[Drink|beverage]] in the country, often enjoyed at various gatherings. This distinct cocktail, known as Chapman or shapman, is a common sight at Nigerian parties. Unlike its non-alcoholic counterpart, mocktail, Chapman falls into the [[cocktail]] category due to the inclusion of Angostura aromatic bitters. Comprising [[Carbonated water|carbonated]] [[Orange (fruit)|orange]] and [[lemon]] or lime drinks, grenadine syrup, fruit juice, ice cubes, and other garnishes, this unique concoction is a highlight at many events.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wande |first=S.-Davies |date=2018-06-26 |title=How to make Nigerian chapman drink |url=https://tribuneonlineng.com/how-to-make-nigerian-chapman-drink/ |access-date=2024-02-06 |newspaper=[[Nigerian Tribune]]|language=en-GB}}</ref> 

While there is no approved standard recipe, a Chapman drink will always include bitters, lemon, lime and cucumber.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.legit.ng/1103078-chapman-recipe-ingredients-preparation.html|title=Chapman recipe: Ingredients and preparation|last=Nnamani|first=Aisha|newspaper=[[Legit.ng]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-02-16 |title=How To Make One Of The Easiest, Non-alcoholic Cocktails - Chapman |url=https://t.guardian.ng/life/how-to-make-one-of-the-easiest-cocktails-chapman/ |location=Lagos, Nigeria|access-date=2022-07-02 |newspaper=[[The Guardian (Nigeria)|The Guardian]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Benguet coffee''', also known as '''Benguet arabica''', is a [[Single-origin coffee|single-origin]] [[coffee varietals|coffee varietal]] grown in the [[Cordillera Central (Luzon)|Cordillera]] highlands of the northern [[Philippines]] since the 19th century. It belongs to the species ''[[Coffea arabica]]'', of the [[List of coffee varieties|Typica variety]]. It is one of the main crops of farmers in the province of [[Benguet]], which has a climate highly suitable for arabica cultivation.<ref name="bsu">{{cite news |title=Arabica coffee, identified diseases in Mountain Province |url=https://www.sunstar.com.ph/article/138856 |work=SunStar Philippines |date=April 26, 2017}}</ref> Benguet coffee is listed in the [[Ark of Taste]] international catalogue of endangered [[food heritage|heritage foods]] by the [[Slow Food]] movement.<ref name="slowfoodbenguet">{{cite web |title=Benguet Coffee |url=https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/benguet-coffee/ |website=Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity |access-date=December 19, 2018}}</ref>

==History==
Arabica coffee is believed to have been introduced to the [[Cordillera Central (Luzon)|Cordillera]] highlands in the mid-19th century. According to William F. Pack, an American governor of Benguet (1909–1912) during the [[History of the Philippines (1898–1946)|American colonial period]], arabica coffee was first introduced to the Cordilleras in 1875 by a Spanish military governor of Benguet, [[Manuel Scheidnegal y Sera]]. He initially planted them in government gardens in the lowlands of the province to evaluate their potential as a regional crop. However, frequent rains and the low altitude were not ideal conditions for the plants. The next governor, Enrique Oraa, had greater success when he transplanted them at higher altitudes in 1877 and distributed seedlings among the native [[Igorot people]]. In 1881 however, the then governor, a certain Villena, attempted to coerce the natives into growing coffee by ordering them to do so. In protest, native communities destroyed arabica plantations at the advice of village elders.<ref name="pack"/>

However, a native chief named Camising from [[Kabayan, Benguet|Kabayan]] purportedly saw the benefits of the crop and introduced arabica coffee to his own people. His successes convinced neighboring communities to take up coffee cultivation on their own. Benguet coffee was part of the booming coffee industry of the Philippines during the 1880s and 1890s, which reached annual coffee exports of up to 16 million pounds. However, [[coffee rust]] devastated the plantations in 1899 and coffee production plummeted. By 1917, annual total export of coffee from the Philippines only amounted to around 3,000 pounds.<ref name="pack"/><ref name="ukers"/>

Pack praised Benguet coffee even then for its flavor and spearheaded a plan to rehabilite the industry while he was governor.<ref name="pack"/> However, his efforts and that of the American colonial government failed.<ref name="ukers">{{cite book|last=Ukers |first=William H.|title=All about Coffee |date=January 1935 |publisher=Library of Alexandria |orig-date=1st Pub. 1935 |isbn=978-1-4655-2397-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oJxpQX4ko7cC }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Benguet coffee cultivation is centered in the province of [[Benguet]], mostly in backyard or small-scale farms. The coffee they produced were both for local consumption and sold as luxury exports to Spain, where they fetched high prices.<ref name="pack">{{cite book|author=William F. Pack|editor =United States Bureau of Census|title =Census of the Philippine Islands: Taken Under the Direction of the Philippine Commission in the Year 1903|chapter =Coffee Culture in the Province of Benguet|publisher =U.S. Government Printing Office|volume=IV|year =1905|pages=84–86|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=HqkJAAAAIAAJ}}</ref> The coffee industry flourished in the mid-20th century as demand increased. But it faltered in the 1990s due to rapidly rising inflation and government neglect, resulting in farmers shifting to other crops like corn.<ref name="slowfoodbenguet"/><ref name="Pasagoy"/>

In recent years, provincial governments are attempting to bring back coffee production for both local and international markets. Production has steadily increased since 2010. In 2016, the [[Department of Trade and Industry (Philippines)|Department of Trade and Industry]] in Cordillera launched a shared service facility and laboratory for processing and cupping arabica in the [[Benguet State University]], the first in the country. Benguet is regarded as the top producer of quality arabica coffee in the Philippines and is in high demand.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dar |first1=Carlito |title=Benguet-grown Arabica coffee dominates 2018 Philippine Coffee Quality Competition |url=https://pia.gov.ph/news/articles/1006110 |website=Philippine Information Agency |publisher=Republic of the Philippines |access-date=December 20, 2018}}</ref><ref name="Pasagoy">{{cite news |last1=Pasagoy |first1=Mark Victor |title=Benguet coffee production key to better economic trade |url=https://www.sunstar.com.ph/article/86906 |access-date=December 19, 2018 |work=SunStar Philippines |date=July 19, 2016}}</ref><ref name="juan">{{cite news |last1=Juan |first1=Chit |title=Coffee from Cordillera in demand |url=https://business.inquirer.net/70565/coffee-from-cordillera-in-demand |access-date=December 19, 2018 |newspaper=Philippine Daily Inquirer |date=July 12, 2012}}</ref>

The Philippine coffee roadmap, which is the blue print of the country's coffee industry, aims to put the Philippines' coffee sufficiency level at 161% by the year 2022. To be able to reach this goal, production volume has to increase by 145, 969.79 metric tons, production area has to expand by 99,879 hectares, and productivity will have to increase by 0.50 MT to make it 1 MT per hectare. In the Cordillera region coffee production is pegged to be at 3,735.86 MT of green beans coming from 6,322 hectares production area.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sagpa-ey |first1=Jaila |title=Coffee Status, Trends, and Opportunities Bared During Farmers Forum |url=https://ati.da.gov.ph/ati-car/news/05152018-1025/coffee-status-trends-and-opportunities-bared-during-farmers-forum |website=Agriculture Training Institute in the Cordillera |date=November 20, 2017 |publisher=Department of Agriculture}}</ref>

Benguet coffee is characterized as having an acidity comparable to Hawaiian [[Kona coffee]] and [[Jamaican Blue Mountain Coffee|Jamaican Blue Mountain coffee]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Our Coffee Beans |url=http://kapeumali.weebly.com/coffee-beans.html |website=Kape Umali |access-date=December 20, 2018}}</ref> Benguet coffee is listed in the [[Ark of Taste]] international catalogue of endangered [[food heritage|heritage foods]] by the [[Slow Food]] movement.<ref name="slowfoodbenguet"/><ref name="rappler">{{cite news |title=Benguet Arabica coffee listed among 'endangered' food products |url=https://www.rappler.com/nation/156380-benguet-arabica-coffee-slow-food-ark-of-taste |access-date=December 19, 2018 |work=Rappler |date=December 23, 2016}}</ref>

{{Infobox brand|name=Akta-Vite|introduced=1943|discontinued=2023|country=Australia|previousowners=[[Sara Lee Corporation]]|type=Chocolate-flavoured drink mix|tagline=Pure Aussie Goodness|logo=AKTA-VITE Logo.png}}
'''Akta-Vite''' was a brand of [[chocolate milk|chocolate flavouring]] for [[milk]] or [[plant milk]]. As it does not itself contain milk products, it is [[lactose]]-free and suitable for people who are [[lactose intolerant]] or avoiding dairy products for other reasons. It was created in 1943 by George Nicholas in [[Chadstone]], a suburb of [[Melbourne]], and initially marketed as a [[nutritional supplement]] available only in [[pharmacy|pharmacies]]. It is owned and manufactured by the Nicholas family through Nicholas Health and Nutrition Pty Ltd. Akta-vite is no longer in production<ref name=times>{{cite news |title=Akta-Vite Returns to its Original Owners |url=https://www.theaustraliatimes.com/akta-vite-returns-to-its-original-owners/ |accessdate=1 January 2019 |work=The Australia Times |date=27 April 2016}}</ref>

==History==
Alfred Nicholas and his brother George Nicholas became wealthy by producing Australian-made [[aspirin]] sold as ''Aspro'' after [[Bayer]] lost their Australian [[patent]] during the [[First World War]]. This wealth enabled them to diversify into nutritional supplements, including Akta-Vite.<ref name=age>{{cite news |last1=Moncrief |first1=Marc |title=Shake up looms for Akta-Vite after family firm buys back Aussie icon |url=https://www.theage.com.au/national/victoria/shake-up-looms-for-aktavite-after-family-firm-buys-back-aussie-icon-20160430-goj42k.html |accessdate=1 January 2019 |work=The Age |date=2 May 2016 |language=en}}</ref> Many nutrients were not readily available in synthetic form in the 1940s, with natural ingredients including [[vitamin A]] from [[shark]] [[liver]]s.<ref name=times /> Akta-Vite was exported to [[Southeast Asia]] in the 1950s, and became a well-known brand in [[Thailand]],<ref>{{cite book |last1=Battersby |first1=Paul |title=To the Islands: White Australia and the Malay Archipelago since 1788 |date=2007 |publisher=Lexington Books |isbn=9780739161784 |page=180 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PHiSkoEwweQC&pg=PA180 |accessdate=1 January 2019 |language=en}}</ref> being sold in an orange [[tin can]].<ref name=age />

The brand was sold to the [[Sara Lee Corporation]] in 1984, and bought back by the Nicholas family in 2016.<ref name=times />

Chatham Artillery punch:
{{Short description|Alcoholic beverage}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2021}}
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Chatham Artillery punch
| image       = File:Chatham Artillery Punch.jpg   
| type        = [[Mixed drink]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|Lemons, sugar, whiskey, brandy, rum, Champagne<ref name="Stern 2014">{{cite web|last=Stern|first=Steven|date=29 April 2014|title=Original Chatham Artillery Punch Recipe|url=https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1013708-original-chatham-artillery-punch|access-date=27 February 2021|website=NYT Cooking}}</ref>}}
| served      = Chilled
| garnish     = Grated nutmeg, cherries
}}

'''Chatham Artillery punch''' is a potent [[Punch (drink)|punch]] containing [[rum]], [[whisky]], [[brandy]], and Champagne.<ref name="McKibben 2016">{{cite web|last=McKibben|first=Beth|date=8 July 2016|title=Chatham Artillery Punch: Maybe the Strongest Drink in American History|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/drink/chatham-artillery-punch-maybe-the-strongest-drink/|access-date=27 February 2021|website=pastemagazine.com}}</ref> It also contains [[lemon]]s and sugar.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> Named after the [[Chatham Artillery|Savannah regiment]], it is well-known in the city of [[Savannah, Georgia]],<ref name="McKibben 2016" /> which is located in [[Chatham County, Georgia|Chatham County]].

== History ==
The original recipe and creator are unknown.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> One legend has it that [[George Washington]] was presented the punch when he arrived at [[Chatham Artillery]] in 1792, and he gave the regiment two [[cannon]]s.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016">{{cite web|date=8 June 2016|title=Drink This: Chatham Artillery Punch|url=https://www.atlantamagazine.com/dining-news/drink-chatham-artillery-punch/|access-date=27 February 2021|website=Atlanta Magazine}}</ref> 

A more plausible story was reported in an 1885 article for the [[The Augusta Chronicle|''Augusta Chronicle'']].<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> It stated that the punch was created in the 1850s, when the [[Republican Blues]] returned from a drill in [[Macon, Georgia|Macon]] and were welcomed back by Sergeant A. B. Luce and the Chatham Artillery.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> The punch was said to have been created by adding a quart of brandy, whiskey, and rum along with Champagne, lemon, and sugar to a horse bucket containing crushed ice.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> According to this story, every man who drank it was [[Alcohol intoxication|inebriated]].<ref name="McKibben 2016"/>

In 1870, a group of [[Southern United States|Southern]] journalists held a convention in Savannah and were served the punch on a [[riverboat]] cruise.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> They became inebriated and reported their encounter with the drink, proposing guesses of the actual content.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> The punch subsequently received national attention.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> President [[Chester A. Arthur|Chester Arthur]] was said to have been bested by the drink.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/>

In 1900, Admiral [[George Dewey]], a war hero from the [[Battle of Manila Bay|1898 Battle of Manila Bay]], also became inebriated when he imbibed the punch.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> One recipe was later named after him.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/>

The drink was later revised to become less potent.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Miller 2011">{{cite web|last=Miller|first=Marleigh Riggins|date=11 April 2011|title=Chatham Artillery Punch Recipe|url=https://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2011/04/drink-the-book-chatham-artillery-punch-original-recipe-wondrich.html|access-date=27 February 2021|website=Serious Eats}}</ref> In a recipe from 1907, it was written: "Experience has taught the rising generation to modify the receipt of their forefathers to conform to the weaker constitutions of their progeny."<ref name="Miller 2011"/><ref name="Wondrich 2010">{{cite book|last=Wondrich|first=D.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t6LabYdVTZ8C|title=Punch: The Delights (and Dangers) of the Flowing Bowl|publisher=Penguin Publishing Group|year=2010|isbn=978-1-101-44512-9|page=|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref>

After the end of [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]] in the late 1930s, the cocktail grew in popularity again.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> One of the last variations was published after Prohibition by the ''[[The New York Sun|New York Sun]]'' in 1939.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> The new recipes were substantially different, and sometimes included [[liquor]]s like [[Scotch whisky|scotch]] and [[gin]] and even excluded Champagne.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/>

Another legend is that during [[Sherman's March to the Sea|Sherman's March]] in the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], the residents of Savannah provided Sherman with so much of the punch that he decided to spare the city.<ref name="Pariseau">{{cite web|last=Pariseau|first=Leslie|title=The Great American Bar Crawl: Nine Bartenders Pick Their Favorite Cocktails|url=https://www.gq.com/story/bar-crawl-bartenders-favorite-cocktails-in-america|access-date=27 February 2021|website=GQ|date=21 June 2012 }}</ref>

== Ingredients ==
Many punch recipes call for Santa Cruz rum, which became more popular after Prohibition.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193">{{cite book|last=Moss|first=R.F.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vELTCwAAQBAJ|title=Southern Spirits: Four Hundred Years of Drinking in the American South, with Recipes|publisher=Ten Speed Press|year=2016|isbn=978-1-60774-867-0|page=193|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref> It is more likely that heavy, dark rum is more similar to one used in the original recipe.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193"/> [[Catawba (grape)|Catawba wine]] is difficult to find in modern times, and is substituted with a white wine or Champagne.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193"/> In the [[Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil (film)|1997 film adaptation]] of the [[John Berendt]] novel ''[[Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil]]'', the punch is referenced as "three parts fruit, seven parts liquor{{snd}} whatever's available on both counts".<ref>{{cite AV media|url=|title=Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil|date=November 21, 1997|people=Eastwood, Clint (director); Hancock, John Lee (screenwriter)|language=English|publisher=Warner Bros. Pictures|trans-title=|location=|time=|access-date=|archive-url=|archive-date=|format=|id=|isbn=|oclc=|quote=|medium=motion picture}}</ref>

== Preparation ==
The drink can be prepared by taking lemon [[Zest (ingredient)|peels]] and [[Muddler|muddling]] them with sugar which will extract oils from the lemon peels.<ref name="Stern 2014"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> This mixture is added to lemon juice and is strained.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> The lemon-sugar mixture is then added to a large bowl with crushed ice along with brandy, rum, whiskey, and Champagne.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> Although not likely traditional, [[Candied fruit|candied cherries]] (and sometimes the juice from the jar) are often added as well.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46">{{cite book|last1=Fowler|first1=D.L.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Y-rCfsqL5cC|title=The Savannah Cookbook|last2=Carrington|first2=J.R.|publisher=Gibbs Smith, publisher|year=2008|isbn=978-1-4236-0224-8|page=46|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref> Similarly, gin is sometimes added in modern recipes.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

== Variations ==
One variation is called Champagne punch.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> This is less potent version of the drink, and uses [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Curaçao]] or [[Cointreau]], a few shot of [[bitters]], fresh [[Strawberry|strawberries]], lemon, [[Syrup|simple syrup]], brandy, and Champagne.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> It is popular at [[wedding reception]]s and Christmas parties.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

There are similar drinks that exist. One is regent's punch, which is popular along the [[East Coast of the United States]].<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> Another is the [[Fish house punch]], which is found in the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast United States]].<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

Airmail (cocktail):
{{Short description|Rum-based cocktail}}
[[File:Air Mail Cocktail.png|thumb|Airmail Cocktail,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=In the mix|url=https://augustine-bar.de/in-the-mix/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=augustine-bar.de|language=English|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140504212541/http://augustine-bar.de:80/in-the-mix/ |archive-date=2014-05-04 }}</ref> garnished with a postal stamp]]
The '''''Airmail'' or ''Air Mail''''' (also ''Airmail cocktail'') is a classic cocktail based on [[rum]], [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] or [[lemon]] juice, [[honey]], and [[sparkling wine]]. It was probably created during or shortly after the period of [[prohibition]] in the [[United States|United States of America]] or on [[Cuba]], i.e. in the 1920s or 1930s.

Airmail Cocktail is also a brand of [https://www.airmailcocktail.com/ ready-to-drink cocktails] created and produced in Cognac (France) since 2020.

== History ==
As with the slightly older [[Aviation (cocktail)|Aviation cocktail]], to whose recipe there is no similarity, the name is reminiscent of [[aviation]] which developed rapidly at that time. In those years when international telephone connections were still a rarity, [[airmail]] was the fastest means of communication across national borders. Because of [[Prohibition in the United States|prohibition]], Americans were only able to legally drink alcohol abroad until 1933. Cuba, among other countries, benefited from this as a pronounced bar and cocktail culture began developing on the island in the 1920s. Since 1925, flights were available from [[Key West]] to [[Havana]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Pioneering Years: Commercial Aviation 1920 – 1930|url=https://www.centennialofflight.net/essay/Commercial_Aviation/1920s/Tran1.htm|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=centennialofflight.net - U.S. Centennial of Flight Commission|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626001311/http://www.centennialofflight.net/essay/Commercial_Aviation/1920s/Tran1.htm|archive-date=2015-06-26}}</ref> and in 1930, a regular [[Airmail|airmail service]] was established to and from the island.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|last=Ford|first=Doug|date=31 December 2014|title=A return to Havana: the Airmail Cocktail|url=https://cold-glass.com/2014/12/31/a-return-to-havana-the-airmail-cocktail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=cold-glass.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150111001408/http://cold-glass.com/2014/12/31/a-return-to-havana-the-airmail-cocktail/|archive-date=11 January 2015}}</ref> Shortly after, the ''Airmail Cocktail'' appeared for the first time in an advertising brochure of the then still Cuba-based rum manufacturer [[Bacardi|Bacardí]].<ref name=":8" />

In 1941, the recipe was published in a mixology book.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Campbell Whitfield|first=William|title=Here's How. Mixed Drinks.|publisher=Three Mountaineers Inc.|year=1941|editor-last=Shell|editor-first=Ted (Illustrator)|edition=1|pages=36}}</ref> In his recipe collections, ''Just Cocktails'' (1939) and ''Here's How'' (1941), the author W.C. Whitfield had collected numerous drinks from the years of prohibition and provided them with comments partly in laconic style. As far as the ''Airmail Cocktail'' is concerned, Whitfield commented on it  ‘It ought to make you fly high’.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|last=Meehan|first=Jim|title=The PDT Cocktail Book|last2=Gall|first2=Chris|publisher=Sterling Epicur|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4027-7923-7|location=New York|pages=48; 30}}</ref> The cocktail gained further popularity when the recipe was mentioned in the ''Handbook for Hosts'' in [[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] magazine in 1949.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Esquire's Handbook for Hosts.|publisher=Grosset & Dunlap Publishers|year=1949|location=New York}}</ref>

In the following decades, the cocktail wasn't very popular, having been published rarely. In the 2010s, however, the cocktail experienced another boom by being mentioned in the ‘[https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/11420025-the-pdt-cocktail-book PDT Cocktail Book]’ (2011) and by the promotion of alcoholic drinks by the brand [[Bacardi|Bacardí]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|date=26 July 2019|title=Rum trifft Champagner: Das völlig verdiente Revival des Air Mail Cocktails|url=https://mixology.eu/air-mail-cocktail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=mixology.eu|language=German|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210614140819/https://mixology.eu/air-mail-cocktail/ |archive-date=2021-06-14 }}</ref>

== Ingredients and similar cocktails ==
The basis for the ''Airmail Cocktail'' is a sour mixture of [[rum]], [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] juice and [[honey]] (or honey syrup), which are first shaken on ice in a [[cocktail shaker]] and then strained into a pre-cooled [[Cocktail glass]]. The mixture is then topped up with sparkling wine. The drink is similar to the [[Canchanchara|Canchánchara]],<ref name=":5" /> which consists of the same ingredients except for the [[sparkling wine]]. ‘Esquire’ magazine calls the ''Airmail Cocktail''  a "combination of the cocktails ''French 75'' and ''Honey Bee''".<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|last=Rense|first=Sarah|date=27 September 2019|title=How to make an Air Mail|url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3760/air-mail-drink-recipe/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=esquire.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150216154029/http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3760/air-mail-drink-recipe/|archive-date=16 February 2015}}</ref> The [[French 75 (cocktail)|''French 75'']] is a Champagne-based drink and a classic mixture of Gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup, while the ''Honey Bee'' consists of white rum, honey and lemon juice<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rense|first=Sarah|date=15 May 2020|title=How to make a Honey Bee|url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3770/honey-bee-drink-recipe/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=esquire.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150215020034/http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3770/honey-bee-drink-recipe/|archive-date=15 February 2015}}</ref> and therefore is akin to a [[Daiquiri]]. A modern cocktail which shares the ingredients rum, lime juice and champagne with the Airmail Cocktail is the [[Old Cuban]], which was created in 2001.

Most recipes feature a mixture ratio of 3 [[Litre|cl]] rum, 1.5 cl lime juice and 1.5 cl honey syrup,<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> which are then topped up with 3 cl champagne<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web|date=6 May 2021|title=Airmail Cocktail|url=https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/recipe-airmail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=imbibemagazine.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927230258/https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/recipe-airmail/ |archive-date=2020-09-27 }}</ref> and either garnished with a slice of lime on the rim of the glass<ref name=":4" /> or not garnished at all<ref name=":5" /> - as usual for cocktails based on sparkling wine. The magazine ''[[Imbibe Magazine|Imbibe]]'' recommends a dash of [[Angostura bitters|Angostura]] (bitters) and a mint leaf,<ref name=":7" /> while the rum manufacturer [[Bacardi|Bacardí]] recommends a postage stamp as garnish.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Air Mail|url=https://www.bacardi.com/de/de/rum-cocktails/air-mail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=bacardi.com|language=German|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422142859/https://www.bacardi.com/de/de/rum-cocktails/air-mail/ |archive-date=2021-04-22 }}</ref>

The Cocktail can be prepared with [[Rum#Grades|dark or white rum]]. Dark rum is best complemented with the addition of a comparatively [[Honey#Acid content and flavor effects|aromatic honey]], while white rum prefers the use of a mild honey like [[Honey#Floral source|Acacia blossom honey]].<ref name=":5" /> Cuban rum is often recommended. Substitution of the lime juice with lemon juice is possible.<ref name=":3" /> The honey syrup used for the cocktail is a mixture of 2 parts honey and 1 part water,<ref name=":4" /> which is easier to incorporate into mixtures and to add to taste than pure honey. In most cases, the cocktail is topped up with [[Champagne#Sweetness|dry champagne]], [[Sparkling wine#Crémant|Crémant]] or [[sparkling wine]] (less so with [[Prosecco]]).<ref name=":7" />

It is usually served [[Bartending terminology#Straight, up, and straight up|straight up]] in a pre-cooled [[Champagne glass#Flute|champagne flute]] or [[Champagne glass#Coupe|coupe]].<ref name=":5" /> Some recipes call for much larger quantities of liquid and proportionally more sparkling wine which therefore suggests serving the cocktail in a [[Collins glass]].<ref name=":6" />

{{Infobox beverage

'''Cohasset Punch''' is a [[brand]] of [[rum]]-based drink introduced in 1899. First created by [[Chicago]] bartenders Lewis A. Williams and Thomas C. Newman, Cohasset Punch was long associated with the Ladner Bros. bar on [[Madison Street (Chicago)|Madison Street]] in the [[Chicago Loop]], who produced it until the 1980s.<ref name="Wondrich">{{cite encyclopedia | last=Wondrich | first=David | encyclopedia=[[The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails]] | title=Cohasset Punch | publisher=Oxford University Press | publication-place=New York | date=2022 | pages=186–187 | isbn=978-0-19-931113-2 | editor1-last=Wondrich | editor1-first=David | editor2-last=Rothbaum | editor2-first=Noah}}</ref> Though officially classified as a [[liqueur]], Cohasset Punch can also be considered a bottled [[cocktail]] or [[punch (drink)|punch]], and has been referred to as "the definitive Chicago cocktail".<ref name="WSJ">{{citation | last=Felten | first=Eric | title=Drinking the Chicago Way | newspaper=WSJ | url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB122973257260622987 | date=December 20, 2008 | access-date=May 20, 2024}}</ref> In 2024, bottled Cohasset Punch was relaunched under new ownership.<ref name="History">{{cite web | title=History | website=Cohasset Punch | url=https://www.cohassetpunch.com/history | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref>

==History==
In the late 1890s, Chicago saloon owner and liquor dealer Lewis A. Williams{{efn | Lewis Williams' name is spelled "Louis" on some records, but his death notice<ref name="WilliamsObit">{{cite news |title=Death Notices | work=Chicago Tribune | date=July 9, 1935 | page=21 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-lewis-a-williams-death/148446528/}}</ref> uses "Lewis."}} was invited to spend a few weeks at the [[Cohasset, Massachusetts]] summer estate of long-time family friend,<ref name="Crane">{{cite book | title=Footprints and Echoes | last=Crane | first=William H. | date=1927 | location=New York | publisher=E.P. Dutton & Company | pages=55–56 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=91dAAAAAIAAJ}}</ref> actor [[William H. Crane]].<ref name="Wondrich" /><ref name="Bonforts">{{cite magazine | title=The Origin of Cohasset Punch | author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> | magazine=Bonfort's Wine & Spirit Circular | date=August 10, 1902 | page=305 | volume=58 | issue=7}}</ref> Williams overheard some of Crane's other guests discussing rum [[punch (drink)|punch]], and [[telegraphy|wired]] Tom Newman, his business partner back in Chicago, to request a mixed drink that would "surpass anything ever before imbibed by any living soul."<ref name="Bonforts" /> Within 24 hours, a cask of the new punch was loaded onto a railcar and bound for Cohasset. Upon tasting the new concoction, Crane and his guests declared Newman the "king of blenders." Crane wired Newman his thanks and asked for the name of the new drink, and Newman simply wired back the name, "Cohasset".<ref name="Bonforts" />

Williams & Newman began mixing Cohasset Punch at their saloon,<ref name="advertisement">{{cite news |title=Have You Had a Cohasset Punch | work=Chicago Inter Ocean | date=October 16, 1898 | page=8 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-inter-ocean-williams-newman-ad-for/167459716/}}</ref>{{efn | The Williams & Newman saloon was located at 124 [[Dearborn Street]] (now 10 N. Dearborn after the 1911 street renumbering). Williams & Newman was located across the street from the saloon of James McGarry, the inspiration for the [[Mr. Dooley]] character in columns by humorist [[Finley Peter Dunne]].<ref name="Recollections">{{cite book | title=Recollections of Life & Doings in Chicago: From the Haymarket Riot to the End of World War I | last=Hermann | first=Charles H. | date=1945 | location=Chicago | publisher=Normandie House | pages=140–141 | url=https://libsysdigi.library.uiuc.edu/OCA/Books2008-09/recollectionsofl00herm/recollectionsofl00herm.pdf}}</ref>}} serving the blend over a [[peach]] slice soaked in [[brandy]].<ref name="Fougner">{{cite news | last=Fougner | first=G. Selmer | title=Along the Wine Trail | work=New York Sun | date=November 11, 1938 | page=23}}</ref> By the fall of 1899 they were selling Cohasset Punch in bottles, with modest but nationwide distribution.<ref name="Wondrich" /> From the very beginning, each bottle had an image of [[Cohasset, Massachusetts|Cohasset]]'s famous [[Minot's Ledge Light]]house on the label.<ref name="trademark">{{US trademark|60035924}} Mixed Spiritous Beverages. Williams & Newman, Chicago, Ill. Essential feature—The pictoral representation of a lighthouse scene. Used since January, 1899. (filed January 15, 1900) (published February 19, 1901)</ref>{{efn | Labels from 1899 to early 1981 also included illustrations of a sailboat and steamship on either side of the lighthouse.<ref name="trademark" /> Labels from 1981<ref name="81COLA">{{cite web | title=Cohasset Punch | website=COLA Public Registry | url=https://ttbonline.gov/colasonline/viewColaDetails.do?action=publicDisplaySearchBasic&ttbid=81090152 | date=September 28, 1981 | access-date=May 31, 2024}}</ref> until the end of original production replaced these with an illustration of one [[square rig|square-rigged]] [[tall ship]] to the right of the lighthouse. The modern label depicts [[William H. Crane]]’s [[catboat]] ''Chloe'' to the left of the lighthouse, and Crane’s [[steam yacht]] ''The Senator'' (designed by [[Edward Burgess (yacht designer)|Edward Burgess]] and named for [[The Senator (play)|one of Crane's most successful plays]]).<ref name="FAQ">{{cite web | title=FAQ | website=Cohasset Punch | url=https://www.cohassetpunch.com/faq | access-date=May 23, 2024}}</ref><ref name="Senator">{{cite news |title=Com. W.H. Crane's Steam Yacht Senator | work=Boston Globe | date=February 14, 1897 | page=28 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-com-w-h-cranes-stea/103338199/}}</ref>}} In 1902, a leading liquor [[trade magazine|trade journal]] remarked that so high was the demand for Cohasset Punch in its city of origin, that "what the [[mint julep]] is to [[Southern United States|the South]], Cohasset Punch is to Chicago."<ref name="Bonforts" /> A recipe appeared for Cohasset Punch in cocktail guides that included sweet [[vermouth]], New England [[rum]], [[lemon]] juice, and [[orange bitters]],<ref name="Sheridan">{{cite book | title=The Complete Buffet Manual | last=Sheridan | first=J.E. | date=1901 | location=Chicago | publisher=Henneberry | pages=47–48 | url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1901-The-Complete-Buffet-Manual-or-How-to-Mix-Fancy-Drinks-by-J-E-Sheridan/46/}}</ref> but regulars believed that this formula did not quite taste like the original.<ref name="Wondrich" /> Of the drink's smoothness compared to its 60-[[Alcohol proof|proof]] strength, a 1938 letter to the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' wrote that after three or four drinks, "a pleasant mellowness steals over you, your imagination glows, you discover humor you never possessed. Then suddenly you push your chair back to stand up, and lo, your legs are merely attached to your body for appearance's sake!"<ref name="Tribune38">{{cite news |title=A Line O' Type or Two | work=Chicago Tribune | date=August 17, 1938 | page=10 | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-cohasset-punch-a-line/148447450/}}</ref>

[[File:Ladner Brothers, Home Of Cohasset Punch, 207 West Madison St., Chicago, Illinois (NBY 416934).jpg|thumb|alt=A postcard image featuring exterior and interior images of a bar, and a glass of Cohasset Punch.|A 1940s postcard for the Ladner Bros. "Home of Cohasset Punch" bar at [[Madison Street (Chicago)|Madison]] and [[Wells Street (Chicago)|Wells]] Streets, Chicago]]
[[File:CohassetPunch-1980s.jpg|thumb|alt=A bottle of Cohasset Punch from the mid-1980s sitting atop a bar.|A bottle of Cohasset Punch from the mid-1980s, on display at Simon's Tavern in [[Edgewater, Chicago#Andersonville|Andersonville]], Chicago]]
After Williams & Newman retired in 1916, they sold the rights to Carl Ladner, who continued to serve the drink at the Ladner Bros. bar as well as bottle it for distribution. The bar reopened after [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]], and a large [[neon sign]] touting "The Home of Cohasset Punch" was hung outside.<ref name="Wondrich" /> During the 1930s and 1940s, bottled Cohasset Punch could be found at many of Chicago's restaurants and nightclubs including [[Chez Paree]] and [[Blackhawk (restaurant)|The Blackhawk]], as well as the "Tip Top Tap" bar cars aboard the [[Milwaukee Road]]'s [[Hiawatha (Milwaukee Road trains)|Hiawatha]] passenger trains.<ref name="ChezParee">{{cite document | type=Menu | title=Dinner Wine List | publisher=Chez Paree | date=1941}}</ref><ref name="Blackhawk">{{cite document | type=Menu | title=Cocktails | publisher=The Blackhawk | date=1943}}</ref><ref name="TipTopTap">{{cite document | type=Menu | title=Tip Top Tap Room | publisher=Milwaukee Road | date=1935}}</ref> Ladner Bros. was demolished in 1986<ref name="SunTimes86">{{cite news | last=Davis | first=Jerry C. | title=Prohibition-era Cohasset Punch to fall for W. Madison skyscraper | work=Chicago Sun-Times | date=March 17, 1986 | page=47 | url=https://chicagosuntimes.newsbank.com/doc/news/0EB36CF74D05F922}}{{subscription required}}</ref> by developer [[Lee Miglin]] to make way for the proposed (but never built) 125-story [[Miglin-Beitler Skyneedle]].<ref name="SunTimes89">{{cite news | last=Davis | first=Jerry C. | title=New skyscraper planned—would tower over Sears | work=Chicago Sun-Times | date=May 23, 1989 | url=https://chicagosuntimes.newsbank.com/doc/news/0EB36E5D94B09125}}{{subscription required}}</ref> Production of Cohasset Punch ceased shortly thereafter.

In 2024, the Cohasset Punch brand was revived by a Chicago-based cocktail history enthusiast using historical accounts of its flavor and ingredients.<ref name="Tribune">{{cite news | last=Hammond | first=David | title=Want to party like it's 1899? One Chicagoan is working to revive Cohasset Punch liqueur | work=Chicago Tribune | date=January 12, 2024 | url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2024/01/12/want-to-party-like-its-1899-one-chicagoan-is-working-to-revive-cohasset-punch-liqueur/ | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref><ref name="Forbes">{{cite web | last=Hurt | first=Jeanette | title=Drinks Historian Revives Chicago's Signature Cocktail, Cohasset Punch | website=Forbes | date=April 28, 2024 | url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeanettehurt/2024/04/28/drinks-historian-revives-chicagos-signature-cocktail-cohasset-punch/?sh=1ff6a0eb1642 | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref>

==Serving==
Historically, Cohasset Punch has been served stirred with ice and strained into a cocktail glass over a peach slice. In the early 20th century, this garnish would have likely been a peach slice preserved in brandy.<ref name="Wondrich" /> In the 1970s and 1980s, Cohasset Punch was increasingly served [[Bartending terminology#On the rocks|on the rocks]] or with [[drink mixer|mixers]].<ref name="SanDiego">{{cite news | last=Riggs | first=Rod | title=Pushing an old punch | work=San Diego Union-Tribune | date=November 24, 1986 | page=E-7 | url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/news/117922C40A3F1B6D}}{{subscription required}}</ref><ref name="TribLetters">{{cite news | author=<!--not stated--> | title=LETTERS: Memories Pack a Punch | work=Chicago Tribune | date=August 31, 2008 | url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2008/08/31/letters-2766/ | access-date=May 22, 2024}}</ref> The current manufacturer suggests a number of cocktails that can be made with Cohasset Punch.<ref name="Recipes">{{cite web | title=Recipes | website=Cohasset Punch | url=https://www.cohassetpunch.com/recipes | access-date=May 19, 2024}}</ref>
