===Southeast Asia===
==== Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore ====
In [[Bruneian cuisine|Bruneian]], [[Malaysian cuisine|Malaysian]] and [[Singaporean cuisine|Singaporean]] cuisines, ginger tea is generally called ''teh halia''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dailyexpress.com.my/read.cfm?NewsID=1773|title=Plen-tea-ful uses|work=[[Daily Express (Malaysia)|Daily Express]]|date=11 November 2015|access-date=22 March 2016}}</ref> It is not a pure ginger tea, as it is brewed of strong sweetened black tea, ginger rhizome, sugar with milk or condensed milk.

<gallery>
File:Lemongrass ginger tea.jpg|''Teh serai halia'' ([[lemongrass]] ginger tea) in Malaysia
File:Teh Halia (Singapore).jpg|''Teh halia'' (Singaporean ginger tea)

</gallery>

==== Indonesia ====
In Indonesia, it is called ''teh jahe''. In [[Java]], a local version of ginger tea enriched with [[palm sugar]] and [[spices]] called ''[[wedang jahe]]'' is more popular.<ref name="IndoEats-WedangJahe">{{cite web | title = Wedang Jahe (Indonesian Ginger Tea) | author = Pepy Nasution | work = Indonesia Eats | date = 12 February 2010 | url = http://indonesiaeats.com/indonesian-ginger-tea-wedang-jahe/ | archive-date = 1 March 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120301125955/http://indonesiaeats.com/indonesian-ginger-tea-wedang-jahe/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>

''Wedang Jahe'' is a type of [[Indonesian cuisine|Indonesian]] ginger tea.<ref name="IndoEats-WedangJahe"/> ''Wedang'' in [[Javanese language|Javanese]] means "hot beverage" while ''jahe'' means "[[ginger]]". Although devoid of any caffeine content, it is often served and enjoyed as an invigorating tea. It is made from the ginger [[rhizome]], usually fresh and cut in thin slices, and [[palm sugar]] or granulated cane sugar, frequently with the addition of fragrant [[pandanus amaryllifolius|pandan]] leaves. Palm sugar can be substituted with [[brown sugar]] or [[honey]]. People traditionally tend to add spices such as [[lemongrass]], [[cloves]], and [[cinnamon]] sticks.<ref name="IndoEats-WedangJahe"/>

Milk, either fresh or [[condensed milk|condensed]], might be added.<ref>{{cite web | title = Wedang Teh Susu Jahe – Ginger Milk Tea | date = 5 August 2013 | author = Anita | work = Daily Cooking Quest | url = http://dailycookingquest.com/by-cuisine/indonesian/wedang-teh-susu-jahe-ginger-milk-tea | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131008232525/http://dailycookingquest.com/by-cuisine/indonesian/wedang-teh-susu-jahe-ginger-milk-tea | archive-date = 8 October 2013 | url-status = dead }}</ref>

<gallery>
File:Wedang Jahe.jpg|''Wedang jahe'' (Javanese ginger tea) in [[Surakarta]], Central Java, with bits of spices
</gallery>

==== Philippines ====
In the Philippines, it is called ''salabat'' and is traditionally made simply with peeled and thinly sliced or crushed raw ginger boiled for a few minutes in water. Sugar, [[honey]], and [[calamansi]] are added for taste, along with other flavoring ingredients as desired.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Garcia |first1=Miki |title=Filipino Cookbook: 85 Homestyle Recipes to Delight Your Family and Friends |date=2012 |publisher=Tuttle Publishing |isbn=9781462905287}}</ref><ref name="Besa-Quirino">{{cite web |last1=Besa-Quirino |first1=Betty |title=Ginger Tea- Filipino Salabat with Lemon Honey |url=https://www.asianinamericamag.com/filipino-salabat-ginger-tea-with-lemon-honey-creme/ |website=Asian in America |date=19 February 2013 |access-date=12 July 2021}}</ref><ref name="baker">{{cite web |last1=Baker |first1=Liren |title=Homemade Fresh Ginger Tea |url=https://kitchenconfidante.com/homemade-fresh-ginger-tea |website=Kitchen Confidante |date=26 November 2018 |access-date=12 July 2021}}</ref> Modern versions can also use ground ginger powder (often called "instant ''salabat''") added to hot boiling water.<ref name="Padilla">{{cite journal |last1=Padilla |first1=L.D.E. |title=Instant salabat [ginger brew] made easier and tastier |journal=BAR Chronicle |date=2012 |volume=13 |issue=8 |pages=16–17|url=https://businessdiary.com.ph/4263/instant-salabat-made-easier-and-tastier/}}</ref> Native ginger varieties (which are small and fibrous) are preferred, as they are regarded as being more pungent than imported varieties.<ref name="fao">{{cite book |title=Ginger value chain study in Nueva Vizcaya, Philippines (GCP/RAS/296/JPN) |date=2019 |publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations |location=Bangkok |isbn=9789251317518 |page=6}}</ref>

''Salabat'' is typically served in the relatively cold month of December.<ref>{{cite book|author=Caroline Joan Picart|title=Inside Notes from the Outside|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VZvSlPp-wycC&pg=PA48|date=January 2004|publisher=Lexington Books|isbn=978-0-7391-0763-8|pages=48–}}</ref> Along with ''[[tsokolate]]'' (traditional [[hot chocolate]]), it is usually paired with various native rice cakes (''[[kakanin]]'') like ''[[bibingka]]'' or ''[[puto bumbong]]''. ''Salabat'' is traditionally sold by early morning street vendors during the ''[[Simbang Gabi]]'' (dawn [[Catholic mass|mass]]) of the [[Christmas in the Philippines|Christmas season]].<ref name="Walker">{{cite book |last1=Walker |first1=Harlan |title=Oxford Symposium on Food and Cookery 1991: Public Eating : Proceedings |date=1992 |publisher=Oxford Symposium |isbn=9780907325475 |page=99}}</ref><ref name="Long">{{cite book |last1=Long |first1=Lucy M. |title=Ethnic American Food Today: A Cultural Encyclopedia |date=2015 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=9781442227316 |page=503}}</ref><ref name="Conopio">{{cite news |last1=Conopio |first1=Camille |title=Christmas special: Top 10 traditional Filipino food |url=https://www.asianjournal.com/life-style/travel/christmas-special-top-10-traditional-filipino-food/ |access-date=12 July 2021 |work=Asian Journal |date=4 December 2013}}</ref>

''Salabat'' is also widely consumed as a throat-soothing remedy for cough, sore throat, and common colds.<ref>{{cite news |title=Fresh Ginger Tea with Honey (Salabat) to help cure Cold, Cough and Flu |url=https://www.manilaspoon.com/2015/11/fresh-ginger-tea-with-honey-salabat-to.html |access-date=12 July 2021 |work=Manila Spoon |date=25 November 2015}}</ref> Drinking ''salabat'' is believed to improve a person's singing voice.<ref>{{cite news |title=Can Salabat Make You A Singing Prodigy? |url=https://www.onemusic.ph/news/salabat-fact-or-folk-d-944 |access-date=12 July 2021 |work=OneMusicPH |date=10 June 2016 |archive-date=12 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712135940/https://www.onemusic.ph/news/salabat-fact-or-folk-d-944 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Besa-Quirino"/><ref name="baker"/><ref name="Tek-Ing">{{cite news |last1=Tek-Ing |first1=Jessa |title=Guide to Tea in the Philippines: Local Flavors, Farm Tours, Tea Brands |url=https://guidetothephilippines.ph/articles/ultimate-guides/tea-philippines-guide |access-date=12 July 2021 |work=Guide to the Philippines}}</ref>

A variant of ''salabat'' that exclusively or partially use [[turmeric]] is known as ''dulaw'', ''duwaw'', or ''duyaw'' in the [[Visayas]] and [[Mindanao]] islands; and ''tsaang dilaw'' (literally "yellow tea") in [[Filipino language|Filipino]].<ref>{{Cite book | isbn=9786214200870|title=Philippine Food, Cooking, and Dining Dictionary|author=Edgie Polistico | year = 2016 | publisher = Anvil Publishing, Inc}}</ref>

===South Asia===
==== India ====
In India, ginger tea is known as ''adrak ki chai'' and is a widely consumed beverage. It is made by grating ginger into brewed black tea along with milk and sugar.

Another common version is ginger lemon tea, prepared by adding ginger root to tepid lemon juice.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Is Ginger High In Potassium - Dietaketocustomplan|url=https://dietaketocustomplan.com/ginger-potassium-vs-kidney/|access-date=2021-11-21|website=dietaketocustomplan.com|date=8 August 2021|language=en-us|archive-date=21 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211121093925/https://dietaketocustomplan.com/ginger-potassium-vs-kidney/|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Masala chai]] is often brewed by adding spices and ginger root to tea leaves, milk, and sugar.<ref>{{Cite web |title=All the Tea (Not) in China: The Story of How India Became a Tea-Drinking Nation |url=https://www.seriouseats.com/indian-tea-history-5221096 |access-date=2023-08-24 |website=Serious Eats |language=en}}</ref>

The beverage has also been acknowledged as having several key health benefits including boosting immunity, relieving nausea and reducing inflammation.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2021-04-08 |title=Ginger Tea Benefits: 8 health benefits of ginger tea |work=The Times of India |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/life-style/health-fitness/diet/8-health-benefits-of-ginger-tea/articleshow/27715978.cms |access-date=2023-11-02 |issn=0971-8257}}</ref> During the Tang Dynasty, tea was flavored to counteract the bitter taste. Ginger was a favorite among tea drinkers, along with onions, orange peel, cloves, and mint.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gxCBfNmnvFEC |title=The Story of Tea |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210705095704/https://books.google.com/books?id=gxCBfNmnvFEC |archive-date=2021-07-05}}</ref>
<gallery>
File:Kullad chai.jpg|''Adrak chai'' (Indian ginger tea) 
</gallery>

====Pakistan====
In Pakistan, ginger tea is often called “adrak wali chai”. It is commonly prepared in winter for warmth and used as a soothing drink for digestion or coughs. It is widely consumed at home and by street vendors.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Bridging Cultures Through Herbal Teas: Shared Traditions in Chinese and Pakistani Wellness Practices
 |website=Youlin Magazine
 |url=https://www.youlinmagazine.com/article/bridging-cultures-through-herbal-teas-shared-traditions-in-chinese-and-pakistani-wellness-practices/MzA5OQ==
 |date=31 July 2023
 |access-date=8 December 2025
}}
</ref>

====Sri Lanka====
In Sri Lanka, a traditional herbal drink called Koththamalli (coriander-ginger tea) is sometimes used in place of plain ginger tea. The drink is made by brewing fresh ginger with coriander seeds (and sometimes pepper or jaggery), and is traditionally consumed to relieve colds, soothe the throat, and aid digestion.<ref>{{cite web |title=Healthy Sri Lankan Herbal Infusions |website=Explore Sri Lanka |url=https://exploresrilanka.lk/healthy-sri-lankan-herbal-infusions/ |access-date=8 December 2025}}
</ref>

====Nepal====
In Nepal, it is common to add ginger to milk-tea (locally called “chiya”), especially in colder or mountainous regions. Many Nepali households include ginger (and sometimes other spices) in milk tea during winter for its warming and soothing properties.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Nepal Milk Tea: A Taste of Authentic Nepali Chiya
 |website=Himalayan Masters
 |url=https://himalayan-masters.com/nepal-milk-tea/
 |date=26 November 2023
 |access-date=8 December 2025
}}
</ref>

Death in the Afternoon (cocktail):
{{short description|Cocktail made up of absinthe and Champagne}} {{Infobox drink | name = Death in the Afternoon | image = Death In The Afternoon.jpg | caption = Death in the Afternoon | type = [[Wine cocktail]] | base = [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne]], [[Absinthe]] | drinkware = [[Champagne flute]] }} '''Death in the Afternoon''', also called the '''Hemingway''' or the '''Hemingway Champagne''',{{cite book|title = Ultimate Bar Book: The Comprehensive Guide to over 1,000 Cocktails|last = Hellmich|first = Mittie|publisher = [[Chronicle Books]]|year = 2006|isbn = 978-0-8118-4351-5|page = 154}}{{cite book |title= Knack Bartending Basics: More Than 400 Classic and Contemporary Cocktails|last= Bourgoin|first= Susan|year= 2009|publisher= Globe Pequot|isbn= 978-1-59921-504-4|page= 132}} is a [[cocktail]] made up of [[absinthe]] and [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne]], invented by [[Ernest Hemingway]]. The cocktail shares a name with Hemingway's 1932 book ''[[Death in the Afternoon]]'', and the recipe was published in ''So Red the Nose, or Breath in the Afternoon'', a 1935 cocktail book with contributions from famous authors.{{cite news |title= Trying to Clear Absinthe's Reputation|author= McGee, Harold|url= https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/03/dining/03curi.html|newspaper= [[The New York Times]]|date= 3 January 2007|access-date=15 July 2011}}{{cite book |title= Diffordsguide Cocktails 7|last= Difford|first= Simon|year= 2008|publisher= Diffordsguide|isbn= 978-0-9556276-0-6|page= 122}} Hemingway's original instructions were:
"Pour one jigger absinthe into a Champagne glass. Add iced Champagne until it attains the proper opalescent milkiness. Drink three to five of these slowly."
It is claimed that the cocktail was invented by Hemingway after he spent time in the [[Rive Gauche|Left Bank]], Paris, and enjoyed the absinthe there. The original printed recipe for the drink claimed that it was invented "by the author and three officers of H.M.S. Danae after having spent seven hours overboard trying to get Capt. Bra Saunders’ fishing boat off a bank where she had gone with us in a N.W. gale."{{Cite web|url=http://belikehemingway.com/2016/02/29/drink-like-hemingway-how-to-make-a-death-in-the-afternoon/|title=Drink Like Hemingway: How to Make a Death in the Afternoon|last=Duffy|website=Be Like Hemingway.|access-date=2016-03-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160405210536/http://belikehemingway.com/2016/02/29/drink-like-hemingway-how-to-make-a-death-in-the-afternoon/|archive-date=2016-04-05|url-status=dead}} Death in the Afternoon is known for both its [[decadence]] and its high [[Alcohol proof|strength]].{{cite news|title= Top 5 Absinthe Cocktails|author= English, Camper|url= http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/drinking/cocktails/top5_absinthecocktails|publisher= [[Epicurious]]|access-date= 15 July 2011|archive-date= 21 July 2011|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110721142043/http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/drinking/cocktails/top5_absinthecocktails|url-status= dead}}{{cite news |title= Ernest Hemingway's Death in the Afternoon|url= http://www.esquire.com/drinks/ernest-hemingway-drink-recipe|newspaper= [[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|access-date=15 July 2011}} There are a number of alternative ways to produce Death in the Afternoon. The absinthe can be added to the glass after the Champagne, as some brands of absinthe will float on the Champagne for a short time. Other alternatives have arisen because of the difficulty of acquiring absinthe; the absinthe can be replaced with [[Absente]], an alternative to absinthe available where it is illegal, or a strong [[pastis]], such as [[Pernod]]. Variants which use an alternative to absinthe are sometimes given a different name, but are also sometimes still referred to as Death in the Afternoon.{{cite book|title= Night+Day San Francisco|author1= Balmain, Julianne|author2= Chynoweth, Kate|year= 2006|publisher= ASDavis Media Group|isbn= 978-0-9759022-9-5|page= [https://archive.org/details/nightdaysanfranc00balm/page/132 132]|url-access= registration|url= https://archive.org/details/nightdaysanfranc00balm/page/132}} Some recipes direct the person making the cocktail to use ingredients in addition to the Champagne and absinthe; Valerie Mellema recommends that a [[sugar|sugar cube]] and several dashes of [[bitters]] be added to the glass prior to the main ingredients.{{cite book |title= The Professional Bartender's Handbook: A Recipe for Every Drink Known|last= Mellema|first= Valerie|year= 2007|publisher= Atlantic Publishing Company|isbn= 978-0-910627-95-5|page= 154}} The cocktail is milky in appearance on account of the [[Ouzo effect|spontaneous emulsification]] of the absinthe (or substitute), and bubbly, which it takes from the Champagne. After the first sip, however, it becomes significantly less bubbly. Harold McGee, dining and wine writer for ''[[The New York Times]]'', said that it "seemed a waste of effervescence" (though substituting Pernod for the absinthe). ==See also== {{Portal|Drink}} *[[List of cocktails]] ==References== {{reflist}} {{Wine cocktails}} [[Category:Cocktails with absinthe]] [[Category:Cocktails with Champagne]] [[Category:Ernest Hemingway]]

'''Kopi''' ({{zh|t=㗝呸/咖啡|poj=ko-pi}}), also known as [[Nanyang (region)|Nanyang]] coffee, is a traditional coffee beverage found in several [[Southeast Asia]]n nations. Often brewed to be highly caffeinated, it is commonly served with sugar and/or milk-based condiments. The drink originated during the [[British Malaya]] era and has [[Hainanese cuisine|Hainanese]] cultural roots. Its name is derived from the [[Malay language|Malay term]] for coffee. The term ''Nanyang'', which means "south sea" in [[Mandarin Chinese|Mandarin]], refers to Southeast Asia.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Traditional Breakfast of Kaya and Kopi|url=https://www.roots.gov.sg/ich-landing/ich/traditional-breakfast-of-kaya-and-kopi|website=www.roots.sg|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> Kopi-culture vocabulary is grounded in the [[Hokkien language]] as a result of historical immigration to Southeast Asia from the [[Minnan region]] of Fujian Province, in southeastern China. The beverage is usually served in coffee shops, [[hawker centre]]s, and [[Kopi tiam|kopitiams]] across the region.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Lai|first=Ah Eng|date=2015|title=The Kopitiam in Singapore: An Evolving Story about Cultural Diversity and Cultural Politics|url=|journal=Food, Foodways and Foodscapes|volume=|pages=103–132|doi=10.1142/9789814641234_0006|isbn=978-981-4641-21-0}}</ref>

In [[Singapore]], kopi is recognized as culturally significant<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal|last=Aljunied|first=Khairudin|s2cid=154985319|date=2014|title=Coffee-shops in Colonial Singapore: Domains of Contentious Publics|doi=10.1093/hwj/dbt011|journal=History Workshop Journal|volume=77|pages=65–85|via=Oxford Academic}}</ref> and part of everyday diet and lifestyle.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Singapore Coffee Association|url=https://www.singaporecoffee.org/|website=Singapore Coffee Association|access-date=19 May 2020|archive-date=4 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200804023440/http://singaporecoffee.org/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Singapore coffee is distinct from other types due to its roasting process and preparation technique involving a variation of the [[Torrefacto]] method.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=Cheryl |last2=McGonigle |first2=Ian |date=2 July 2020 |title=Kopi culture: consumption, conservatism and cosmopolitanism among Singapore's millennials |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1683478X.2020.1726965 |journal=Asian Anthropology |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=213–231 |doi=10.1080/1683478X.2020.1726965 |s2cid=216228666 |issn=1683-478X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Concerns over the elevation of [[diabetes]] cases have caused the creation of government-led nationwide campaigns in Singapore to reduce sugar intake, especially with regard to sweet drinks or drinks that add large amounts of sugar, such as kopi.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Sugar? No thanks: Patrons opt for healthier option when asked to sweeten beverages themselves|url=https://www.todayonline.com/singapore/sugar-no-thanks-patrons-opt-healthier-option-when-asked-sweeten-beverages-themselves|last=Ng|first=Kelly|date=2018|website=TODAYonline|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> The significance of kopi in Singapore's culture can be explored in greater detail in the country's kopi museum.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|title=Order kopi like a local|url=https://www.visitsingapore.com/en_au/editorials/order-kopi-like-a-local/|website=visitsingapore.com|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref>

==Etymology and Hokkien roots==
[[File:Ya Kun Koya toast, eggs and coffee.jpg|250px|thumb|right|Kopi (background) and kopi O (foreground). Kopi paired with [[kaya toast]] and half-boiled egg, is a popular breakfast option in [[Singapore]] (widely available in coffee-shops as "Set A").]]

This prominence of the [[Hokkien]] language in local kopi culture can be linked to the prominence of Hokkien [[Immigration|immigrants]] in [[British Malaya|Malaya]] and [[Singapore in the Straits Settlements|colonial Singapore]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last1=Guan|first1=Kwa Chong|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xxeeDwAAQBAJ|title=A General History of the Chinese in Singapore|last2=Lim|first2=Kua Bak|date=21 June 2019|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-981-327-765-6|language=en}}</ref> According to the history of Chinese immigration, millions of [[China]] residents left due to natural calamities and political instability during the 19th century.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|last=Leong-Salobir|first=Cecilia|title=Singapore: Tasting the Citypublisher=Palgrave Macmillan|year=2019|isbn=978-1-137-52223-8|location=New York|pages=83–111}}</ref> In the beginning, 50,000 Chinese landed in Singapore—many of them Chinese traders.<ref name=":4" /> This number grew to 200,000 in 1900 as more passed through the Malay States and [[Dutch East Indies]] into Singapore. Amongst the arrivals, the Hokkiens made up the largest proportion of Chinese dialect groups in Singapore.<ref name=":4" /> Thus, they also came to possess a dominant share of the banking, manufacturing and trade industries.<ref name=":3" />

==Variations==
Variations in style of traditional [[coffee]] revolve around denseness, sugar level, and additions of [[evaporated milk]], [[condensed milk]] or ice. Local kopi vocabulary governs the way consumers order their preferred style of kopi in [[Malaysia]] and [[Singapore]].

''Kopi'' is a term from Malay and is used in conjunction with terms from different Chinese languages, including [[Hokkien language|Hokkien]] and [[Cantonese language|Cantonese]]. In Singapore, there are at least 54 core variations<ref name="How to make a Kopi">{{cite web |title=How to make a Kopi |url=https://www.finecoffeecompany.com/how-to-make-a-kopi-that-tastes-much-better-with-an-espresso-machine/ |website=Fine Coffee Company|date=2 March 2023 }}</ref> of kopi with different customisation on sugar, temperature and thickness. These terms are recognised in hawkers and coffee shops nationally.

Younger generations of [[Singaporeans]] have created modern twists on kopi, such as almond ginger kopi.<ref name=":8" />

==Processing==
===Beans and sources===
{{See also|Coffea canephora}}
[[File:Canephora.jpg|thumb|Unroasted robusta beans]]

Kopi traditionally uses [[Coffea canephora|Robusta]] coffee beans. During [[Singapore in the Straits Settlements|colonial Singapore]], the Chinese partook in exchanges with [[Arabs|Arab]] traders who carried with them [[Indonesia]]n Robusta beans, and these beans grew better in Singapore's conditions as opposed to [[Coffea arabica|Arabica]] beans.<ref name=":9">{{Cite book|last=Loh|first=Jahan|title=One Kopi at a Time: Retracing Singapore's Coffee Culture|publisher=Invasion Studios Pte Ltd|year=2015|location=Singapore}}</ref> The common type of Robusta beans used in Singapore is the Indonesia EK-1 species.<ref name=":2" /> In 21st-century Singapore, Robusta beans continue to be largely imported from Indonesia and [[Vietnam]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite web|title=Singapore's Cosmopolitan Coffee and Tea Culture|url=https://stir-tea-coffee.com/api/content/faed2808-f417-11e8-a1c3-120e7ad5cf50/|last=Doyle|first=Josh|date=7 December 2018|website=STiR Coffee and Tea Industry International - STiR is the international coffee and tea industry bi-monthly magazine website, local, global, equipment, machinery, supplies, services, market, intelligence, raw, product, retail, service news|language=en-us|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> In a bid to modernize, heritage brands such as Lam Yeo Coffee Powder Factory choose to use gourmet beans from [[South Africa]] and [[Central America]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lam Yeo Coffee Powder Factory |url=https://www.roots.gov.sg/en/places/places-landing/Places/landmarks/balestier-food-trail/lam-yeo-coffee-powder-factory |access-date=19 May 2020 |website=roots.sg}}</ref>

===Roasting===
{{See also|Torrefacto}}

The general traditional preparation process for [[Hainan people|Hainanese]]-style kopi involves using a combination of 80% beans, 20% sugar and margarine in the roasting process for a duration of 25 minutes at 180 degrees Celsius.<ref name=":0" /> Halfway into the roasting time, salt is added. Sugar is also added at the end to provide a caramelized finish and takeaway any bitter aftertaste.<ref name=":0" /> The result is a richer and more fragrant coffee than Western-style coffee.<ref name=":9" /> This method has been said to hold slight similarities to the common [[Torrefacto]] roasting method in [[Argentina]], [[Costa Rica]], [[France]], [[Portugal]] and [[Spain]].<ref name=":2" />

===Serving===
[[File:Stainless Steel Kopi Pot (1).jpg|thumb|A kopi pot]]

To serve, the ground kopi powder is placed in a [[muslin]] bag and boiling water is poured over it.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web|title=Brass coffee dispenser kettle|url=http://roots.sg/learn/collections/listing/1022248|website=www.roots.sg|language=en|access-date=19 May 2020|archive-date=14 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814022517/https://www.roots.sg/learn/collections/listing/1022248|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is then stirred using a long stick or [[Chopsticks|chopstick]]. After, the brew is transferred back and forth between two large cylindrical kettles with upright tubular spouts tapering to the pouring end.<ref name=":11" /> The purpose is to aerate and cool the kopi.

===Nutrition===
Kopi has twice the amount of [[caffeine]] found in [[Coffea arabica|Arabica]] coffee.<ref>{{Cite web|title=10 differences Between Robusta & Arabica Coffee|url=https://theroasterspack.com/blogs/news/15409365-10-differences-between-robusta-arabica-coffee|last=Pabari|first=Suneal|date=2014|website=The Roasters Pack|language=en|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> A regular cup of kopi contains three teaspoons of [[sugar]] whereas kopi ''siew dai'' has one.{{tspUS|5}}.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|title=Reduce Sugar in Your Coffee for a Healthier Drink|url=https://www.healthhub.sg/live-healthy/1829/yum-seng-how-to-order-healthier-drinks|website=www.healthhub.sg|language=en-US|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> The [[World Health Organization]] recommends that an optimal sugar intake would border {{tspUS|5}} to bring about health benefits.<ref name=":12" />

==History==
===Singapore===
The origin of kopi in Singapore is intertwined with the demographic, industrial and cultural history of colonial Singapore. In 1821, the [[Hainan people|Hainanese]] arrived in Singapore to trade medicinal herbs, umbrellas and wax amongst other things.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lai|first=Chee Kien|date=2006|title=Multi-ethnic Enclaves around Middle Road: An Examination of Early Urban Settlement in Singapore|journal=BiblioAsia|volume=2|issue=2|pages=4–20|via=NLB}}</ref> They did not immigrate to Singapore until much later in the 1870s due to conservative attitudes and delayed open trade and seafaring activities.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|title=Hainanese community {{!}} Infopedia|url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_1492_2009-03-25.html|website=eresources.nlb.gov.sg|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref>

This left the Hainanese at an employment disadvantage compared to earlier arrivals like the [[Hoklo people|Hokkien]], [[Teochew people|Teochew]] and [[Cantonese people|Cantonese]], who had already entrenched themselves into industries like commerce and agriculture, due to aid from exclusivist clan associations.<ref name=":5" /> The Hainanese were a small group, unable to communicate easily with other Chinese groups due to language barriers and were both illiterate and poor.<ref name=":6" /> These circumstances forced them into the service sector, where they found work as rubber tapers, waiters, and more popularly, cooks and domestic servants in rich European and [[Peranakan]] households.<ref name=":5" />

From the late 1920s to early 1930s, the economic downturn incentivized the Hainanese to turn to the hotel, bar and restaurant landscape due to lower rental rates.<ref name=":6" /> The competition from [[Cantonese people|Cantonese]] single women immigrants and reduction of British and Peranakan families after [[World War II]] also impacted the viability of remaining in the services sector.<ref name=":5" /> Thus, the Hainanese relied upon their culminated culinary and personal service skills, and increasingly ventured into setting up their own coffeeshops or [[Kopi tiam|kopitiams]] from the 1920s to 1950s.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Yap|first=Mui Teng|title=Hainanese in the restaurant and catering business|publisher=Opinion books|year=1990|location=Singapore|pages=78–90}}</ref> The support from the Hainanese association members aided this successful transition.<ref>Low, C. G. (1983). Chinese Dialect Groups. On ''Oral History Centre'' [MP3]. Singapore: National Archives of Singapore.</ref> It is recognized that the Hainanese community played a pioneering and pivotal role in the emergence of the kopitiam culture in Singapore.<ref>{{Cite news|last=The Straits|first=Times|date=2007|title=Kopi connection|work=The Straits Times}}</ref> It was through these Hainanese kopitiams that distinctive techniques of roasting [[coffee bean]]s and brewing coffee were created, and kopi along with its variations in Singapore was birthed.<ref name=":5" />

During the [[Japanese occupation of Singapore|Japanese Occupation]], [[black market]] traders often used coffee shops to sell rice, salt and sugar to the public.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book|last=Kratoska|first=Paul H.|title=The Japanese Occupation of Malaya: A Social and Economic History|publisher=C. Hurst & Co. Publishers|year=1998|isbn=9780824818890}}</ref> By mid-1944, tighter restrictions and increased scarcity forced most coffee shops to close.<ref name=":7" /> The remaining only offered kopi without sugar and milk.<ref name=":7" /> This meant consumption and availability of kopi O greatly reduced. Key events also shaped the kopi landscape in late 1900s [[Singapore]], affecting the price, availability and consumption.

The rapid trend of buying kopitiams in Singapore began in 1988.<ref name=":5" /> A direct effect of a change in policy, that enabled privatization of ownership of kopitiams previously under the [[Housing and Development Board|Housing Development Board]].<ref name=":5" /> Kopitiams became attractive property investments.<ref name=":5" /> This caused the prices of kopitiam properties for sale and resale to rise sharply.<ref name=":5" /> The result also encompassed the practice of selling new purchases to another owner, who would then renovate the place to justify increased rents onto the tenants.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Han|first=Fook Kwang|date=2013|title=HDB coffee shops are not district 10 bungalows|page=40|work=The Sunday Times}}</ref> Another pattern of holding the kopitiam for short periods of time and selling them off to make money quickly also emerged.<ref name=":5" />

The overarching economic result directly impacting stallholders and consumers, was an exponential growth in food and rent prices. Examples included increases of rent by S$1000, a 30% to 70% hike in prices of dishes, and a close to 100% increase in price for a cup of Kopi.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Chan|first1=Francis|last2=Kua|first2=Z.Y.|date=2007|title=Record price for coffee shop means higher rents|work=The Straits Times}}</ref> In 2006, the price of a kopi O rose from 60 cents to 70 cents.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Lim|first=D|date=2006|title=Kopi-O likely to cost more soon|work=The Straits Times}}</ref> Similarly, in 2016, due to increased rent and labor costs, kopi prices rose to $1.30, which caused unhappiness in patrons.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Wong|first=Siew Ying|date=2016|title=Budget 2016: Of coffee prices and hopes of a helping hand|work=The Straits Times|url=https://www.straitstimes.com/opinion/of-coffee-prices-and-hopes-of-a-helping-hand}}</ref>

The reactions of the public towards raised kopi prices – writing complaint letters to ''[[The Straits Times]]'' and involving The Consumers Association of Singapore – serve as evidence with regard to the constant of kopi in Singapore's food culture and the integral role it plays in the everyday lifestyles of [[Singapore]] residents.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Chang|first1=Rachel|last2=Ong|first2=A|date=2011|title=Wrestling with the beast – again|pages=36–37|work=The Straits Times}}</ref>

===Malaysia===
[[File:A mug of Tenom coffee.jpg|upright|thumb|A mug of kopi brewed from Tenom-grown ground coffee beans]]

In [[East Malaysia]], the town of [[Tenom]] in the state of Sabah is a major producer of [[Robusta coffee|Robusta variety]] coffee beans used to make kopi, which is widely consumed throughout the state and the neighbouring kingdom of [[Brunei]].<ref name="Capital">{{cite web|url=http://www.bt.com.bn/features/2014/11/17/sabah%E2%80%99s-coffee-capital-tenom|title=Sabah's coffee capital of Tenom|agency=Bernama|via=The Brunei Times|date=17 November 2014|access-date=20 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320042943/http://www.bt.com.bn/features/2014/11/17/sabah%E2%80%99s-coffee-capital-tenom|archive-date=20 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bharian.com.my/bhplus-old/2015/06/64088/kopi-popularkan-daerah-tenom|title=Kopi popularkan daerah Tenom|trans-title=Coffee popularises Tenom district|lang=ms|work=Berita Harian|date=28 June 2015|access-date=24 April 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sabah.com.my/borneotrade/h3.htm|title=Directories - Manufacturer (Federation of Sabah Manufacturers)|work=Borneo Trade|access-date=20 January 2016|archive-date=7 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141207144228/http://www.sabah.com.my/borneotrade/h3.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sabah.gov.my/md.tnm/background.html|title=Background (Agriculture)|work=Tenom District Council|access-date=20 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320134355/http://www.sabah.gov.my/md.tnm/background.html|archive-date=20 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> The beans are processed using traditional firewood and drum rotation methods and typically without addition of any artificial ingredients or colourings.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://asean-gidatabase.org/sites/default/files/gidocs/MYGI000GI06-00005-en.pdf|title=Tenom Coffee|work=ECAAP III|access-date=20 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320134531/http://asean-gidatabase.org/sites/default/files/gidocs/MYGI000GI06-00005-en.pdf|archive-date=20 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Coffee was first planted in Sabah during the administration of [[British North Borneo]], concentrated mainly in the area of the east coast on the [[forest reserve]] near mangrove areas with the ''[[coffea arabica]]'' variety. However, due to a severe outbreak of disease, the plantation efforts were initially abandoned by 1910.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.etawau.com/Agriculture/Coffee/Yit_Foh.htm|title=Yit Foh Coffee Powder Factory|publisher=e-tawau|date=16 January 2012|access-date=20 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320025939/http://www.etawau.com/Agriculture/Coffee/Yit_Foh.htm|archive-date=20 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> Since then, coffee production was concentrated in the west coast area. [[Tenom]] received attention when the [[British North Borneo Chartered Company]] (BNBCC) established coffee and other plantations in the area. To take the resources to major towns, a [[Sabah State Railway|railway line]] from Melalap to Jesselton (now [[Kota Kinabalu]]) was built by the British in the late 1890s. To increase the coffee production, many labourers from [[Republic of China (1912–49)|China]], mainly those of [[Hakka people|Hakka]] and [[Cantonese people|Cantonese]] descent were brought to Tenom by the British as local workforce.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.flyingdusun.com/005_Places/008_Tenom.htm|title=Sabah Cities, Towns and Villages - Tenom|last=Scholz|first=Herman|work=Flying Dusun|accessdate=20 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320134131/http://www.flyingdusun.com/005_Places/008_Tenom.htm|archive-date=20 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> Today, Tenom is widely known as an [[agriculture]] site with large coffee production and has been dubbed as the "Sabah's coffee capital".<ref name="Capital"/> Due to its large demand from other countries since 2010s, the government began to help to address the shortage of raw coffee supply in Tenom.<ref name=Shortage>{{cite news|url=http://www.dailyexpress.com.my/news.cfm?NewsID=126020|title=Tenom raw coffee shortage|last=Mathew|first=Mail|work=Daily Express|date=24 July 2018|access-date=25 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180725083505/http://www.dailyexpress.com.my/news.cfm?NewsID=126020|archive-date=25 July 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Thailand===
Kopi, or koopi, is a popular drink in [[Southern Thailand]].<ref name=Thai>{{Cite web|title=Robusta coffee, native to Satun Province...a gem to preserve in the community|url=http://rdo.psu.ac.th/en/index.php/features/231-robusta-coffee|website=[[Prince of Songkla University]]|date=28 January 2019|access-date=24 April 2022}}{{Dead link|date=June 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Farmers from certain plantations in the region would process locally grown coffee and brew it in the style of Malaysian kopi culture.<ref name=Thai/>

==Sale and distribution==
===Consumer market===
[[File:Hawker Center, Singapore.jpg|thumb|Hawker centre in Singapore]]

In Singapore there are an estimated 322 coffee shops and hundreds of them are found in the [[New towns of Singapore|HDB estates]].<ref name=":5" /> This is alongside hundreds of [[food court]]s and [[hawker centre]]s.<ref name=":5" /> Almost all of them sell Singapore kopi and its many variations. The established coffee shops include Tong Ah Eating House in [[Chinatown, Singapore|Chinatown]] that has been passed down through four generations,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Snapshots from Singapore: A Guide to Singaporean Coffee.|url=https://drinks.seriouseats.com/2012/08/snapshots-from-singapore-a-guide-to-singaporean-coffee-kop-how-to-order-how-its-made.html|last=Falkowitz|first=Max|date=2012|website=Serious Eats}}</ref> [[Killiney Kopitiam|Killiney kopitiam]] that has received a heritage award, Heap Seng Leong – one of the few traditional coffee shops serving kopi with butter,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Heap Seng Leong – Old-school coffeeshop with Kopi Gu You & kaya toast|url=https://www.ladyironchef.com/2019/05/heap-seng-leong/|last=Chua|first=Gin|date=2019|website=Ladyironchef}}</ref> and Ah Seng Coffee that began in the 1960s.<ref name=":8" />

There are also commercialized outlets that specialize in the Singapore traditional breakfast and kopi. The household names include:
* [[Ya Kun Kaya Toast|Ya Kun]], a [[Hainan people|Hainanese]] business that began in 1944. The chain is largely seen as culturally significant to [[Singaporeans|Singaporean]] life<ref>{{Cite news|last=Low|first=Shi Ping|date=2007|title=A toast to expansion in Asean|work=The Edge Singapore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Leveraging on the Singaporean Government's strong support – Interview with Ya Kun Kaya Toast.|url=https://hkmb.hktdc.com/en/1X0A4P8P/hktdc-research/Leveraging-on-the-Singaporean-Government's-Strong-Support-Interview-with-Ya-Kun-Kaya-Toast|last=HKTDC Research|date=2015}}</ref> and is also recognized for its [[kaya toast]].
* [[BreadTalk|Toast Box]], that integrates heritage items into its décor and is known for their butter mountain display. It also conducts [[Nanyang (region)|Nanyang]] coffee appreciation workshops.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Toast Box Singapore|url=https://www.facebook.com/toastboxsingapore/posts/923089234405267|website=www.facebook.com|language=en|access-date=28 May 2020}}</ref>
* and Nanyang Old Coffee, conceptualised in the 1940s and winner of 'The Search for The Best Coffee Competition 2013'.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Awards to Nanyang Old Coffee|url=http://nanyangoldcoffee.com/awards.html|website=nanyangoldcoffee.com|access-date=28 May 2020|archive-date=5 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190105045835/http://nanyangoldcoffee.com/awards.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The brand also runs workshops.

An initiative by [[NTUC FairPrice|NTUC Foodfare]] and [[Kopitiam (company)|Kopitiam]] that began in 2019, continues to provide kopi at discounted prices of $0.50 for Singaporeans part of the Pioneer and Merdeka generations, and the NTUC Union.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web|title=Coffee, tea at 50 cents for seniors and workers.|url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/coffee-tea-at-50-cents-for-seniors-and-workers|last=Seow|first=Joanna|date=2019|website=The Straits Times.}}</ref> A regular cup of kopi usually costs around $0.90 to $1.60 at [[Kopitiam (company)|Kopitiam]] outlets.<ref name=":13" />

===Instant kopi===
The [[instant coffee]] market in Singapore is set to grow annually by 3.1% according to Statista.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Instant Coffee - Singapore {{!}} Statista Market Forecast|url=https://www.statista.com/outlook/30010200/124/instant-coffee/singapore|website=Statista|language=en|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> In 2016 and 2017, the movement against [[diabetes]] negatively impacted sales numbers.<ref name=":10" /> This occurred alongside the growing appeal of [[Single-serve coffee container|coffee pods]] to consumers in Singapore.<ref name=":10" /> One of the major contributing factors towards this trend is the ability to control the amount of sugar and creamer used.<ref name=":10" />

National brands such as [[BreadTalk|Toast Box]] produce their own instant kopi products.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Toast Box|url=https://www.toastbox.com.sg/signatures.html|website=www.toastbox.com.sg|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> Instant kopi can also be found in local supermarkets. The brands which provide traditional kopi variations such as kopi O include [[OldTown White Coffee|Old Town]], OWL, Gold Kili, Aik Cheong and Ah Huat.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Results For instant coffee {{!}} FairPrice|url=https://www.fairprice.com.sg/search?query=instant%20coffee|website=www.fairprice.com.sg|access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref>

==Society and culture==
===Consumption (colonial Singapore)===
During the early 1900s, [[porcelain]] cups were typically used to serve the kopi.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |title=Porcelain cup with 'Kilang Serbuk Kopi Sin Seng' logo |url=https://www.roots.gov.sg/Collection-Landing/listing/1063084 |access-date=28 May 2020 |website=www.roots.sg |language=en}}</ref> These cups were decorated by the motifs or logos of the coffee suppliers.<ref name=":15" /> Consumers would cool their kopi by pouring it into the saucer and then drinking from it.<ref name=":15" /> In the 1930s, some coffee roasters would use [[opium]]-infused water to roast their beans in order to make customers addicted to their brew.<ref name=":9" /> There was also a practice of warming cold coffee in ceramic cups on a [[charcoal]] burner, to give the impression that the coffee was freshly made.<ref name=":9" /> [[Blue-collar worker|Blue-collared]] workers began to drink coffee instead of tea due to its stronger caffeine effect.<ref name=":9" />

More than 80% of the coffee-shops were run by [[Hainan people|Hainanese]] and [[Fuzhou people|Foochows]], but they were often patronized by members of other communities such as [[Malays (ethnic group)|Malays]] and [[Indian people|Indians]].<ref name=":14" /> The main consumers of kopi at these coffee-shops were men.<ref name=":5" /> This was partly due to the small population of women [[Immigration|immigrants]], and the cultural expectation for them to remain at home or in their quarters.<ref name=":5" />

Another reason was the nature of [[Kopi tiam|kopitiams]] in [[Singapore in the Straits Settlements|colonial Singapore]], which served as recreation venues for men, gambling dens, and meeting places for [[secret society]] members.<ref name=":14" /> The prevalence of [[Prostitution|prostitutes]] and [[Call girl|escort girls]] at the kopitiams also discouraged women from sitting around.<ref name=":14" />

===Consumption (modern Singapore)===
Kopi makes up over 70% of the coffee consumed in 21st-century Singapore.<ref name=":2" /> People from all income brackets, gender, age and communities can be found drinking the widely available kopi – with some enjoying four to six cups a day.<ref name=":10" /> The original ceramic cups have been widely replaced by [[glass]] at many coffee shops.<ref name=":0" /> In hawker centres, the [[Take-out|takeaway]] option is served in a plastic bag.

This beverage is often paired with a traditional Singapore breakfast which consists of kaya and butter on charcoal-grilled toast, paired with two [[Boiled egg|soft-boiled]] eggs.<ref name=":0" /> Kaya is an egg jam combined with [[coconut milk]] and [[sugar]].<ref name=":0" /> The [[Hainan people|Hainanese]] version is brown in color due to the use of caramelized sugar.<ref name=":0" /> The [[Peranakan]] version is instead green in color due to the infusion of [[Pandanus|pandan]] leaves.<ref name=":0" /> Both types are equally prevalent in Singapore. The breakfast holds links to the British style of breakfast and was popularized by the Hainanese.<ref name=":0" />

===Health===
In 2016, Singapore launched a nationwide campaign to tackle [[diabetes]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Singapore's War on Diabetes|url=https://www.healthhub.sg/live-healthy/1273/d-day-for-diabetes|website=www.healthhub.sg|language=en-US|access-date=28 May 2020}}</ref> A survey conducted by YouGov found that 42% of [[Singaporeans]] were supportive of a [[Sugary drink tax|sugar tax]] in Singapore whereas 58% would favor a ban of drinks containing high sugar levels.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Almost 3 in 5 Singaporeans would support a total ban on high-sugar drinks: Survey, Business Insider - Business Insider Singapore|url=https://www.businessinsider.sg/almost-3-in-5-singaporeans-would-support-a-total-ban-on-high-sugar-drinks-survey|last=Tay|first=Rachel|website=www.businessinsider.sg|language=en-US|access-date=28 May 2020|archive-date=5 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191205071012/https://www.businessinsider.sg/almost-3-in-5-singaporeans-would-support-a-total-ban-on-high-sugar-drinks-survey/|url-status=dead}}</ref> The attitudes of Singaporeans towards sugar has a direct impact on their preference of kopi, since kopi O involves addition of sugar. The 2018 healthier drinks policy has created mandatory guidelines for many food and beverage outlets, putting a control on the sugar content.<ref name=":1" /> Coffee shop operator [[Kopitiam (company)|Kopitiam]] has also started the practice of serving sugar-free beverages, and leaving the sugar at the side of stalls for customers to add for themselves.<ref name=":1" /> A trial conducted at the Health Promotion Board's public canteen saw a 75% drop in the amount of sugar used, when the self-help practice was implemented.<ref name=":1" /> With 430,000 Singaporeans with diabetes in 2018, the dwindling appeal of kopi O shows potential of being a long-term constant.<ref name=":1" />

==Museum==
The Nanyang Old Coffee Mini Singapore Coffee Museum is a museum dedicated to kopi history.<ref name=":8" /> It traces the traditional roasting methods and features photographs, vintage items, and information regarding the kopi landscape in Singapore, as well as those who partake in creating it. An example of an interesting tidbit of information is how empty [[condensed milk]] cans were reused as takeaway containers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Home of Nanyang Old Coffee {{!}} 南洋老咖啡|url=http://nanyangoldcoffee.com/|website=nanyangoldcoffee.com|access-date=28 May 2020}}</ref>

Goombay Smash:
{{Short description|Rum-based beverage from the Bahamas}}
[[File:Goombay Smash upon arrival (5435890609).jpg|thumb]]
'''Goombay Smash''' is a [[rum]] based beverage in the [[Bahamas]].<ref name=gulls>{{cite book |title=Where the Gulls Are: Fishing with Joe |last=Burroughs |first=Bob |date=2011}}</ref> It is traditionally served in a sling or collins glass. The Goombay Smash was created by Emily Cooper, aka Miss Emily, at the Blue Bee Bar in [[Green Turtle Cay|New Plymouth]]. The original recipe is a secret, but it is believed to have contained [[coconut]] rum, [[dirty rum]], [[apricot]] [[brandy]], and [[pineapple juice]].<ref name=gulls/> Imitators and variations commonly use rum, coconut and pineapple juice.<ref name=gulls/> Apricot [[liqueur]] is sometimes used and dark, amber or spiced rums (dirty rums) are preferred. In place of coconut rum, coconut cream can be used. Other variations include [[Creme de Banane]], [[orange juice]] and [[grenadine]].<ref name=gulls/>

Egg in beer:
{{Short description|English idiom}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2021}}
{{Orphan|date=December 2020}}

'''Egg in beer''' refers to the practice, literally or figuratively, of cracking a raw [[Egg as food|egg]] into a glass of [[beer]]. The term is used [[metaphor]]ically, commonly as "what do you want, egg in your beer?" implying that the listener already has something good but is undeservedly asking for more.<ref name="MelilloMelillo2005">{{cite book|author1=Joseph Melillo|author2=Edward M. Melillo|title=American Slang: Cultural Language Guide to Living in the USA|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gvHzNsQoeH4C&pg=PA106|year=2005|publisher=Mottobene Inc|isbn=978-1-59404-017-7|pages=106–}}</ref>

==Literal==
In England, where the consumption of the egg in beer is centuries old, a mix of beer, raw egg, honey and other herbs could be prescribed to the sick.  [[Posset]], famously consumed in ''[[Macbeth]]'' and ''[[The Merry Wives of Windsor]]'', consists partly in eggs whipped with cream, sugar, and beer or wine.  [[Syllabub]] is made by mixing egg whites cream and wine. The egg also clears out cloudier beers.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Hezel |first=Anna |date=6 July 2016 |title=A Brief History of Drinking Raw Eggs, from 'Macbeth' to 'Orange Is the New Black' |url=http://www.extracrispy.com/culture/328/a-brief-history-of-drinking-raw-eggs-from-macbeth-to-orange-is-the-new-black |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170630023034/http://www.extracrispy.com/culture/328/a-brief-history-of-drinking-raw-eggs-from-macbeth-to-orange-is-the-new-black |archive-date=30 June 2017 |website=Extra Crispy}}</ref>

According to the [[Elizabethan era|Elizabethan]] theories, out of the four fundamentals characters (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic), eggs are sanguine and beer is choleric.<ref name=":0" />

In 1915, industry journal ''The Mixer and Server'' noted a [[Seattle]] case where a judge decreed that an egg, once cracked into a glass of beer, qualified as a drink and was not in violation of ordinances against giving free food in bars.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= |first1= |last2= |first2= |date=1915 |title=Egg in Beer is Considered Drink |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.li53p3&view=1up&seq=911 |journal=The Mixer and Server |volume=XXIV |issue=10 |pages=49 |doi= |access-date= |publisher=Hotel and Restaurant Employee's International Alliance and Bartenders' International League of America.}}</ref>

A 1939 article in ''Printing'' magazine notes that Pennsylvania State Brewers' Association had launched a public-relations campaign to "sell the idea that eggs and beer make a pleasing combination."<ref>{{cite book|title=Printing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ShwhAQAAMAAJ|year=1939}}</ref> Other Pennsylvania sources refer to this as a "miner's breakfast".<ref name="Smiles2005">{{cite book|author=Jack Smiles|title="Ee-Yah": The Life and Times of Hughie Jennings, Baseball Hall of Famer|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CL2KTvU6jdoC&pg=PA9|date=10 May 2005|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-0-7864-8428-7|pages=9–}}</ref><ref name="Noon2011">{{cite book|author=Mark A. Noon|title=Yuengling: A History of America's Oldest Brewery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KfZ3k6iz3NQC&pg=PA33|date=23 November 2011|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-0-7864-8659-5|pages=33–}}</ref>

Since 1999, Giang Cafe (located in [[Hanoi]], Vietnam) has served an egg beer consisting of beer mixed with whipped egg yolks—a variant on traditional Vietnamese [[egg coffee]].<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=2019-04-10 |title=Hanoi egg beer: the frothy Vietnamese cocktail that's hard to beat |url=https://www.scmp.com/lifestyle/travel-leisure/article/3005381/hanoi-egg-beer-frothy-vietnamese-cocktail-thats-hard-beat |work=South China Morning Post |access-date=2023-09-28}}</ref>

==Metaphorical==
{{wiktionary|egg in one's beer}}
Sources differ as to the origin of the [[colloquialism]], with some stating it dates to [[World War II]]<ref name="Sala2013">{{cite book|author=Jenny La Sala|title=Comes A Soldier's Whisper: A Collection of Wartime Letters with Reflection and Hope for the Future|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lbrMUHXIUlEC&pg=PA93|date=15 February 2013|publisher=Trafford Publishing|isbn=978-1-4669-7687-0|pages=93–}}</ref> while others speculate that it dates to the 19th century.<ref name="Axelrod2011">{{cite book|author=Alan Axelrod|title=The Cheaper the Crook, the Gaudier the Patter: Forgotten Hipster Lines, Tough Guy Talk, and Jive Gems|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hYYkAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT112|date=20 July 2011|publisher=Skyhorse Publishing|isbn=978-1-62873-017-3|pages=112–}}</ref> However, a 1933 article in the ''[[Stevens Indicator]]'', mentioning an employee who had not received a raise, notes: "What do you expect, Carl? Egg in your beer?"<ref>{{cite book|title=Stevens Indicator ...|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WrUnAQAAMAAJ|year=1933}}</ref>

== Flips ==
Mixing beer, an egg and liquor is called a "flip". According to The Whistler's lead bartender in Chicago, Marina Holter, flips date back to as far as the 1690s. Some assume that the liquor kills the [[salmonella]] risks linked to raw eggs consumption.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-02-21 |title=Beer flips are the beer-and-whole egg cocktail—wait, hear me out |url=https://thetakeout.com/beer-flips-how-to-make-beer-and-whole-egg-cocktail-1832759172 |access-date=2024-01-25 |website=The Takeout |language=en}}</ref> It may also be a revisited version of the classic raw egg+alcohol consumed across ages and cultures (and referred to as "Fallujah omelets" in the series ''[[Orange Is the New Black]]'').<ref name=":0" />

== Products ==
In 2021, for [[Easter]], [[Cadbury]] partnered with [[Goose Island Brewery|Goose Island]] to release a [[Cadbury Creme Egg|Creme Egg]]-flavored beer.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cadbury Creme Eggs Now Come in Beer Form |url=https://www.foodandwine.com/news/cadbury-creme-eggs-beer-goose-island |access-date=2024-01-25 |website=Food & Wine |language=en}}</ref>

'''Dried lime tea''', also known as '''chai noomi basra''' ({{langx|ar|شاي نومي بصرة}}<ref name="alsumaria">{{cite news |title=بالفيديو: تعرف إلى فوائد النومي بصرة المشروب العراقي الرمضاني! |url=https://www.alsumaria.tv/infograph-details/303636/infographics/%D8%A8%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%81%D9%8A%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%88-%D8%AA%D8%B9%D8%B1%D9%81-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D9%81%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%AF-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D9%88%D9%85%D9%8A-%D8%A8%D8%B5%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B4%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%A8-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%82%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B1%D9%85%D8%B6%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%8A |access-date=12 October 2025 |work=[[Al Sumaria]] |language=ar |trans-title=Video: Learn about the benefits of Noumi Basra, the Iraqi Ramadan drink!}}</ref>), '''noomi basra tea''' or '''loomi tea''', is a type of [[herbal tea]] made from [[dried lime]]s that is traditional to [[Iraq]] and the [[Arabian Peninsula]].<ref name="Basan">{{cite book|title=Middle Eastern Kitchen|last=Basan|first=Ghillie|pages=78|location=NY, USA|publisher=Hippocrene Books Inc.|isbn=9780781811903|year=2007}}</ref><ref name="nasrallah2013">{{cite book |last1=Nasrallah |first1=Nawal |author1-link=Nawal Nasrallah |title=Delights from the Garden of Eden: A Cookbook and History of the Iraqi Cuisine |date=2013 |publisher=Equinox Pub. |isbn=978-1-84553-457-8 |page=545 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Delights_from_the_Garden_of_Eden/4RZAPgAACAAJ |access-date=8 October 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

==Preparation==
Loomi tea is made by seeding the dried limes (''noomi [[Basra]]'') where they are cracked into several pieces, or just pricked, and their peels are simmered in water for 15 to 30 minutes until boiled. Afterwards, they are drained and the tea is sweetened with sugar. At times, [[honey]] may be preferred instead and [[saffron]] threads may also be added.<ref>{{cite web|title=What is Noomi Basra?|author=Ayelet's Comfort|date=2015|url=http://ayeletscomfort.com/2012/03/04/what-is-noomi-basra|access-date=10 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151202101219/http://ayeletscomfort.com/2012/03/04/what-is-noomi-basra/|archive-date=2 December 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Usage==
Served hot, the drink is also consumed as a remedy to aid [[indigestion]], upset stomach, [[diarrhea]], and [[nausea]]. It is very sour and aromatic, but can also be mildly sweet, depending on how much sugar is added. Omani dried limes have a pleasant tart [[citrus]] flavor and are rich in [[vitamin C]].<ref name="Basan" />

*[[Ginger tea]], another herbal tea used to treat upset stomach

'''Kahawa Sūg''', also known as '''Sulu coffee''' or '''Sulu robusta''', is a [[Single-origin coffee|single-origin]] [[coffee varietals|coffee varietal]] grown by the [[Tausug people]] of the [[Sulu Archipelago]], [[Philippines]]. It is a [[robusta coffee|robusta]] [[cultivar]], belonging to the species ''[[Coffea canephora|Coffea canephora]]''. It originates from robusta plants introduced to [[Sulu]] in the 1860s. It is an important part of traditional [[Tausug people|Tausug]] culture. It is mostly consumed locally, though it has started being exported more widely in recent years. It is currently endangered by the introduction of modern higher yield coffee varieties.

==History==
Kahawa Sūg has a unique origin, in comparison to other traditional coffee varieties in the Philippines. Robusta coffee was introduced to the Sulu archipelago in the 1860s by [[Herman Leopold Schück]], a Prussian [[merchant mariner]] originally from [[Upper Silesia]]. Schück had become a close friend to the ruler of the [[Sulu Sultanate]], Sultan [[Jamalul Alam]]. He eventually became a blood brother to the Sultan through [[blood compact]] and decided to settle in the Philippines. He established a plantation of robusta coffee in the village of Lukut Lapas (now [[barangay]] Anuling, [[Patikul, Sulu]]) with 20,000 plants. Cultivation spread to the locals and the coffee became known as kahawa Sūg.<ref name="CNNBueno"/><ref name="Montemayor">{{cite book |last1=Montemayor |first1=Michael Schuck |title=Captain Herman Leopold Schück : the saga of a German sea captain in 19th century Sulu-Sulawesi seas |date=2007 |publisher=University of the Philippines Press |isbn=9789715424851}}</ref> It literally means "Sulu coffee", from [[Arabic language|Arabic]] [[wikt:قهوة|قهوة]], ''qahwah'' ("coffee"), and Sūg ("sea currents"), the native [[Tausug language|Tausug]] name for the Sulu archipelago.<ref name="polistico">{{cite book|author =Edgie Polistico|title =Philippine Food, Cooking, & Dining Dictionary|publisher =Anvil Publishing, Incorporated|year =2017|isbn =9786214200870|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=iz8_DwAAQBAJ&q=Arroz+caldo}}{{Dead link|date=February 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Cultural significance==
Kahawa Sūg is an important part of [[Tausug people|Tausug]] culture in Sulu. It is the traditional accompaniment to ''bangbang'' (''[[merienda]]'' snacks) or ''latal'' (a platter with a variety of native dishes).<ref name="CNNBueno">{{cite news |last1=Bueno |first1=Anna |title=The untold heritage of Sulu's fascinating coffee culture |url=http://cnnphilippines.com/life/leisure/food/2016/11/11/sulu-coffee.html |access-date=December 21, 2018 |work=CNN Philippines |date=November 11, 2016 |archive-date=December 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181221090536/http://cnnphilippines.com/life/leisure/food/2016/11/11/sulu-coffee.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="RapplerMadarang">{{cite news |last1=Madarang |first1=Rhea Claire |title=Sweet tradition: A peek at Tausug treats |url=https://www.rappler.com/life-and-style/best-eats/203473-tausug-treats-sweet-tradition-ramadan |access-date=December 21, 2018 |work=Rappler |date=May 27, 2018}}</ref> It is usually served with an extra empty glass, so the hot coffee can be poured back and forth to cool while swirling it at the same time and releasing the aroma. The coffee is described as being non-acidic and not too bitter.<ref name="CNNBueno"/>

Kahawa Sūg are sold in Muslim communities in the Philippines in ''kahawahan'', the native [[Coffeehouse|coffee shop]]s.<ref name="polistico"/> It is usually taken black.<ref name="Blueboard">{{cite news |last1=Veneracion-Rallonza |first1=Maria Lourdes |title=Tales from the 'Margins:' A Tausug Girl and Kahawa Sug |url=http://www.ateneo.edu/news/research/tales-%E2%80%98margins%E2%80%99-tausug-girl-and-kahawa-sug-blueboard-ma-lourdes-veneracion-rallonza |work=Blueboard |publisher=Ateneo de Manila University |date=March 8, 2016 |archive-date=December 21, 2018 |access-date=December 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181221182518/http://www.ateneo.edu/news/research/tales-%E2%80%98margins%E2%80%99-tausug-girl-and-kahawa-sug-blueboard-ma-lourdes-veneracion-rallonza |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Kahawa Sūg is widely grown in Sulu, producing around 7,300 [[metric tons]] each year because of Sulu's naturally fertile soil. However, it is mostly consumed locally in Mindanao and rarely exported because of the problems brought by the [[conflict in Muslim Mindanao]] in recent decades. Most Filipinos outside of Mindanao are unaware that Sulu even has a native coffee variety. Coffee are traditionally harvested by hand, plucking individual ripe red [[coffee berry|berries]], as opposed to the modern methods of harvesting robusta where the branches are stripped entirely.<ref name="CNNBueno"/> Kahawa Sūg are traditionally soaked in water before being depulped, then washed again and fermented overnight before rinsing and drying.<ref name="Perez">{{cite news |last1=Perez |first1=Ace June Rell S. |title=Attaining peace through coffee |url=https://www.sunstar.com.ph/article/38808 |access-date=December 21, 2018 |work=SunStar Philippines |date=October 26, 2015}}</ref>

In recent years, the [[Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao|ARMM]] branch of the [[Department of Agrarian Reform]] has started investing in local coffee farmers through the ARCCESS Project (Agrarian Reform Community Connectivity and Economic Support Services). They provide training, equipment, and funds. In 2017, 10 metric tons of Kahawa Sūg were purchased by the Filipino company, [[Universal Robina Corporation]].<ref name="Cayon">{{cite news |last1=Cayon |first1=Manuel |title='Pick red' farm group in ARMM gets coffee purchase order from URC |url=https://businessmirror.com.ph/pick-red-farm-group-in-armm-gets-coffee-purchase-order-from-urc/ |access-date=December 21, 2018 |work=BusinessMirror |date=May 21, 2017}}</ref><ref name="dararmm">{{cite news |title=Sulu Royal Coffee now distributor to large food corporation |url=http://dar.armm.gov.ph/sulu-royal-coffee-now-distributor-to-large-food-corporation/ |publisher=Department of Agrarian Reform, Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Republic of the Philippines |date=May 14, 2017 |archive-date=December 20, 2018 |access-date=December 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181220221522/http://dar.armm.gov.ph/sulu-royal-coffee-now-distributor-to-large-food-corporation/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Garcia">{{cite news |last1=Garcia |first1=Teofilo P. |title=Coffee processing plants to rise in four Sulu towns |url=http://balita.ph/2009/11/08/coffee-processing-plants-to-rise-in-four-sulu-towns/ |access-date=December 21, 2018 |work=Balita |date=November 8, 2009 |archive-date=December 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181221134619/http://balita.ph/2009/11/08/coffee-processing-plants-to-rise-in-four-sulu-towns/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

A notable leader in local coffee growers is Kumalah Sug-Elardo, a full-blooded Tausug [[Royal house of Sulu|princess]] (''Putlih'') and a descendant of the two Royal houses of Sulu. She is often dubbed as the "Coffee Princess". She founded and leads the People's Alliance for Progress Multipurpose Cooperative (PAP-MPC) in 2009, with the goal of improving the livelihoods of the people in the conflict-torn region.<ref name="Cayon"/><ref name="Kumalah">{{cite web |title=The Benefits of Coffee Farming |date=October 25, 2016 |url=http://philcoffeeboard.com/the-benefits-of-coffee-farming/ |access-date=December 21, 2018 |ref=October 26, 2016}}</ref><ref name="tayao">{{cite news |last1=Tayao-Juego |first1=Annelle |title=To end war, plant coffee |url=https://business.inquirer.net/216347/to-end-war-plant-coffee |access-date=December 21, 2018 |newspaper=Philippine Daily Inquirer |date=October 9, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Del Mundo">{{cite news |last1=Del Mundo |first1=Anita Q. |title=The Coffee Princess |url=https://www.philstar.com/other-sections/starweek-magazine/2012/02/12/776219/coffee-princess |access-date=December 21, 2018 |work=PhilStar Global |date=February 12, 2012}}</ref><ref name="Dino">{{cite web |last1=Dino |first1=Nelson |title=Behind this kahawa sug, a woman |url=https://www.layagsug.com/home/-behind-this-kahawa-sug-a-woman |website=Layag Sug |access-date=December 21, 2018 |archive-date=December 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181221182509/https://www.layagsug.com/home/-behind-this-kahawa-sug-a-woman |url-status=usurped }}</ref>

Kahawa Sūg is also used to make [[kahawa kubing]], a local [[civet coffee]].<ref name="dararmm"/><ref name="slowfoodkubing">{{cite web |title=Sulu zibet coffee |url=https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/sulu-zibet-coffee/ |website=Slow Food Foundation Biodiversity |access-date=December 21, 2018}}</ref>

==Conservation==
Kahawa Sūg is listed in the [[Ark of Taste]] international catalogue of endangered [[food heritage|heritage foods]] by the [[Slow Food]] movement. It is threatened by modern higher yield fast-growing coffee [[cultivar]]s that are being introduced to Sulu.<ref name="slowrobusta">{{cite web |title=Sulu robusta coffee |url=https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/sulu-robusta-coffee/ |website=Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity |access-date=December 21, 2018}}</ref>

An '''''emoliente''''' ({{IPA|es|emolˈjente}}) is a traditional drink consumed principally in [[Peru]]. It is customary to drink it in the morning or evening. Various medicinal properties are attributed to ''emolientes'' and they are used to treat [[Digestion|digestive]], [[Reproductive system|reproductive]], [[Respiratory system|respiratory]] and [[Circulatory system|circulatory]] problems.<ref>{{Cite news |date=20 February 2015 |title=¿Cuáles son los beneficios de consumir emoliente? |language=es |agency=laprensa.peru.com |url=https://laprensa.peru.com/actualidad/noticia-beneficios-consumir-emoliente-39571 |access-date=21 February 2018 |archive-date=21 February 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180221100819/https://laprensa.peru.com/actualidad/noticia-beneficios-consumir-emoliente-39571 |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Emolientes'' were introduced to Peru during the [[Viceroyalty of Peru|colonial era]] as a medicinal drink or [[Herbal tea|tisane]]. In [[Lima]] they became popular to the point that there was an ''emolientero'' (emoliente seller) on practically every street corner.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Acurio |first=Gastón |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MID-tgAACAAJ |title=Larousse de la gastronomía peruana: diccionario gatronómico ilustrado |date=2008 |publisher=Q.W. Editores |isbn=9789972589379 |editor-last= |location=Lima |page=159 |language=es |chapter= |author-link=Gastón Acurio |access-date= |archive-date=2021-11-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130205540/https://books.google.es/books?id=MID-tgAACAAJ& |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=EMOLIENTE |url=http://comidasperuanas.net/emoliente/ |access-date=28 August 2017 |publisher=Comidas Peruanas |archive-date=28 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828230026/http://comidasperuanas.net/emoliente/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
[[File:Emolientera_Cusco_02012009.JPG|thumb|300x300px|An ''emoliente'' seller in [[Cusco]], [[Peru]].]]

== Characteristics ==
An ''emoliente'' is a drink based on roasted grains of [[barley]], medicinal herbal extracts, [[sugar]] and [[lemon]] juice. Amongst the most commonly used herbs are [[Equisetum bogotense|Andean horsetail]], [[Flax|linseeds]], [[alfalfa]], [[Plantago lanceolata|ribwort plantain]] and ''[[boldo]]''.<ref name=":0" />

In recent years, ''emolliente'' sellers, especially those with mobile street carts, have been incorporating a range of medicinal plants into their drinks, some of which have been chosen due to their diuretic properties.<ref name=":0" /> These include [[Uncaria tomentosa|cat's claw]], [[Lepidium meyenii|maca]], [[Phyllanthus niruri|gale of the wind]], [[Croton lechleri|''sangre de grado'']], [[Minthostachys mollis|''muña'']] and ''[[Aloe]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Propiedades del Emoliente |url=http://www.lineayforma.com/nutricion/propiedades-del-emoliente.html |access-date=28 August 2017 |publisher=Mujeractiva.com |archive-date=28 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828230703/http://www.lineayforma.com/nutricion/propiedades-del-emoliente.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Other so-called "special" ''emolientes'' may include [[pollen]], [[honey]], ''[[algarrobina]]'', [[corn silk]], spices (such as [[cinnamon]]) or infusions made from fruit ([[quince]] or [[pineapple]]) or [[potato]] skins.<ref name=":0" />

'''Doodh soda''' ({{Lit|milk soda}} in [[Hindustani language|Hindi-Urdu]] and [[Punjabi language|Punjabi]]) is a cold drink made by mixing a lemon- or lime-flavored soda, such as [[Sprite (drink)|Sprite]] or [[7 Up]], with milk. A variant uses a [[cola]]-flavored soda, such as [[Pepsi]] and some use [[cream soda]] such as [[Pakola]]. It is popular in the [[Punjab]] region of both [[Pakistan]] and [[India]], and is especially popular during [[Ramadan]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite magazine|first=Haneen J. |last=Iqbal |date=2021-04-16 |title=My Iftar Table Isn't Complete Without Doodh Soda |url=https://www.bonappetit.com/story/doodh-soda |access-date=2023-03-11 |magazine=[[Bon Appétit]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Imtiaz|first=Saba|date=2017-06-20|title=You Should Mix Soda with Milk|url=https://www.eater.com/2017/6/20/15793584/doodh-soda-doodh-7up-milk-pakistan|access-date=2023-03-11|website=[[Eater (website)|Eater]]|language=en|author-link=Saba Imtiaz}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |first=Anne|last=Ewbank|title=Doodh Soda|url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/foods/doodh-soda-milk|access-date=2023-03-11|website=[[Atlas Obscura]]|language=en}}</ref> It is considered to be healthier than regular soda, and is often paired with spicy foods.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite news  |date=May 12, 2022|first= Sharon |last=Benjamin|title=A viral food trend that is a popular summer drink in Pakistan called 'doodh soda' |url=https://gulfnews.com/food/a-viral-food-trend-that-is-a-popular-summer-drink-in-pakistan-called-doodh-soda-1.1652361784604 |access-date=2023-03-11 |work=[[Gulf News]] |language=en}}</ref> The combination of soda and milk was first created in [[Victorian era|Victorian]] England, and from there it spread to India and Pakistan through the [[British Empire]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Struble|first=Cristine|date=2021-04-20|title=What Is Doodh Soda And What Does It Taste Like?|url=https://www.mashed.com/387786/what-is-doodh-soda-and-whats-it-taste-like/|access-date=2023-03-11|website=[[Mashed (website)|Mashed]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

Similar drinks using 7 Up and Pepsi have been promoted in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Emery|first=David|date=2023-03-06|title=Is This Vintage '7-Up and Milk' Promotion Real?|url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/7-up-and-milk/|access-date=2023-10-29|website=[[Snopes]]|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wiener-Bronner|first=Danielle|date=2022-12-01|title=Pepsi wants you to drink soda mixed with milk this holiday season|url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/12/01/business/dirty-soda-pepsi/index.html|access-date=2023-10-29|website=[[CNN Business]]|language=en}}</ref> The Pepsi-based version, nicknamed "[[Pilk]]" in the brand's marketing campaign, has been compared to Doodh soda.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://runnermag.ca/2023/02/the-true-meaning-behind-dudh-soda-the-real-pilk/|title=The Runner | the true meaning behind dudh soda, the real "pilk"|website=The Runner|access-date=2024-01-28|author=Sandhu|date=2023-02-03|first=Sukhmani Kaur}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thejuggernaut.com/doodh-soda-origins-pepsi-lindsay-lohan-ad|title=In Defense of Doodh Soda|website=The Juggernaut|access-date=2024-01-28|author=Ahsan|date=2022-12-23|first=Sadaf}}</ref>

== Preparation ==
There are multiple methods of creating doodh soda. One method is pouring boiling milk into a metal bucket submerged and spun in a container of iced water. Once chilled, the milk is mixed with the soda. Other times, vendors mix the drink by pouring between glasses, aerating the mixture.<ref name=":1" /> At home, people create it by filling a glass with equal parts ice, soda, and milk.<ref name=":0" /> Other ingredients are sometimes added in small amounts such as [[Rooh Afza]], fruit syrup, sugar, honey,<ref name=":1" /> or the zest of a lemon or lime.<ref name=":0" />

== In popular culture ==
The drink gained mainstream popualrity due to its mention in the 2025 Indian film ''[[Dhurandhar]]'' by a character named Mohammed Aalam (played by [[Gaurav Gera]]) who rhymed it with a [[jingle]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Desk |first=Trending |date=2026-03-20 |title='Darling dil kyu toda, peelo Aalam soda': Dhurandhar's iconic line made doodh soda a viral drink at theatre stalls |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/new-updates/darling-dil-kyu-toda-peelo-aalam-soda-dhurandhars-iconic-line-made-dhoodh-soda-a-viral-drink-on-theatre-stalls/articleshow/129696627.cms?from=mdr |access-date=2026-04-18 |work=The Economic Times |issn=0013-0389}}</ref>

Tonic water}} }} '''Espresso and tonic''' or '''espresso tonic''' is a [[List of non-alcoholic mixed drinks|non-alcoholic mixed drink]] made by mixing [[espresso]] and [[tonic water]]. First recorded in 2007, the drink became popular in [[Scandinavia]] before spreading to North America, Japan, and around the world. The key ingredients are espresso and tonic water, but other flavourings may be added. == History == Tonic water was patented in 1858 in London{{Cite web |title=Just the tonic: A natural history of tonic water {{!}} Kew |url=https://www.kew.org/read-and-watch/just-the-tonic-history |access-date=2023-12-02 |website=www.kew.org |language=en}} and espresso machines were invented in 1905 in Italy.Morris, Jonathan (2007), [https://www.academia.edu/379110 "The Cappuccino Conquests. The Transnational History of Italian Coffee"], University of Hertfordshire, p.5. However, the earliest record of this drink is from 2007 in [[Oslo]]. There it was mixed by a [[barista]] working with the future founders of the Swedish company Koppi Roasters, [[Anne Lunell]] and Charles Nystrand.{{Cite web |title=Deep Dive: What Is an Espresso Tonic? {{!}} Trade Coffee |url=https://www.drinktrade.com/blog/education/what-is-espresso-tonic |access-date=2023-11-19 |website=www.drinktrade.com |language=en}} Later that year, it was featured on the Koppi Roasters menu in [[Helsingborg]] as Kaffe & Tonic.{{Cite web |date=2023-11-19 |title=Coffee Drinks Stake a Claim at the Bar - The New York Times |website=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/06/17/dining/coffee-drinks-stake-a-claim-at-the-bar.html |access-date=2023-11-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231119014859/https://www.nytimes.com/2015/06/17/dining/coffee-drinks-stake-a-claim-at-the-bar.html |archive-date=2023-11-19 }} Its popularity grew in Scandinavia and by the 2010s, the drink had spread to North American coffee culture as a result of international barista competitions. By 2015, the drink had also spread to Japan.{{Cite web |last=Martin |first=Deborah |date=2023-01-16 |title=What Makes Japan's Sparkling Coffee Unique? |url=https://www.tastingtable.com/1168475/what-makes-japans-sparkling-coffee-unique/ |access-date=2023-11-19 |website=Tasting Table |language=en-US}} The drink has been associated with "barista fashion" by historian [[Wendy Pojmann]].{{Cite journal |last=Pojmann |first=Wendy |date=2020-05-20 |title=Barista Cool: Espresso Fashion Transformed |url=https://zmj.unibo.it/article/view/10567 |journal=ZoneModa Journal |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1S |pages=213–227 |doi=10.6092/issn.2611-0563/10567 |issn=2611-0563}} In 2019, the British coffee chain [[Caffè Nero]] partnered with the beverage company [[Fever-Tree]] to sell two versions of the drink.{{Cite web |last=Woolfson |first=Daniel |title=Fever-Tree partners with Caffè Nero for 'Espresso & Tonic' drinks |url=https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/new-product-development/fever-tree-partners-with-caffe-nero-for-espresso-and-tonic-drinks/592482.article |access-date=2023-11-19 |website=The Grocer |language=en}} == Presentation == [[File:Espresso tonic.jpg|thumb|Espresso tonic, with head ([[Montevideo]], 2023)]] The drink is traditionally created by pouring espresso over iced tonic water, creating a [[layered drink]]. If the tonic is poured onto espresso, a head of foam is created on the drink.{{Cite web |title=We're Calling It Now, the Espresso Tonic Is the Drink of the Summer |url=https://www.foodandwine.com/espresso-tonic-7481464 |access-date=2023-11-19 |website=Food & Wine |language=en}} The drink can also include sugar syrup, a lemon garnish, or other flavours such as cherry,{{Cite web |last=Qureshi |first=Hira |title=Philly baristas are obsessed with espresso tonics — and you should be, too |url=https://www.inquirer.com/food/drink/what-is-an-espresso-tonic-where-to-find-philadelphia-20230621.html |access-date=2023-11-19 |website=Inquirer |date=5 July 2023 |language=en}} lime, or honey.{{Cite web |last=Janzen |first=Emma |date=2021-08-17 |title=Five Takes on the Coffee & Tonic |url=https://imbibemagazine.com/five-takes-on-the-coffee-tonic/ |access-date=2023-11-19 |website=Imbibe Magazine |language=en-US}} It is Japanese baristas who are credited with adding additional flavours to the drink first. Suggestions for serving include using a [[Collins glass]], and with a straw.{{Cite book |last=Alchemist |first=The |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zAfSDwAAQBAJ&dq=espresso+tonic&pg=PT167 |title=The Alchemist Cocktail Book: Master the dark arts of mixology |date=2021-05-06 |publisher=Random House |isbn=978-1-4735-8350-4 |language=en}} ==See also== * {{portal-inline|Coffee}} == References == {{Commons category|Espresso and tonic}} [[Category:Coffee drinks]] [[Category:Coffee in Europe]] [[Category:Norwegian drinks]] [[Category:Non-alcoholic mixed drinks]] [[Category:Food and drink introduced in 2007]]
