'''Milo''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|m|aɪ|l|oʊ}} {{respell|MY|loh}};<ref>{{cite news|last=Khong|first=Rachel|date=6 March 2017|url=https://www.bonappetit.com/story/nestle-milo-malted-chocolate-drink|title=An Ode to Milo, the Malted Chocolate Drink I Grew Up With|work=Bon Appétit|access-date=21 December 2021}}</ref> stylised in [[all caps]] as '''MILO''') is a chocolate-flavoured [[malt]]ed powder product produced by [[Nestlé]], typically mixed with [[milk]], hot water, or both, to produce a [[beverage]]. It was originally developed in Australia by [[Thomas Mayne (inventor)|Thomas Mayne]] (1901–1995) in 1934.

Most commonly sold as a powder in a green can, often depicting various sporting activities like badminton or [[football]], Milo is available as a premixed beverage in some countries and has been subsequently developed into [[Milo (chocolate bar)]], [[breakfast cereal]] and protein [[granola]]. Its composition and taste differ from country to country.

Milo maintains significant popularity in a diverse range of countries throughout the world, particularly in [[Australasia]], Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

== History ==
[[File:1940s Nestlé Milo tin.jpg|thumb|150px|1940s Milo can]]
In 1934, Australian [[industrial chemist]] and inventor Thomas Mayne, who was working at Nestlé, developed "Milo"<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article118190410 |title=60 years on and Milo is still a sweet success |newspaper=[[The Canberra Times]] |volume=69 |issue=21,636 |location=Australian Capital Territory, Australia |date=12 July 1994 |access-date=28 April 2021 |page=3 |via=National Library of Australia}} </ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nestle.com.au/aboutus/history |title= History |website=Nestle |access-date=24 November 2017}}</ref> and launched it at the [[Sydney Royal Easter Show]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.milo.com.au/about/ |title=About Milo |access-date=2015-05-11 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518095738/http://www.milo.com.au/about/ |archive-date=18 May 2015 |df=dmy-all }}</ref> Mayne came up with his formula for Milo combining [[malt]] extract (made from malted barley), full cream [[milk powder]], [[Cocoa solids|cocoa]], sugar, mineral salts, iron and [[vitamin]]s A, D and B1, in an attempt "to develop a completely balanced food drink which contained all the necessary [[protein]]s and [[Mineral (nutrient)|minerals]]".<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article118136319 |title=Milo: 60 years of a winning formula |newspaper=[[The Canberra Times]] |volume=70 |issue=21,693 |location=Australian Capital Territory, Australia |date=7 September 1994 |access-date=28 April 2021 |page=26 |via=National Library of Australia}} </ref> It was intended to help children to obtain enough [[nutrient]]s in their diet.<ref name=100yearsabc>{{cite web | last=Johnson | first=Keely | title=Smithtown Milo factory celebrates 100 years of sweet success | website=ABC News |publisher=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] | date=30 May 2021 | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2021-05-30/nestle-milo-factory-in-smithtown-turns-100/100160818 | access-date=30 May 2021}}</ref>

Nestlé, which had taken ownership of a milk-processing plant in [[Smithtown, New South Wales|Smithtown]], [[New South Wales]], in 1921, started producing the product not long after the show.<ref name=100yearsabc/> The name was derived from the famous [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greek]] athlete [[Milo of Croton]], after his legendary strength.<ref name=":0">[https://milo.com.au/all-about-milo All about Milo].</ref> The product was even noted as "tonic food".<ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article58731596 |title=Nestles Milk Company |newspaper=[[Sunday Times (Perth)]] |issue=1915 |location=Western Australia |date=7 October 1934 |access-date=28 April 2021 |page=12 (First Section) |via=National Library of Australia}} </ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article75718771 |title=Nestle's exhibits at the show |newspaper=Mirror |volume=13 |issue=702 |location=Western Australia |date=12 October 1935 |access-date=28 April 2021 |page=23 |via=National Library of Australia}} </ref>

== Manufacture ==
[[File:Food snacks Nestle Milo refill pack and milo.jpg|thumb|Milo powder (Australian form)]]
Milo is made by evaporating the water content from a thick syrup at reduced pressure, using a [[Vacuum drying|vacuum dryer]] to reduce the mix to [[Granularity|granular ]]form.<ref>{{cite book | last=Higman | first=B.W. | title=How Food Made History | publisher=Wiley | year=2011 | isbn=978-1-4443-4465-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YIUoz98yMvgC&pg=RA1-PA1889 | access-date=November 24, 2017 | page=1889}}</ref> The thick opaque syrup is obtained from malted [[wheat]] or [[barley]] sourced from companies that produce these raw products.<ref>{{cite book | last=Brewers' Society (London | first=England) | title=Brewing Review | publisher=Brewing Publications. | issue=v. 77, no. 2 | year=1963 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dFMEAQAAIAAJ | access-date=November 24, 2017 | page=416}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Lim | first=T.K. | title=Edible Medicinal And Non-Medicinal Plants: Volume 5, Fruits | publisher=Springer Netherlands | year=2013 | isbn=978-94-007-5653-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_ZZEAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA27 | access-date=November 24, 2017 | page=27}}</ref>

Milo's composition and taste differ in some countries due to logistics limitations and personal preferences among different regions.

{{as of|2021}}, the Smithtown factory, which produces the product for Australia and New Zealand, produces more than 13,000 tonnes of Milo a year.<ref name="100yearsabc" /> Nestlé Singapore states that Milo is produced locally at its factory in [[Jurong]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Milo sold in Singapore is made here, no counterfeit problems, say Nestle and retailers |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/milo-sold-in-singapore-is-made-here-no-counterfeit-problems-say-nestle-and-retailers |website=The Straits Times |access-date=5 November 2021 |language=en |date=16 March 2015|author1=Chew Hui Min|author2=Jalelah Abu Baker|author3=Lim Yi Han|author-first4=Jessica|author-last4=Lim}}</ref> Milo in [[Japan]] is manufactured using ingredients imported from Singapore.<ref name="MOJPSG">{{cite web |author=Guan Zhen Tan |date=December 8, 2020 |title=Japan to stop selling Milo until March 2021 after viral tweet leads to high demand |url=https://mothership.sg/2020/12/japan-milo/ |access-date=November 4, 2021 |website=mothership.sg}}</ref><ref name="CAMPSG">{{cite web |author=Ed |date=December 9, 2020 |title=Japan suspends sale of Milo due to shortage of ingredients from Singapore |url=https://www.campus.sg/japan-suspends-sale-of-milo-due-to-shortage-of-ingredients-from-singapore-campus-sg/ |access-date=November 4, 2021 |website=campus.sg}}</ref><ref name="MAINJP">{{cite news |author=Mainichi Japan |date=December 9, 2020 |title=Japan sales of Milo malt drink to be halted over difficulty obtaining imported ingredients |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20201208/p2a/00m/0bu/022000c |access-date=November 4, 2021 |newspaper=Mainichi Daily News}}</ref>

== Nutritional information ==
The recipe for the standard product has remained almost exactly the same since its creation in 1934, the only variation being in the added [[Mineral (nutrient)|minerals]] and vitamins.

Standard Milo consists of four main ingredients: malted barley, milk powder, sugar and cocoa.<ref>{{cite web |website=Milo |url=https://milo.com.au/products/powders/milo-powder#ingredients |title=What's in Milo? |access-date=30 May 2021}}</ref> It contains 1,680 [[Kilojoules|kJ]] (402 [[kilocalories]]) in every 100 [[Gram|g]] of the powder, mostly from [[carbohydrates]]. Carbohydrates can be used for [[Food energy|energy]] by the body, which is the basis of Milo being marketed as an [[energy drink]]. Most of the carbohydrate content is sugar. The New Zealand version of Milo is 46 percent sugar.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.milo.co.nz/milo-products/milo-powders-liquids/milo |title=MILO® – MILO New Zealand |website=www.milo.co.nz |access-date=24 August 2018}}</ref>

Milo dissolved in water has a [[glycemic index]] (GI) of 55.<ref>{{cite web |title=Glycemic Index for Milo (Nestlé, Australia) dissolved in water |url=http://www.dietandfitnesstoday.com/glycemicIndexDetails.php?id=71 |work=Diet & Fitness Today |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref> However, milk has a much lower GI of 30 to 33, so mixing a very small amount of Milo into a mug of milk yields an overall GI closer to 33, whereas adding a lot of Milo into a mug of milk, yields an overall GI that is closer to 55.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-06-12 |title=Shocking & Fun Facts You Should Know About Milo (Drink) |url=https://www.foodsng.com/shocking-fun-facts-you-should-know-about-milo-drink/ |access-date=2021-01-22 |website=FoodsNG |language=en-US}}</ref>

Milo is high in [[calcium]], iron and the vitamins B<sub>1</sub>, B<sub>2</sub>, B<sub>6</sub>, B<sub>12</sub>. Milo is advertised as containing "Actigen-E" which is Nestlé's trademarked name for the vitamins in the Milo recipe.<ref>{{cite web |title=What is Actigen-E? |url=http://milkpowd.blogspot.com.au/2008/07/what-is-actigen-e.html |date= 22 July 2008 |website=Milkpowder is too Danger |access-date=15 August 2013}}</ref> It also contains some [[theobromine]], a [[xanthine]] alkaloid similar to [[caffeine]], which is present in the cocoa used in the product.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.biomedsearch.com/nih/Caffeine-theobromine-levels-in-selected/10798344.html |title=Caffeine and theobromine levels in selected Nigerian beverages |website=BioMedSearch |access-date=1 February 2015 |archive-date=13 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161013215750/http://www.biomedsearch.com/nih/Caffeine-theobromine-levels-in-selected/10798344.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | author=William Gervase Clarence-Smith| title=Cocoa and Chocolate, 1765–1914 | year=2000 | publisher=Routledge | location=London | pages=10, 31 | isbn = 0-415-21576-5 }}</ref>

A study conducted in Malaysia by the 'Nutrition Society of Malaysia' suggested that Milo and similar products made children who consumed them "more likely to be physically active and spend less time in front of a computer or television".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=b. Jan Mohamed |first1=Hamid Jan |last2=Loy |first2=S. L. |last3=Mohd Taib |first3=Mohd Nasir |last4=A Karim |first4=Norimah |last5=Tan |first5=S. Y. |last6=Appukutty |first6=M. |last7=Abdul Razak |first7=Nurliyana |last8=Thielecke |first8=F. |last9=Hopkins |first9=S. |last10=Ong |first10=M. K. |last11=Ning |first11=C. |last12=Tee |first12=E. S. |date=2015-12-30 |title=Characteristics associated with the consumption of malted drinks among Malaysian primary school children: findings from the MyBreakfast study |journal=BMC Public Health |volume=15 |article-number=1322 |doi=10.1186/s12889-015-2666-5 |doi-access=free |issn=1471-2458 |pmc=4697324 |pmid=26718818}}</ref> A 2017 ''[[New York Times]]'' article found that Nestlé had been financing the society and vetting the articles before publication, leading to questions of scientific impartiality.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Fuller |first1=Thomas |last2=O'Connor |first2=Anahad |last3=Richtel |first3=Matt |date=2017-12-23 |title=In Asia's Fattest Country, Nutritionists Take Money From Food Giants |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/12/23/health/obesity-malaysia-nestle.html |access-date=2021-04-24 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-02-06 |title=Here's All You Need to Know About The Viral Milo Sugar Controversy |url=https://worldofbuzz.com/heres-need-know-viral-milo-sugar-controversy/ |access-date=2021-04-24 |website=World of Buzz |language=en-US}}</ref> The high concentration of sugar, and the presence of [[maltodextrin]], also raised whether the product should be marketed as a health product.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hong |first=Tan Heng |date=2018-03-03 |title=Milo drops health rating following pressure from health groups |url=https://www.minimeinsights.com/2018/03/03/13102/ |access-date=2021-04-24 |website=Mini Me Insights |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Versions ==
Since 2017, Nestle Philippines has produced Milo using its "protomalt" formulation.<ref name="Reuters 2016">{{cite web |author=Reuters Staff |date=August 2, 2016 |title=Nestle Philippines invests $43 mln in new Milo chocolate drink plant |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/nestle-philippines/nestle-philippines-invests-43-mln-in-new-milo-chocolate-drink-plant-idUSL3N1AJ126 |access-date=November 24, 2017 |website=U.S.}}</ref><ref name="Lacson 2017">{{cite web |author=Lacson, Nonoy E. |date=July 23, 2017 |title=ARMM wants to supply Nestlé plant with cassava from Marawi and Lanao |url=https://news.mb.com.ph/2017/07/23/armm-wants-to-supply-nestle-plant-with-cassava-from-marawi-and-lanao |access-date=November 24, 2017 |website=Manila Bulletin News |archive-date=23 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200223130640/https://news.mb.com.ph/2017/07/23/armm-wants-to-supply-nestle-plant-with-cassava-from-marawi-and-lanao/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> The protomalt is composed of carbohydrates derived from barley and [[cassava]].<ref name="Reuters 2016" /><ref name="Lacson 2017" />

In Australia, a version of Milo called Milo B-Smart was released in 2008, which had a finer texture, added B vitamins and [[iodine]], and a different taste from the original Milo formula, and was marketed as a health food for children.<ref>{{cite web |date=13 August 2008 |title=Nestlé Urges Kids to B-Smart |url=http://www.can-news.com.au/detail.asp?sectionID=1&rowID=590 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161112144333/http://www.can-news.com.au/detail.asp?sectionID=1&rowID=590 |archive-date=12 November 2016 |access-date=12 November 2016 |website=Can and Aerosol News}}</ref> However, {{as of|lc=yes|2021}}, this product is no longer available.<ref name="milopowders">{{cite web |title=Powders |url=https://milo.com.au/products/powders |access-date=30 May 2021 |website=MILO Australia}}</ref> A higher malt content form also existed in Australia and was marketed in brown and maroon coloured cans. Nestlé stopped advertising this higher malt form on their Australian products website sometime between March and April 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-04-11 |title=MILO's Extensive Range of Delicious Products - MILO {{!}} MILO |url=http://www.milo.com.au/products/ |access-date=2024-07-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150411090629/http://www.milo.com.au/products/ |archive-date=11 April 2015 }}</ref>

{{as of|2021}}, three other varieties are manufactured at the Australian plant: high protein, reduced sugar and a [[plant-based]] version.<ref name="100yearsabc" />

As of 2021, Nestlé has launched dairy-free plant-based versions of Milo and other drinks under the brand. The new version of these drinks contain almond and soy milk, the two core ingredients{{snd}} cocoa and malt{{snd}} remain the same.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cornall |first=Jim |date=8 April 2021 |title=Nestlé launches dairy free Milo in Asia |url=https://www.dairyreporter.com/Article/2021/04/08/Nestle-launches-dairy-free-Milo-in-Asia |access-date=24 July 2021 |website=Dairy Reporter}}</ref>

==Consumption==
Milo is typically mixed with milk, hot water, or both, to produce a [[beverage]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Knowles |first1=Sarah |date=13 July 2015 |title=Nestle's new Milo recipe tested by a dietitian |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff.co.nz]] |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/life-style/food-wine/drinks/70189262/nestles-new-milo-recipe-tested-by-a-dietitian |access-date=12 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170728133230/https://www.stuff.co.nz/life-style/food-wine/drinks/70189262/nestles-new-milo-recipe-tested-by-a-dietitian |archive-date=28 July 2017}}</ref>

===Australia and New Zealand===
Traditionally in Australia and New Zealand, Milo is served mixed with either hot or cold milk, or sprinkled on top.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-07-16|title='Don't understand': Fitzy's surprise over Milo debate result| url=https://www.news.com.au/lifestyle/food/drinks/should-you-drink-milo-hot-or-cold-poll-settles-infamous-debate/news-story/2b6c328910a49548b0e97074c289f460|access-date=2020-09-07|website=NewsComAu|language=en}}</ref>

===Latin America===
Milo is very popular in all Latin American countries, especially in [[Colombia]], where people often think of it as a local product, and it is not only consumed with milk, but also in drinks with fruits, such as bananas and strawberries, even in drinks with oatmeal.<ref>{{Cite web |title='Milo te da energía, la meta la pones tú': la receta exitosa de esta marca icónica, que cumple 80 años en Colombia |url=https://www.elcolombiano.com/negocios/bebida-milo-cumple-80-anos-como-obtuvo-su-exito-CH25554215 |access-date=2025-06-22 |website=www.elcolombiano.com |date=4 October 2024 |language=es-419}}</ref>

===Asia===
[[File:Iced Milo.jpg|thumb|150px|Iced Milo aka "Milo Ais", "Milo Peng", or "Es Milo". A popular drink in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and South American countries like Colombia]]
Milo manufactured outside Australia is customised for local methods of preparation. In [[Malaysia]], as well as [[Brunei]] and some other parts of Asia, Milo with ice added is known as "Iced Milo", "Milo Ais" in [[Malay language|Malay]], or "Es Milo" in [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]] (alternatively, "bing" or "peng", meaning ice in [[Cantonese]] and [[Hokkien]] respectively). Iced Milo is even available at fast food restaurants such as [[KFC]] and [[McDonald's]] in certain countries within southeast Asia.<ref>{{cite web|title=Nutrition Information: Desserts & Beverages|url=http://www.kfc.com.my/menu/desserts-beverages|work=Kentucky Fried Chicken|access-date=10 November 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161111061148/http://www.kfc.com.my/menu/desserts-beverages/|archive-date=11 November 2016|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Nutrition Information: Beverages|url=http://www.mcdonalds.com.my/ourfood/nutritions_beverages.asp|work=McDonald's|access-date=15 August 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130220213641/http://www.mcdonalds.com.my/ourfood/nutritions_beverages.asp|archive-date=20 February 2013|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref>[http://www.mcdonalds.com.sg/eatsmart_nutriinfo.html] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130319063942/http://www.mcdonalds.com.sg/eatsmart_nutriinfo.html|date=19 March 2013}}</ref>

In [[Malaysia]], Milo is also served locally in [[kopitiam]]s and [[mamak stall]]s in versions such as "[[Milo Dinosaur]]" (a cup of Milo with an extra heaped spoonfuls worth of undissolved Milo powder added on top of it), "Milo [[Godzilla]]" (a cup of Milo with ice cream and/or topped with whipped cream), "Neslo" (combined with [[Nescafé]] powdered coffee), and "Milo Mangkuk" (Iced Milo that is served with shaved ice inside a plastic bowl). The Milo powder is also usually used in the making of [[Batik cake]]. In [[Hong Kong]], Milo is served in [[Cha chaan teng]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kong Sihk Tong {{!}} Eat the World NYC|url=http://www.eattheworldnyc.com/2019/05/kong-sihk-tong.html|website=www.eattheworldnyc.com|access-date=2020-05-27}}</ref>

In [[Malaysia]], Milo is also sometimes sprinkled on ice cream or breakfast cereals, or mixed with milk into a paste and spread on bread.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pinch|first1=Annika|url=https://cornellsun.com/2017/03/22/from-roti-canai-to-roti-milo-malaysia-night-2017/#:~:text=Roti%20Milo%20is%20a%20chocolate,the%20bread%20looked%20pretty%20unappealing.|title=From Roti Canai to Roti Milo: Malaysia Night 2017|accessdate=20 August 2020|website=Cornell Sun|date=22 March 2017 }}</ref> Milo can be used as an ingredient in [[roti canai]], where it is usually called "roti Milo".<ref>{{cite web|title=Food Tour Malaysia|url=http://www.tripadvisor.com/LocationPhotoDirectLink-g298570-d1955672-i62785777-Food_Tour_Malaysia-Kuala_Lumpur_Wilayah_Persekutuan.html|publisher=Trip Advisor|accessdate=17 April 2015}}</ref>

At the present time {{when|date=February 2025}}, [[Malaysia]] has the world's highest per capita consumption of Milo, [[Singapore]] coming second.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Jonas|first=Patrick|date=9 January 2009|title=Nestled in Nicely|work=Tabla|url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Page/tabla20090109-1.1.6?ST=1&AT=advanced&K=badminton&KA=badminton&DF=23/12/1979&DT=&NPT=&L=&CTA=&P=463|access-date=24 July 2021}}</ref>

In Malaysia milo's ingredients consist of: Cereal Grains [Wholegrain Wheat (gluten) (35.2%), Wheat Flour (gluten), Corn Semolina], Sugar, Extract of Malt Barley (gluten) and Starch, Fat-Reduced Cocoa Powder, Minerals (Calcium Carbonate, Reduced Iron), Palm Oil, Skimmed Milk Powder (Cow's Milk), Iodized Salt (Sodium Chloride, Potassium Iodate), Emulsifier (Soya Lecithin E322), Natural Flavourings, Antioxidant (Tocopherols), Vitamins (B3, B5, B6, B2, B9).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Milo Ingredients |url=https://www.nestle-cereals.com/my/my-en/cereals/milo}}</ref>

== Marketing ==
[[File:Kota-Kinabalu Sabah Borneo-International-Marathon-2015-95.jpg|thumb|Milo being served at an athletics event]]
Apart from Australia, Milo is popular in many countries and regions, including [[New Zealand]], [[Malaysia]], [[Singapore]], [[Brunei]], [[Pakistan]], [[Philippines]], [[Vietnam]], [[India]], [[Indonesia]], [[Hong Kong]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[Maldives]], [[Thailand]], [[Japan]], [[Jamaica]], [[Trinidad and Tobago]], [[Guyana]], [[Chile]], [[Colombia]], and countries in [[Southern Africa]], [[Central Africa]], [[East Africa]], [[West Africa]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.news.com.au/lifestyle/food/things-you-never-knew-about-milo/news-story/00f15276bdcb5ab5697b2e0edb8700ea |title=10 things you never knew about MILO |date=2014-04-15 |website=NewsComAu |language=en |access-date=2020-03-30}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.beveragedaily.com/Article/2014/10/13/Nestle-backs-beverage-belief-in-Vietnam-with-36m-Milo-investment |title=Nestle backs beverage 'belief' in Vietnam with $36m Milo investment |work=beveragedaily.com |access-date=2018-08-08 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/milo-under-the-spotlight-after-fake-products-seized-in-malaysia-10-facts-about-milo |title=Milo under the spotlight after fake products seized in Malaysia: 10 facts about Milo |last=migration |date=2015-03-16 |work=The Straits Times |access-date=2018-08-08 |language=en}}</ref> In Australia and most other countries, the packaging is a green can and depicts people playing various sports. 

In Australia, the MILO in2CRICKET and MILO T20 Blast programs, operated in most areas by volunteers, teach children age 5–12 how to play the game of [[cricket]]. In the 2016–2017 season, over 78,000 children participated in the programs.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cricket Australia and Milo celebrate 25 years of junior cricket |date=17 September 2017 |url=https://www.nestle.com.au/en/media/newsandfeatures/cricket-australia-and-milo-celebrate-25-years-of-junior-cricket |publisher=Nestle}}</ref>

Milo is very popular in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore, where the brand name is synonymous with chocolate flavoured drinks: Milo has a 90% market share in Malaysia,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nestle.com/Resource.axd?Id=9EE4B633-5B80-4CC6-9CF1-F61EFD87A1CA |title=Nestlé: Our transformational opportunity |access-date=3 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101205175937/http://www.nestle.com/Resource.axd?Id=9EE4B633-5B80-4CC6-9CF1-F61EFD87A1CA |archive-date=5 December 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and [[Malaysians]] were said to be the world's largest consumers of Milo.<ref>{{cite news |location=[[Petaling Jaya]] |title=Shahrir urges restaurants to lower price of Milo |url=http://www.thestar.com.my/story.aspx?file=%2f2009%2f2%2f24%2fnation%2f3333128&sec=nation%3a |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130815073739/http://www.thestar.com.my/story.aspx?file=/2009/2/24/nation/3333128&sec=nation: |url-status=dead |archive-date=15 August 2013 |access-date=15 August 2013 |newspaper=The Star Online |date=24 February 2009 }}</ref> In Malaysia and Singapore, specialised trucks or vans, affectionately called Milo vans, serving up to three thousand cups of the drink are commonly seen at sports and community events and schools.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Why does Milo from Milo vans taste different? Is there really a secret recipe? We tried to find out |url=https://cnalifestyle.channelnewsasia.com/dining/why-does-milo-van-milo-taste-different-better-384106 |access-date=2024-02-03 |website=CNA Lifestyle |language=en}}</ref> 

In Peru, during the 1970s [[Juan Velasco Alvarado|military dictatorship]], Milo labels displayed Peruvian motifs, such as photos and pictures of Peruvian towns, history, crops, fruits, animals, plants,<ref>{{cite web|author=Arkivperu |url=http://www.arkivperu.com/blog/?p=337 |title="Zoología botánica" de Milo (1973) | |publisher=Arkivperu.com |date=5 August 2013 |access-date=11 September 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.arkivperu.com/zoologia-botanica-de-milo-1976/|title="Zoología botánica" de Milo (1973)|date=2 December 2007|publisher=Arkivperu|access-date=9 August 2013}}</ref> as an educational aid. After 1980, when the military left power, sports predominated on the labels.

Milo is sold by Nestlé in Canada at all major food retailers. Although Milo has been available since the 1970s, a Canadian-specific flavour launched within the last decade{{When|date=December 2019}} that dissolves more quickly but maintains the sweet malt flavour profile. It competes with the British brand [[Ovaltine]].{{cn|date=May 2021}}

Aside from the International section of specific grocery stores and certain Asian grocery stores, Nestlé does not market Milo in the United States. In 2017 Colombian-manufactured Milo started appearing on shelves in supermarkets in the United States such as [[Walmart]].{{cn|date=May 2021}}

It can also be found in the United Kingdom in some [[Sainsbury's]] and [[Tesco]] supermarkets, which import it from Kenya and South Africa. [[Asian supermarket|Asian food specialists]] also stock it. Ovaltine is more popular with UK consumers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fung |first=Lynn |date=2012-01-12 |title=A History of Malted Milk |url=https://www.tatlerasia.com/dining/digest/a-history-of-malted-milk |access-date=2021-01-22 |website=Tatler Hong Kong}}</ref>

In Ireland, it can be found in many Asian or African stores. Typically they will stock Kenyan or Filipino Milo.

In China, it is commonly sold in Western supermarkets, but also smaller convenience stores. Usually packaged in a 240gram flexible foil pouch, single-drink packets can also be purchased. The Milo itself contains more milk solids than the Australian Milo.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Milo minus the milk |url=https://www.dairyreporter.com/Article/2020/03/12/Milo-minus-the-milk |website=dairyreporter.com |date=12 March 2020 |language=en-GB |access-date=2020-05-27}}</ref>

In the past, it was available in Portugal and Brazil. Nestlé Brazil discontinued production of Milo in Brazil, to focus on the much-popular domestic brands [[Nescau]] and [[Nesquik]]. The Chilean version of Milo is still in production and is identical in taste and texture to the one that was once produced in Brazil.{{cn|date=May 2021}}

In May 2013, more than 20 years out of the Portuguese market, Nestlé reintroduced the brand, aiming at the high-end market.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nestle.pt/SaboreiaaVida/Noticias/Pages/MILOregressa20anosdepois.aspx |title=Milo reintroduced |access-date=2013-06-23 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131023160226/http://www.nestle.pt/SaboreiaaVida/Noticias/Pages/MILOregressa20anosdepois.aspx |archive-date=23 October 2013 |df=dmy-all }}</ref>

In the Philippines, Nestlé partnered with the [[Department of Education (Philippines)|Department of Education]] in 2017, in a marketing response to the "energy gap" within school-aged children whose athletic and academic performance were impacted due to low energy. This raised the ethical question of advertising to children.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Diyco|first=Nanette Franco|title=Milo scores big on activation and false advocacy|work=BWorld News|url=https://www.bworldonline.com/milo-scores-big-on-activation-and-advocacy/|access-date=April 2, 2021}}</ref>

Prairie oyster:
{{Short description|Drink with a raw egg and sauce}}
{{about||the music group|Prairie Oyster|the food euphemism|Rocky Mountain oysters}}
{{more citations needed|date=December 2016}}
[[File:Prairie_Oyster_.jpg|thumb|A simple prairie oyster in a glass.]]
{{wikt | prairie oyster}}

A '''prairie oyster''' (sometimes also '''prairie cocktail'''), a traditional beverage, consists of a raw egg (often [[yolk]] alone), [[Worcestershire sauce]], vinegar and/or hot sauce, salt, and ground black pepper. A small amount of tomato juice is sometimes added, reminiscent of a [[Bloody Mary (cocktail)|Bloody Mary]]. Occasionally a spirit such as brandy, vodka, or gin is also included, transforming the drink into a [[hair of the dog]]. The egg is broken into a glass so as not to break the yolk. The mixture is quickly swallowed.

The unbroken yolk gives the drink a texture similar to that of an [[oyster]]. An early account from 1859 associates the recipe with the [[prairie]]s of "the [[Great Plains | Plains]]" and with "the Rocky Mountains"<ref>
{{oed | prairie oyster}}
</ref>
of western North America.

This mixture has a reputation as a classic traditional remedy for [[hangover]]s, and has featured in media for many years.

== Supposed hangover remedy properties ==
{{See also|Hair of the dog}}
Though considered a traditional hangover remedy, the prairie oyster has not been scientifically proven to treat hangover symptoms. Headache experts say that a prairie oyster will not work as a remedy for a hangover.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Health/TreatingPain/called-hangover-cures-helps-hurts/story?id=9457713#.UOHt-m97vg8 |website=ABC News |last=Cox |first=Lauren |title=Hangover 'Cures': What Helps and What Hurts |date= December 31, 2009 |accessdate=May 26, 2020}}</ref>

It has been suggested that the raw egg in a prairie oyster may alleviate the symptoms of a hangover since eggs contain cysteine, an amino acid which helps the body break down acetaldehyde, a by-product of processing alcohol.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.eater.com/drinks/2016/3/7/11169320/prairie-oyster-cocktail-television-media-film |website=Eater |title=The Prairie Oyster: A Survey of 100 Years in Pop Culture |last=Stevens |first=Ashlie |date=March 7, 2016 |accessdate=May 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://nowtoronto.com/news/hangover-cure-4-the-prairie-oyster/ |website=Now Toronto |title=Hangover cure #4: The Prairie Oyster  |date=November 17, 2012 |accessdate=May 26, 2020}}</ref> However, there is no reliable evidence showing that consuming foods with this amino acid relieves hangover symptoms.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20181224-no-you-cant-eat-your-way-out-of-a-hangover |website=BBC Future |publisher=BBC |last=Greenwood |first=Veronique |title=No, you can't eat your way out of a hangover |date= December 31, 2018 |accessdate=May 26, 2020}}</ref>

It has also been suggested that a prairie oyster may seem to relieve hangover symptoms by acting as a distraction and a placebo.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20151215-whats-the-secret-to-avoiding-hangovers |website=BBC Future |publisher=BBC |title=What's the secret to dodging hangovers? |last=Robson |first=David |date=December 15, 2015  |accessdate=May 26, 2020}}</ref>

== In popular culture ==
The prairie oyster has appeared in popular media since the early 20th century. Its most notable appearance is in [[P. G. Wodehouse]]'s [[Jeeves]] novels. It first appeared in the 1916 short story "[[Jeeves Takes Charge]]", where Jeeves cures [[Bertie Wooster]]'s hangover with his version of a prairie oyster.<ref>{{cite book|last=Cawthorne |first=Nigel |authorlink=Nigel Cawthorne |title=A Brief Guide to Jeeves and Wooster |location=London |publisher=Constable & Robinson |date=2013 |page=47| isbn=978-1-78033-824-8}}</ref> The drink is not named in the story but it fits the description of a prairie oyster. As Jeeves says, "It is a little preparation of my own invention. It is the Worcester Sauce that gives it its colour. The raw egg makes it nutritious. The red pepper gives it its bite."<ref>{{cite book|last=Wodehouse|first=P. G.|title=Come On, Jeeves|page=13|chapter=Jeeves Takes Charge|publisher=Arrow Books|isbn=9780099513698|year=2008|orig-year=1925|edition=Reprinted}}</ref> Jeeves also serves this hangover cure in other stories. It is very effective, and Bertie suspects that there is more to the drink than the ingredients mentioned by Jeeves.<ref>{{cite book|last=Wodehouse|first=P. G.|title=Right Ho, Jeeves|page=48|chapter=Chapter 5|publisher=Arrow Books|orig-year=1934|year=2008|isbn=9780099513742|edition=Reprinted}} Bertie narrates: "I have had occasion, I fancy, to speak before now of these pick-me-ups of Jeeves's [...] What they consist of, I couldn't tell you. He says some kind of sauce, the yolk of a raw egg and a dash of red pepper, but nothing will convince me that the thing doesn't go much deeper than that."</ref>

[[Gary Cooper]]'s character Longfellow Deeds is served a prairie oyster in the 1935 film ''[[Mr. Deeds Goes to Town]]'' after "a binge" (not "a bender") the night before with reporter Babe Bennett ([[Jean Arthur]]).<!--as seen on-screen, Primary Source-->

[[Sally Bowles]] in the 1939 novel ''[[Goodbye to Berlin]]'' (the inspiration for the 1966 [[Musical theatre|musical]] [[Cabaret (musical)|''Cabaret'']] and the [[Cabaret (1972 film)|1972 film of the same name]]) appears to survive almost exclusively on prairie oysters.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Isherwood |first=Christopher |title=Goodbye to Berlin |date=2012 |publisher=New Directions |isbn=978-0-8112-2024-8 |location=New York}}</ref>

The 1998 anime [[Cowboy Bebop]] also features an episode called Heavy Metal Queen where the main character Spike Spiegel tries to cure his hangover with a prairie oyster.

'''Mate''' ({{IPAc-en|'|m|ɑː|t|eɪ}} {{respell|MAH-tay}}; Spanish: {{lang|es|mate}} {{IPA|es|ˈmate|}}, Brazilian Portuguese: {{IPA|pt|ˈmatʃi|}}) is a traditional Argentine, Paraguayan, Uruguayan and Brazilian [[caffeine]]-rich infused [[herbal drink]]. It is also known as '''{{lang|pt|chimarrão}}'''{{efn|Portuguese: {{IPA|pt|ʃimɐˈʁɐ̃w|}}}} in Portuguese, '''{{lang|es|cimarrón}}'''{{efn|Spanish: {{IPA|es|simaˈron|}}}} in Spanish, and '''{{lang|gn|ka'ay}}''' in [[Guarani language|Guarani]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3tYkDwAAQBAJ&dq=ka'ay+mate&pg=PA183 |title=Guarani Linguistics in the 21st Century |date=2017-05-15 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-32257-8 |language=en}}</ref> It is made by soaking dried [[yerba mate]] (''Ilex paraguariensis'') leaves in hot water and is traditionally served with a metal straw ({{lang|es|[[bombilla]]}}) in a container typically made from a [[calabash gourd]] (also called the {{lang|es|mate}}), from water-resistant hardwoods such as [[Lapacho]] or [[Palo Santo]],{{citation needed|reason=Palo Santo is an aromatic wood, wouldn't work for mate|date=October 2025}} and also made from a cattle horn ({{lang|es|guampa}}) in some areas. A very similar preparation, known as {{lang|es|[[mate cocido]]}}, removes some of the plant material and sometimes comes in tea bags. Today, mate is also sold commercially in tea bags and as bottled [[iced tea]].

Mate has been originally consumed by the [[Guaraní people|Guaraní]] and [[Tupi people|Tupi]] peoples native to Paraguay, north-east of Argentina and South of Brazil. After European colonization, it was spread across the [[Southern Cone]] countries, namely [[Paraguay]], [[Argentina]], [[Uruguay]] and [[Chile]], but it is also consumed in the [[South Region, Brazil|South of Brazil]] and the Bolivian [[Gran Chaco|Chaco]]. Mate is the [[List of national drinks|national beverage]] of Argentina,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.infoleg.gob.ar/infolegInternet/anexos/215000-219999/218040/norma.htm |title=Ley 26.871 - Declárase al Mate como infusión nacional |work=InfoLEG |publisher=[[Minister of Economy (Argentina)|Argentinean Ministry of Economy]] |access-date=7 October 2010 |language=es }}</ref> Paraguay and Uruguay. In Chile, mate is predominantly consumed in the [[Central Chile|central]] and [[Southern Chile|southern]] regions. Mate is also popular in [[Lebanon]], [[Syria]], [[Israel]] — where it was brought by immigrants from Argentina.<ref name="donald">{{cite book |title=Medical Toxicology of Drug Abuse: Synthesized Chemicals and Psychoactive Plants |last=Barceloux |first=Donald |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-1-11810-605-1 |date=3 February 2012 }}</ref><ref name="Middle East Online">{{cite web |url=http://www.middle-east-online.com/english/?id=64763 |title=South American 'mate' tea a long-time Lebanese hit |work=Middle East Online |access-date=11 March 2014 |archive-date=12 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140312014840/http://www.middle-east-online.com/english/?id=64763 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Accessories ==
The metal straw is known as a {{lang|es|[[bombilla]]}} or {{lang|es|bomba}} and is traditionally made of [[silver]]. Modern straws are typically made of [[nickel silver]], [[stainless steel]], or hollow-stemmed [[Cane (grass)|cane]]. The {{lang|es|bombilla}} functions both as a straw and as a [[sieve]]. The submerged end is flared, with small holes or slots that allow the brewed liquid in, but block the chunky yerba mate leaves that make up much of the mixture. A modern {{lang|es|bombilla}} design uses a straight tube with holes or a spring sleeve to act as a sieve.<ref>{{cite news|last=Goodfriend|first=Anne|date=2 March 2006|title=Yerba maté: The accent is on popular health drink|page=1|work=USA Today|url=https://www.usatoday.com/travel/destinations/2006-03-02-yerba-mate_x.htm|access-date=29 May 2011}}</ref>

The container the {{lang|es|mate}} is served in is also known as {{lang|es|mate}}.<ref group="lower-alpha">Known as {{lang|es|mate}} or a {{lang|es|guampa}} in Spanish, or {{lang|pt|cuia}} or {{lang|pt|cabaça}} in Brazil.</ref> It is commonly made from [[calabash gourd]] but may also be made out of other materials.

== History ==
{{main|History of yerba mate}}
[[File:Schmidtmeyer, Peter & Scharf, G - Tertulia & Mate Party -JCB Library f1.2 (cropped).jpg|thumb|[[Tertulia]] and Mate party in [[Santiago de Chile]], in 1821, by [[George Johann Scharf|Scharf]] and Schmidtmeyer. [[John Carter Brown Library]].<ref>{{cite book|author1=Peter Schmidtmeyer |author2=[[George Johann Scharf]]|publisher=[[Daler-Rowney|Rowney & Forster]]|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EzcB9j2y-XIC|title=Travels Into Chile, Over the Andes, in the Years 1820 and 1821: With Some Sketches of the Productions and Agriculture; Mines and Metallurgy; Inhabitants, History, and Other Features, of America; Particularly of Chile, and Arauco|year=1821|page=266}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://americana.jcblibrary.org/search/object/jcbcap-ljcb-1-1-4604-7270004/|website=[[John Carter Brown Library]] website|year=1821|title=Tertulia and Mate Party}}</ref>]]
[[File:Dr francia.JPG|right|thumb|upright=1.02|Lithograph of [[José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia]], a 19th-century ruler of Paraguay, with a {{lang|es|mate}} and its {{lang|es|bombilla}} (a straw)]]

Mate was first consumed by the indigenous [[Guaraní people|Guaraní]] who live in what is now Paraguay, southeastern Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Uruguay,<ref name="EB">{{cite encyclopedia |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/mate-beverage|title=Mate - beverage |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]] |access-date=8 October 2015 |editor-first=Melissa |editor-last=Petruzzello }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Del Techo, Ximénez, Dobrizhoffer|first=Nicolás, Bartolomé, Martín|title=Tres encuentros con América, Asunción, p. 40.|publisher=editorial del Centenario|year=1967}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title = The Guaraní and Their Legacy | editor-first=Barbara |editor-last=Ganson | work = Oxford Bibliographies | access-date = 25 March 2021 | url = https://www.oxfordbibliographies.com/view/document/obo-9780199766581/obo-9780199766581-0222.xml }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.oxfordbibliographies.com/view/document/obo-9780199766581/obo-9780199766581-0222.xml|title = The Guaraní and Their Legacy}}</ref><ref name="Preedy">{{Cite book |last=Preedy |first=Victor R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k3HK2WuZrsYC&q=Goddesses&pg=PT204 |title=Tea in Health and Disease Prevention |publisher=Academic Press |year=2013 |isbn=9780123849373 |pages=165–6 |quote=The Indians known as the Guarani began drinking yerba mate in the region that now includes Paraguay, southern Brazil, southeastern Bolivia, Northeastern Argentina and Uruguay.}}</ref> and  the [[Tupí people]] who lived in neighbouring areas. Later, it spread to parts of southern Brazil and northeast Argentina, particularly areas that were Paraguayan territory before the [[Paraguayan War]].{{citation needed|date=March 2021}} Therefore, the scientific name of the yerba mate is ''Ilex paraguariensis''.

With the Spanish colonization of Paraguay in the late 16th century the consumption of yerba mate spread to Spanish settlers, and in the 17th century to the [[Río de la Plata]] and from there to Peru and Chile.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.yerba-mate.com/yerba_mate_history.htm|title=Regional History of Yerba Mate|website=www.yerba-mate.com|access-date=30 October 2019}}</ref> This widespread consumption turned it into Paraguay's main [[commodity]] above other wares such as tobacco, cotton and beef.

Aboriginal labour was originally used to harvest wild stands of yerba mate. In the mid-17th century, [[Jesuit]]s managed to domesticate the plant and establish plantations in [[Jesuit Reductions|their Indian reductions]] in the Argentine province of [[Misiones]], sparking severe competition with the Paraguayan harvesters of wild stands. After [[Suppression of the Society of Jesus|their expulsion]] in the 1770s, the [[Jesuit missions]] – along with the yerba mate plantations – fell into ruins. The industry continued to be of prime importance for the Paraguayan economy after independence, but development in benefit of the Paraguayan state halted after the [[Paraguayan War]] (1864–1870) that devastated the country both economically and demographically.

Brazil then became the largest producer of mate. In Brazilian and Argentine projects in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the plant was domesticated once again, opening the way for plantation systems. When Brazilian entrepreneurs turned their attention to coffee in the 1930s, Argentina, which had long been the prime consumer, took over as the largest producer, resurrecting the economy of [[Misiones Province]], where the Jesuits had once had most of their plantations. For years, the status of largest producer shifted between Brazil and Argentina.<ref>{{cite web|title=History of Mate|url=http://comex.lasmarias.com.ar/eng/detalle.php?a=yerba-mate-tea&t=3&d=1|publisher=Establecimiento Las Marías|access-date=8 November 2011|archive-date=12 November 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111112130854/http://comex.lasmarias.com.ar/eng/detalle.php?a=yerba-mate-tea&t=3&d=1|url-status=dead}}</ref>

As of 2018, Argentina was the largest producer with 56–62%, followed by Brazil, 34–36%, and Paraguay, 5%.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://segundoenfoque.com/la-produccion-yerba-mate-argentina-registro-record-historico-2018-02-09|title=segundoenfoque|access-date=13 July 2018|date=9 February 2018|archive-date=10 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180210175347/http://segundoenfoque.com/la-produccion-yerba-mate-argentina-registro-record-historico-2018-02-09|url-status=dead}}</ref> Uruguay is the largest per capita consumer, consuming around 19 liters per person per year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.euromonitor.com/2016/10/as-consumption-stagnates-in-south-america-will-yerba-mate-move-north.html|title=As Consumption Stagnates in South America, will Yerba Mate Move North?|date=19 October 2016|access-date=23 June 2017|archive-date=24 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171124234301/http://blog.euromonitor.com/2016/10/as-consumption-stagnates-in-south-america-will-yerba-mate-move-north.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Name ==
The English word comes from the French {{lang|fr|maté}} and the American Spanish {{lang|es|mate}}, which means both mate and the vessel for drinking it, from the [[Quechuan languages|Quechua]] word {{lang|qu|mati}} for the calabash gourd used to make it.<ref>{{MW|maté}}</ref><ref>[https://www.cnrtl.fr/etymologie/mat%C3%A9/0 Etymology of ''maté''] in the ''[[Trésor de la langue française informatisé]]''.</ref>

Both the spellings "mate" and "maté" are used in English. The acute accent indicates that the word is pronounced with two syllables, like [[café]], rather than like the one-syllable English word "[[wikt:mate|mate]]".<ref>Although the order of spelling variants in dictionaries is not necessarily meaningful in any particular case, ''Webster's Third New International Dictionary of the English Language Unabridged'', the ''Oxford English Dictionary'', ''Collins English Dictionary'', the ''Random House Dictionary of the English Language'' and Lexico.com all give the accented form "maté" before the unaccented form "mate", or refer the reader to see "maté" if they look up "mate".</ref> An [[acute accent]] is not used in the Spanish spelling, because the first syllable is [[Stress in Spanish|stressed]]; "{{lang|es|maté}}" with the stress on the second syllable means "I killed".<ref name=EB/>

In Brazil, traditionally prepared mate is known as {{lang|pt|chimarrão}}, although the Portuguese word {{lang|pt|mate}} and the expression "{{lang|es|mate amargo}}" (bitter mate) are also used in Argentina and Uruguay. The Spanish {{lang|es|cimarrón}} means "rough", "brute", or "barbarian", but is most widely understood to mean "feral", and is used in almost all of Latin America for domesticated animals that have become wild. The word was then used by the people who colonized the region of the [[Río de la Plata]] to describe the natives' rough and sour drink, drunk with no other ingredient to sweeten the taste.

== Culture ==
[[File:Pope Francis with Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner 4.jpg|thumbnail|[[Pope Francis]] holds a {{lang|es|guampa}} and {{lang|es|bombilla}} given as a gift while speaking with Argentine President [[Cristina Fernández de Kirchner]] (2013)]]

Mate has a strong cultural significance for both national identity and society. Yerba mate is the national drink of Paraguay, where it is also consumed with either hot or ice cold water (see [[tereré]]);<ref>{{cite book|vauthors=Conran C, Conran T, Hopkinson S|title=The Conran Cookbook|year=2001|publisher=Conran-Octopus|isbn=978-1-84091-182-4}}</ref> Argentina;<ref>{{cite news|last=Sanders|first=Kerry|title=Next time you're in Argentina, try a cup of mate|page=1|publisher=MSNBC|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna24315283|url-status=live|access-date=29 May 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121001185454/http://today.msnbc.msn.com/id/24315283/ns/today-where_in_the_world/t/next-time-youre-argentina-try-cup-mate/|archive-date=1 October 2012}}</ref> and Uruguay. Drinking mate is a common social practice in all of the territory of Paraguay and Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, southern Chile, and eastern Bolivia. Throughout the [[Southern Cone]], it is considered to be a tradition taken from the Guaraní people and drunk by the {{lang|es|[[gaucho]]s}} or {{lang|es| [[vaqueros]]}}, terms commonly used to describe the historical residents of the South American {{lang|es|[[pampas]]}}, {{lang|es|[[Gran Chaco|chacos]]}}, or [[Patagonian grasslands]], found principally in parts of Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay, southeastern Bolivia, southern Chile and southern Brazil. Argentina has celebrated National Mate Day every 30 November since 2015.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://inym.org.ar/noticias/yerba-mate-argentina/78956-30-de-noviembre-dia-nacional-del-mate-en-la-argentina.html |title= ¡Al gran mate argentino salud! 30 de noviembre: Día Nacional del Mate en la Argentina|last= |first= |date= |website= |publisher=INSTITUTO NACIONAL DE LA YERBA MAT |access-date=25 January 2021 |quote=El Congreso de la Nación Argentina, sancionó en diciembre de 2014 la Ley 27.117, la cual establece que el día 30 de noviembre de cada año se celebre el "Día Nacional del Mate", en homenaje al caudillo Andrés Guacurarí y Artigas, conocido popularmente como "Andresito".}}</ref>

{{ill|Parque Histórico do Mate|pt}}, funded by the state of [[Paraná (state)|Paraná]] (Brazil), is a park aimed to educate people on the sustainable harvesting methods needed to maintain the integrity and vitality of the oldest wild forests of yerba mate in the world.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.museuparanaense.pr.gov.br/modules/conteudo/conteudo.php?conteudo=56 |title=Museu Paranaense |publisher=Museuparanaense.pr.gov.br |access-date=13 February 2013 |archive-date=6 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006151726/http://www.museuparanaense.pr.gov.br/modules/conteudo/conteudo.php?conteudo=56 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Mate is also consumed as an [[iced tea]] in various regions of Brazil, originating both from a sweetened industrialized form, produced by [[Matte Leão]], and from artisanal producers. It is part of the beach culture in [[Rio de Janeiro]], where it is widely sold by beach vendors;<ref>{{cite news |last=Barrionuevo |first=Alexei |date=9 February 2010 |title=Clamping Down on the Kaleidoscope of Rio's Beaches |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/02/10/world/americas/10rio.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0 |location=New York City |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=30 August 2014}}</ref> the hot infused variation being uncommon in the area.

== Preparation ==
{{originalresearch|section|date=August 2023}}
{{multiple image
| width             = 200
| image1            = Mate_tradicional_con_pava.jpg
| alt1              = 
| caption1          = A traditional [[calabash gourd]] with a [[kettle]]
| image2            = Mate_moderno_con_pava_electrica.jpg
| alt2              = 
| caption2          = A modern {{lang|es|mate}} with an electric kettle, note that the kettle has a specific {{lang|es|mate}} temperature setting

The preparation of mate is a simple process, consisting of filling a container with {{lang|es|yerba}}, pouring hot, but not boiling, water over the leaves, and drinking with a straw, the {{lang|es|bombilla}}, which acts as a filter so as to draw only the liquid and not the yerba mate leaves. The method of preparing the mate infusion varies considerably from region to region, and which method yields the finest outcome is debated. However, nearly all methods have some common elements. The beverage is traditionally prepared in a gourd vessel, also called {{lang|es|mate}} in Spanish and {{lang|pt|cuia}} (= gourd) in Portuguese, from which it is drunk. The gourd is nearly filled with {{lang|es|yerba}}, and hot water,<ref name="Brooke 3">{{Cite news | first = Elizabeth | last = Brooke | title = Yerba Mate, Ancient Antidote To South America's Heat | url = https://www.nytimes.com/1991/04/24/garden/yerba-mate-ancient-antidote-to-south-america-s-heat.html | work=[[The New York Times]] | date = 24 April 1991 | access-date = 28 May 2011 }}</ref> typically at {{convert|70|to|85|C|F}}, never boiling,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ma-tea.com/pages/Traditional-Method.html |title=Traditional Method |website=ma-tea.com |access-date=30 May 2013}}</ref> is added. The drink is so popular within countries that consume it, that several national electric kettle manufacturers just refer to the range 70 to 85 °C on its thermostat as "mate" temperature.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Albiston |first=Isabel |title=How to drink mate like a local in Argentina |url=https://www.lonelyplanet.com/articles/how-to-drink-mate-in-argentina |access-date=2025-12-11 |website=Lonely Planet |language=en}}</ref>

The most common preparation involves a careful arrangement of the {{lang|es|yerba}} within the gourd before adding hot water. In this method, the gourd is first filled one-half to three-quarters of the way with {{lang|es|yerba}}. Too much {{lang|es|yerba}} will result in a "short" {{lang|es|mate}}; conversely, too little {{lang|es|yerba}} results in a "long" {{lang|es|mate}}, both being considered undesirable. After that, any additional herbs ({{lang|es|yuyo}}, in Portuguese {{lang|pt|jujo}}) may be added for either health or flavor benefits, a practice most common in Paraguay, where people acquire herbs from a local {{lang|es|yuyera}} (herbalist) and use the {{lang|es|mate}} as a base for their herbal infusions. When the gourd is adequately filled, the preparer typically grasps it with the full hand, covering and roughly sealing the opening with the palm. Then the {{lang|es|mate}} is turned upside-down, and shaken vigorously, but briefly and with gradually decreasing force, in this inverted position. This causes the finest, most powdery particles of the {{lang|es|yerba}} to settle toward the preparer's palm and the top of the {{lang|es|mate}}.

Once the yerba mate has settled, the {{lang|es|mate}} is carefully brought to a near-sideways angle, with the opening tilted just slightly upward of the base. The {{lang|es|mate}} is then shaken very gently with a side-to-side motion. This further settles the yerba mate inside the gourd so that the finest particles move toward the opening and the {{lang|es|yerba}} is layered along one side. The largest stems and other bits create a partition between the empty space on one side of the gourd and the lopsided pile of {{lang|es|yerba}} on the other.

{{multiple image
| total_width       = 625
| image1            = Straw mate.jpg
| alt1              = 
| caption1          = A typical {{lang|es|[[bombilla|bomba/bombilla]]}} or straw
| image2            = Bambusové bombilly.JPG
| alt2              = 
| caption2          = Homemade bamboo {{lang|es|bombillas}}
| image3            = Bombilla.jpg
| alt3              = 
| caption3          = An ornate silver {{lang|es|bombilla}}
}}

After arranging the {{lang|es|yerba}} along one side of the gourd, the {{lang|es|mate}} is carefully tilted back onto its base, minimizing further disturbances of the {{lang|es|yerba}} as it is re-oriented to allow consumption. Some [[settling]] is normal, but is not desirable. The angled mound of {{lang|es|yerba}} should remain, with its powdery peak still flat and mostly level with the top of the gourd. A layer of stems along its slope will slide downward and accumulate in the space opposite the {{lang|es|yerba}} (though at least a portion should remain in place).

All of this careful settling of the {{lang|es|yerba}} ensures that each sip contains as little particulate matter as possible, creating a smooth-running {{lang|es|mate}}. The finest particles will then be as distant as possible from the filtering end of the straw. With each draw, the smaller particles would inevitably move toward the straw, but the larger particles and stems filter much of this out. A sloped arrangement provides consistent concentration and flavor with each filling of the {{lang|es|mate}}.

[[File:Matero en Posadas.jpg|thumb|right|upright|Statue of a man serving mate, in [[Posadas, Misiones|Posadas]], Misiones, Argentina]]

Now the {{lang|es|mate}} is ready to receive the straw. Wetting the {{lang|es|yerba}} by gently pouring cool water into the empty space within the gourd until the water nearly reaches the top, and then allowing it to be absorbed into the {{lang|es|yerba}} before adding the straw, allows the preparer to carefully shape and "pack" the {{lang|es|yerba}}<nowiki>'</nowiki>s slope with the straw's filtering end, which makes the overall form of the {{lang|es|yerba}} within the gourd more resilient and solid. Dry {{lang|es|yerba}}, though, allows a cleaner and easier insertion of the straw, but care must be taken so as not to overly disturb the arrangement of the {{lang|es|yerba}}. Such a decision is entirely a personal or cultural preference. The straw is inserted with one's thumb and index finger on the upper end of the gourd, at an angle roughly perpendicular to the slope of the {{lang|es|yerba}}, so that its filtering end travels into the deepest part of the {{lang|es|yerba}} and comes to rest near or against the opposite wall of the gourd. It is important for the thumb to form a seal over the end of the straw when it is being inserted, or the air current produced in it will draw in undesirable particulates.

=== Brewing ===

After the above process, the {{lang|es|yerba}} may be brewed. If the straw is inserted into dry {{lang|es|yerba}}, the {{lang|es|mate}} must first be filled once with cool water as above, then be allowed to absorb it completely (which generally takes no more than two or three minutes). Treating the {{lang|es|yerba}} with cool water before the addition of hot water is essential, as it protects the yerba mate from being scalded and from the chemical breakdown of some of its desirable nutrients. Hot water may then be added by carefully pouring it, as with the cool water before, into the cavity opposite the {{lang|es|yerba}}, until it reaches almost to the top of the gourd when the {{lang|es|yerba}} is fully saturated. Care should be taken to maintain the dryness of the swollen top of the {{lang|es|yerba}} beside the edge of the gourd's opening.

Once the hot water has been added, the {{lang|es|mate}} is ready for drinking, and it may be refilled many times before becoming {{lang|es|lavado}} (washed out) and losing its flavor. When this occurs, the mound of {{lang|es|yerba}} can be pushed from one side of the gourd to the other, allowing water to be added along its opposite side; this revives the {{lang|es|mate}} for additional refillings and is called "{{lang|es|reformar o/el mate}}" (reforming the {{lang|es|mate}}).

== Etiquette ==
{{singlesource|section|date=August 2023}}
{{disputed section|date=August 2023}}

Mate is traditionally drunk in a particular social setting, such as family gatherings or with friends. The same gourd ({{lang|es|[[wikt:cuia|cuia]]}}''/mate'') and straw ({{lang|es|[[wikt:bomba|bomba]]/[[wikt:bombilla|bombilla]]}}) are used by everyone drinking. One person (known in Portuguese as the {{lang|es|[[wikt:preparador|preparador]]}}, {{lang|es|[[wikt:cevador|cevador]]}}, or {{lang|es|[[wikt:patrão|patrão]]}}, and in Spanish as the {{lang|es|[[wikt:cebador|cebador]]}}) assumes the task of server, which most of the time is the house owner in family gatherings. Typically, the {{lang|es|cebador}} fills the gourd and drinks the mate completely to ensure that it is free of particulate matter and of good quality. In some places, passing the first brew of mate to another drinker is considered bad manners, as it may be too cold or too strong; for this reason, the first brew is often called {{lang|es|[[wikt:mate del zonzo|mate del zonzo]]}} ({{lang|es|fool's mate}}). The {{lang|es|cebador}} possibly drinks the second filling as well, if they deem it too cold or bitter. The {{lang|es|cebador}} subsequently refills the gourd and passes it to the drinker to their right, who likewise drinks it all (there is not much; the {{lang|es|mate}} is full of {{lang|es|yerba}}, with room for little water), and returns it without thanking the server; a final {{lang|es|gracias}} or {{lang|pt|obrigado}} (thank you) implies that the drinker has had enough.<ref>[http://www.lanacion.com.ar/1156709-se-toma-un-mate-segunda-parte La Nación newspaper: ¿Se toma un mate? (Segunda parte)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180805112620/https://www.lanacion.com.ar/1156709-se-toma-un-mate-segunda-parte |date=5 August 2018 }} {{in lang|es}}.</ref> The only exception to this order is if a new guest joins the group; in this case the new arrival receives the next mate, and then the {{lang|es|cebador}} resumes the order of serving, and the new arrival will receive theirs depending on their placement in the group. When no more tea remains, the straw makes a loud sucking noise, which is not considered rude. The ritual proceeds around the circle in this way until the mate becomes {{lang|es|[[wikt:lavado|lavado]]}} (washed out), typically after the gourd has been filled about 10 times or more depending on the {{lang|es|yerba}} used (well-aged yerba mate is typically more potent, so provides a greater number of refills) and the ability of the {{lang|es|cebador}}. When one has had one's fill of mate, they politely thank the {{lang|es|cebador}}, passing the {{lang|es|mate}} back at the same time. It is impolite for anyone but the {{lang|es|cebador}} to move the {{lang|es|bombilla}} or otherwise mess with the {{lang|es|mate}}; the {{lang|es|cebador}} may take offense to this and not offer it to the offender again. When someone takes too long, others in the round ({{lang|es|[[wikt:roda|roda]]}} in Portuguese, {{lang|es|[[wikt:ronda|ronda]]}} in Spanish) will likely politely warn them by saying "bring the talking gourd" ({{lang|es|cuia de conversar}}); an Argentine equivalent, especially among young people, being {{lang|es|no es un micrófono}} ("it's not a microphone"), an allusion to the drinker holding the {{lang|es|mate}} for too long, as if they were using it as a microphone to deliver a lecture.

Some drinkers like to add [[sugar]] or [[honey]], creating {{lang|es|[[wikt:mate dulce|mate dulce]]}} or {{lang|es|[[wikt:mate doce|mate doce]]}} (sweet mate), instead of sugarless {{lang|es|[[wikt:mate amargo|mate amargo]]}} (bitter mate), a practice said to be [[Brazilian tea culture|more common in Brazil]] outside its southernmost state. Some people also like to add lemon or orange peel, some herbs or even coffee, but these are mostly rejected by people who like to stick to the "original" mate.
Traditionally, natural gourds are used, though wood vessels, bamboo tubes, and gourd-shaped {{lang|es|mates}}, made of ceramic or metal (stainless steel or even silver) are also common, as are vessels made from cattle horns. The gourd is traditionally made out of the porongo or {{lang|pt|cabaça}} fruit shell. Gourds are commonly decorated with silver, sporting decorative or heraldic designs with floral motifs. Some gourd {{lang|es|mates}} with elaborated silver ornaments and silver {{lang|es|bombillas}} are true pieces of jewelry and are sought after by collectors.

==Contaminants==
{{See also|Yerba mate#Cancer}}
[[File:Benzo(a)pyrene Concentration in Processed Yerba Maté Leaves Sampled in 2006, 2008, and 2010 - Column Chart.svg|thumb|[[Column chart]] displaying [[Benzo(a)pyrene]] concentration in processed yerba mate leaves sampled in 2006, 2008, and 2010: {{legend|#8b5a2b|2006 batches}}
{{legend|#654321|2008 batches}}
{{legend|#423629|2010 batches}}]]
Traditional preparation of yerba mate leaves involves [[Smoking (cooking)|smoking]] them and for this reason they contain a high number of [[polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons]] (PAHs), such as [[benzo(a)pyrene]], which are [[carcinogen]]ic.<ref name="Golozar-2012">{{cite journal |last1=Golozar |first1=Asieh |last2=Fagundes |first2=Renato B. |last3=Etemadi |first3=Arash |last4=Schantz |first4=Michele M. |last5=Kamangar |first5=Farin |last6=Abnet |first6=Christian C. |last7=Dawsey |first7=Sanford M. |title=Significant Variation in the Concentration of Carcinogenic Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons in ''Yerba Maté'' Samples by Brand, Batch, and Processing Method |journal=[[Environmental Science & Technology]] |date=18 December 2012 |volume=46 |issue=24 |pages=13488–13493 |doi=10.1021/es303494s |pmid=23101992 |pmc=3525749|bibcode=2012EnST...4613488G }}</ref> It has been suggested that this may explain cancers associated with mate consumption, such as [[Lung cancer|lung]] and [[bladder cancer]], that cannot be attributed to its hot temperature. Instead, the hot temperature of mate (above 65°C) is specifically linked to [[oesophageal cancer]].<ref name="Oranuba-2018">{{cite journal |last1=Oranuba |first1=Ebele |last2=Deng |first2=Hua |last3=Peng |first3=Jiangnan |last4=Dawsey |first4=Sanford M |last5=Kamangar |first5=Farin |title=Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons as a potential source of carcinogenicity of mate |journal=[[Journal of Environmental Science and Health, Part C]] |date=2 January 2019 |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=26–41 |doi=10.1080/10590501.2019.1555323 |pmid=30596334 |pmc=6443446|bibcode=2019JESHC..37...26O }}</ref> However, the occurrence of PAHs in yerba mate leaves and infusion is based on small studies with non-representative sampling.<ref name="IARC-Book-2018">{{Cite book |title=Drinking Coffee, Mate, and Very Hot Beverages |year=2018 |publisher=International Agency for Research on Cancer |isbn=978-92-832-0183-0 |url=https://publications.iarc.fr/Book-And-Report-Series/Iarc-Monographs-On-The-Identification-Of-Carcinogenic-Hazards-To-Humans/Drinking-Coffee-Mate-And-Very-Hot-Beverages-2018 |format= |issn=1017-1606 |author-link=International Agency for Research on Cancer |access-date=2024-04-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240429063524/https://publications.iarc.fr/Book-And-Report-Series/Iarc-Monographs-On-The-Identification-Of-Carcinogenic-Hazards-To-Humans/Drinking-Coffee-Mate-And-Very-Hot-Beverages-2018 |archive-date=29 April 2024 |url-status=live |archive-format=}}</ref> In any case, the use of mate with potentially lower PAHs content, such as unsmoked mate, has been suggested as a preventive approach.<ref name="Golozar-2012"/><ref name="Oranuba-2018"/>[[File:Mate gaucho.jpg|thumb|Brazilian-style {{lang|pt|chimarrão}}]]

== Other properties ==

Mate is a rich source of [[caffeine]]. On average, mate tea contains 92 mg of [[chlorogenic acid]] per gram of dry leaves, and no [[catechin]]s, giving it a significantly different [[polyphenol]] profile from other teas.<ref name="Journal of Food Science">{{cite journal | doi = 10.1111/j.1750-3841.2007.00535.x | pmid = 18034743| title = Yerba Mate Tea: A Comprehensive Review on Chemistry, Health Implications, and Technological Considerations| journal = Journal of Food Science | date = 17 October 2007 | volume=72| issue = 9| pages = R138-51| last1 = Heck| first1 = C. I.| last2 = De Mejia| first2 = E. G.| s2cid = 32413555| doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1111/j.1750-3841.2007.00535.x | pmid = 18034743| title = Polyphenols in green tea, black tea, and Mate tea| journal = Journal of Food Science | date = 17 October 2007 | volume=72 | issue = 9| pages=R138–R151| last1 = Heck| first1 = C. I.| last2 = De Mejia| first2 = E. G.| s2cid = 32413555| doi-access = free}}</ref>

{{anchor|Mateína}}According to Argentine culture in part promoted by marketers, the stimulant in mate is actually a substance called '''{{lang|es|mateína}}'''<!-- Bolded because [[Mateína]] redirects here. --> (named after the drink). However, analysis of the active [[Yerba mate#Chemical composition and properties|chemicals in yerba mate]] has found that {{lang|es|mateína}} is caffeine.<ref>{{Cite web|date=14 October 2011|title=La mateína no existe|url=https://www.unl.edu.ar/noticias/leer/8809/La_mateina_no_existe.html|access-date=23 July 2020|website=[[Universidad Nacional del Litoral]]}}</ref>

== Legendary origins ==
{{see also|Guaraní creation myth}}

The Guaraní people started drinking mate in a region that currently includes Paraguay, southern Brazil, southeastern Bolivia, northeastern Argentina and Uruguay. They have a legend that the Goddesses of the Moon and the Cloud came to visit the Earth one day. An old man saved them from a {{lang|es|yaguareté}} ([[jaguar]]) that was going to attack them. The goddesses gave him a new kind of plant, from which he could prepare a "drink of friendship" as compensation for his actions.<ref name="Preedy" />

== Variants ==

[[File:Mate cocido frio.jpg|thumb|Iced {{lang|es|[[mate cocido]]}}]]
There various types of yerba mate used to make the drink, depending on the processing and composition. Some key types include:

* {{lang|es|Con palo}} – a mix of stems and ground leaf
* {{lang|es|Sin palo}} – despalada: without stems or very little stem content
* {{lang|es|Compuesta}} – Mixed with other herbs and plants, like mint
* {{lang|es|Saborizada}} – in which the leaf has been flavored with flavorings and [[Food additive|food additives]]
* {{lang|es|Para tereré}} – made specifically for {{lang|es|[[tereré]]}}, usually with other herbs like mint etc
* {{lang|es|Barbacuá}} – toasted mate
* {{lang|es|Cocido/Saquitos}} – bagged, similar to tea bags

Another drink can be prepared with specially cut dry leaves, very cold water, and, optionally, [[lemon]] or another fruit juice, called {{lang|es|[[tereré]]}}. It is very common in Paraguay, northeastern Argentina and in the state of [[Mato Grosso do Sul]], Brazil. After pouring the water, it is considered proper to "wait while the saint has a sip" before the first person takes a drink. In southern Brazil, {{lang|pt|tererê}} is sometimes used as a derogatory term for a not hot enough {{lang|pt|chimarrão}}.

In Uruguay and Brazil, the traditional gourd is usually big with a corresponding large hole. In Argentina (especially in the capital [[Buenos Aires]]), the gourd is small and has a small hole and people sometimes add sugar for flavor.

In Uruguay, people commonly walk around the streets toting a {{lang|es|mate}} and a [[vacuum flask|thermos]] with hot water. In some parts of Argentina, gas stations sponsored by yerba mate producers provide free hot water to travelers, specifically for the purpose of drinking during the journey. Disposable mate sets with a plastic mate and straw and sets with a thermos flask and stacking containers for the yerba mate and sugar inside a fitted case are available.

In Argentina, {{lang|es|[[mate cocido]]}} (boiled mate), in Brazil, {{lang|pt-BR|chá mate}}, is made with a [[tea bag]] or leaves and drunk from a cup or mug, with or without sugar and milk. Companies such as Cabrales from [[Mar del Plata]] and [[Establecimiento Las Marías]] produce tea bags for export to Europe.<ref>[http://www.lanacion.com.ar/nota.asp?nota_id=340787 ''Cabrales abrirá locales en la Capital''] [[La Nación (Buenos Aires)|La Nación]] online, 6 October 2001 {{in lang|es}}.</ref>

[[File:A bottle of an ice tea variataion of mate and a glass of it.jpg|thumbnail|upright=.8|Mate is consumed as an ice tea in various regions of Brazil, in both artisanal and industrial forms. This is a bottle of industrialized mate ice tea, bought from a local supermarket in Rio de Janeiro.]]
Travel narratives, such as [[Maria Graham]]'s ''Journal of a Residence in Chile'', show a long history of mate-drinking in central Chile. Many rural Chileans drink mate, in particular in the southern regions, particularly [[Magallanes Region of Chile|Magallanes]], [[Aysén Region|Aysén]] and [[Chiloé Archipelago|Chiloé]].

In Peru, mate is widespread throughout the north and south, first being introduced to [[Lima]] in the 17th century. It is widespread in [[Rural area|rural zones]], and it is prepared with coca (plant) or in a sweetened tea form with small slices of lemon or orange.''<ref>{{Cite book|title=EL MATE Arte de Cebar|last=Villanueva|first=Amaro|publisher=La compañia general fabril financiera S. A.|year=1960|location=Buenos Aires|pages=200 (In Spanish)}}</ref>''

In some parts of Syria, Lebanon and other Eastern Mediterranean countries, drinking mate is also common. The custom came from Syrians and Lebanese who moved to South America during the late 19th and early parts of the 20th century, adopted the tradition, and kept it after returning to Western Asia. Syria is the biggest importer of yerba mate in the world, importing 15,000 tons a year. Mostly, the [[Druze]] communities in Syria and Lebanon maintain the culture and practice of mate.<ref name="donald" /><ref name="Middle East Online" />

According to a major retailer of mate in [[San Luis Obispo, California]], by 2004, mate had grown to about 5% of the overall natural tea market in North America.<ref>{{cite press release |title=Guayaki Honored With 2004 Socially Responsible Business Award |date=28 October 2004 |publisher=Guayaki |url=http://www.csrwire.com/News/3184.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120723173128/http://www.csrwire.com/News/3184.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 July 2012 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Laura |last=Everage |title=Trends in Tea |work=The Gourmet Retailer |date=1 November 2004 |url=http://www.gourmetretailer.com/gourmetretailer/magazine/article_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1000696346 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061105141723/http://www.gourmetretailer.com/gourmetretailer/magazine/article_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1000696346 |archive-date=5 November 2006 }}</ref> Loose mate is commercially available in much of North America. Bottled mate is increasingly available in the United States. Canadian bottlers have introduced a cane sugar-sweetened, carbonated variety, similar to soda pop. One brand, Sol Mate, produces {{convert|10|usfloz|ml|adj=on}} glass bottles available at Canadian and U.S. retailers, making use of the translingual pun (English 'soul mate'; Spanish/Portuguese 'sun mate') for the sake of marketing.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/graphic/2007/01/19/GR2007011900577.html | title = Tip Sheet: Lowdown on Liquid Power-Ups | access-date = 29 May 2011 | last = Rude | first = Justin | date = 19 January 2007 | newspaper=The Washington Post }}</ref>

In some parts of the [[Southern Cone]] bitter mate is preferred, especially in Paraguay, Uruguay, the south of Brazil, and parts of Argentina and Bolivia. This is referred to in Brazil and a large part of Argentina as {{lang|es|cimarrón}} –which also an archaic name for wild cattle, especially, to a horse that was very attached to a cowboy – which is understood as unsweetened mate.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://circleofdrink.com/yerba-mate-terms-and-glossary|title=Mate Terms and Glossary|website=Circle of Drink|access-date=22 February 2019}}</ref> Many people are of the opinion that mate should be drunk in this form.

Unlike bitter mate, in every preparation of {{lang|es|mate dulce}}, or sweet mate, sugar is incorporated according to the taste of the drinker. This form of preparation is very widespread in various regions of Argentina, like in the [[Santiago del Estero]] province, [[Córdoba, Argentina|Córdoba]], [[Cuyo (Argentina)|Cuyo]], and [[Greater Buenos Aires|the metropolitan region of Buenos Aires]], among others. In Chile, this form of mate preparation is widespread in mostly [[Rural area|rural zones]]. The spoonful of sugar or honey should fall on the edge of the cavity that the straw forms in the {{lang|es|yerba}}, not all over the {{lang|es|mate}}. One variation is to sweeten only the first mate preparation in order to cut the bitterness of the first sip, thus softening the rest. In Paraguay, a variant of {{lang|es|mate dulce}} is prepared by first caramelizing refined sugar in a pot then adding milk. The mixture is heated and placed in a thermos and used in place of water. Often, chamomile ({{lang|es|manzanilla}}, in Spanish) and coconut are added to {{lang|es|yerba}} in the gumpa.

In the sweet version [[sugar substitute|artificial sweeteners]] are also often added. As an alternative sweetener, natural {{lang|gn|ka'á he'é}} (''[[Stevia rebaudiana]]'') is preferred, which is an herb whose leaves are added in order to give a touch of sweetness. This is used principally in Paraguay.

The gourd in which bitter mate is drunk is not used to consume sweet mate due to the idea that the taste of the sugar would be detrimental to its later use to prepare and drink bitter mate, as it is said that it ruins the flavor of the mate.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-08-10-mn-143-story.html|title=More Than a Drink : Yerba Mate: Argentina's Cultural Rite|last=SMITH|first=JAMES F.|date=10 August 1988|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=22 February 2019|issn=0458-3035}}</ref>

[[Materva]] is a sweet, carbonated [[soft drink]] based on yerba mate. Developed in Cuba in 1920, and produced since the 1960s in [[Miami, Florida]], it is a staple of the Cuban culture in Miami.<ref name="Wong-2014">{{cite news |last=Wong |first=Samantha |title=Materva: Un Buchito de Cuba |url=http://www.jwu.edu/uploadedFiles/Documents/Academics/studentwork/JWUStuFoodWritingNMI.pdf |access-date=10 September 2020 |newspaper=Johnson and Wales: Student Food Writing |page=8 (PDF p. 11) |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140113000105/https://www.jwu.edu/uploadedFiles/Documents/Academics/studentwork/JWUStuFoodWritingNMI.pdf |archive-date=13 January 2014}}</ref><ref name="Roque-2011">{{Cite book |title=The Cuban Kitchen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vmJlvl1mVUgC&pg=PA6 |first=Raquel Rábade |last=Roque |date=2011 |edition=1st |page=6 |publisher=Alfred A. Knopf |access-date=10 September 2020 |isbn=9780375711961 |language=en}}</ref>

The '''New Englander''' is a [[cocktail]] made from two to three parts [[Moxie]] to one part gin. The name derives from Moxie's regional popularity in parts of [[New England]]. Some people also detect a slight resemblance in taste to [[Necco]] wafers, another regional product.{{cite news |last=Burnham |first=Emily |url= https://bangordailynews.com/2015/02/10/living/food/it-makes-mainers-mighty-6-moxie-cocktails-to-mix-up-this-winter/ |title=It makes Mainers mighty: 6 Moxie cocktails to mix up this winter |work=[[Bangor Daily News]] |date=February 10, 2015 |accessdate=August 4, 2019}}
==Recipe== 1 part [[Gordon's Gin]]
2-3 parts Moxie
a large slice of lime
a dash of [[Worcestershire sauce]]
The Worcestershire sauce cuts the drink's sweetness. While some prefer to leave it out, purists argue that a New Englander is incomplete without it. {{short description|Vodka-based cocktail}}
{{Infobox drink
