Smoothie:
{{Short description|Drink made from fruit or vegetables}}
{{For multi|the professional gamer|Smoothie (gamer)|the subculture|Nullo (body modification)}}
[[File:Kiwi Smoothie.jpg|thumb|[[Kiwifruit]] smoothie]]

A '''smoothie''' is a beverage made by [[purée]]ing ingredients in a [[blender]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/smoothie|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181025190038/https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/smoothie|archive-date=October 25, 2018|title=Smoothie|publisher=Oxford Dictionary, Oxford University Press|date=2018}}</ref> A smoothie commonly has a liquid base, such as fruit juice or [[milk]], [[yogurt]] or [[ice cream]]. Other ingredients may be added, including fruits, vegetables, [[Plant milk|non-dairy milk]], [[crushed ice]], [[Whey|whey powder]] or [[nutritional supplement]]s. 
== History ==

[[Health food store]]s on the [[West Coast of the United States|west coast of the United States]] began selling smoothies with the invention of the [[Blender|electric blender]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brown |first=Ellen |title=The Complete Idiot's Guide to Smoothies |year=2005 |isbn=1-59257-318-5 |page=3|publisher=Penguin }}</ref> The actual term "smoothie" was being used in [[recipe]]s and [[trademarks]] by the mid-1980s.<ref>{{cite web |date=2018 |title=Smoothie |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/smoothie |access-date=25 October 2018 |publisher=Online Etymology Dictionary, Douglas Harper}}</ref>  In the 1960s Steve Kuhnau was inspired by his work as a [[soda jerk]] and began experimenting with smoothies. They were an alternative for the lactose intolerant Kuhnau to taste his own concoctions using unique blends of fruit juices, vegetables, protein powder, and vitamins. Kuhnau discovered early success in his smoothie sales and founded [[Smoothie King]]. Smoothie King expanded throughout the United States and would pioneer other smoothie businesses. The smoothie was then modified by fast food chains with the addition of sweeter ingredients like chocolate and [[Splenda]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Moffitt |first=Sally |date=2014-06-01 |title=Sources: Food and Drink in American History: A "Full Course" Encyclopedia. |journal=Reference & User Services Quarterly |volume=53 |issue=4 |page=377 |doi=10.5860/rusq.53n4.377a |issn=1094-9054|doi-access=free }}</ref> In the 2000s, consumers began making smoothies at home, in part as an alternative for daily consumption of fruits and vegetables.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Walkling-Ribeiro |first1=Markus |last2=Noci |first2=Francesco |last3=Cronin |first3=Denis A. |last4=Lyng |first4=James G. |last5=Morgan |first5=Desmond J. |date=2010-09-01 |title=Shelf life and sensory attributes of a fruit smoothie-type beverage processed with moderate heat and pulsed electric fields |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0023643810000708 |journal=LWT - Food Science and Technology |language=en |volume=43 |issue=7 |pages=1067–1073 |doi=10.1016/j.lwt.2010.02.010 |issn=0023-6438|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Nutrition ==
[[File:Fruit_smoothie_(8475314736).png|thumb|upright=0.6|Blueberry smoothie topped with blueberries and pineapple pieces]]

The nutrition of a smoothie depends on its ingredients and their proportions. Many smoothies include large or multiple servings of fruits and vegetables, which are recommended in a healthy diet and intended to be a [[meal replacement]].<ref name="mayo">{{cite web |author1=Jeff Olsen |title=Mayo Clinic Minute: Get smart about smoothies |work=Mayo Clinic News Network |url=https://newsnetwork.mayoclinic.org/discussion/mayo-clinic-minute-get-smart-about-smoothies/ |access-date=25 October 2018 |date=26 July 2017}}</ref> However, fruit juice containing high amounts of [[sugar]] can increase [[calorie|caloric intake]] and promote [[weight gain]].<ref name="cdc2018">{{cite web |title=Get the Facts: Sugar-Sweetened Beverages and Consumption |url=https://www.cdc.gov/nutrition/data-statistics/sugar-sweetened-beverages-intake.html |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, US Department of Health and Human Services |access-date=25 October 2018 |date=23 October 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2013/sep/07/smoothies-fruit-juices-new-health-risk|title=Smoothies and fruit juices are a new risk to health, US scientists warn|last=Boseley|first=Sarah|date=2013-09-07|newspaper=The Guardian|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077|access-date=2016-03-27}}</ref> Ingredients such as [[protein powder]]s, sweeteners, or ice cream may be used.<ref name="mayo" /><ref>{{Cite web |publisher=Nutrition Extension - Utah State University |title=Smoothies—Helpful or Harmful?|author=Darla Stoker |author2=Carrie Durward | url=https://extension.usu.edu/nutrition/research/smoothies-helpful-or-harmful |access-date=2022-03-01 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="cdc2015">{{cite web |date=23 September 2015 |title=Rethink Your Drink |url=https://www.cdc.gov/healthyweight/healthy_eating/drinks.html |access-date=25 October 2018 |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, US Department of Health and Human Services}}</ref> One study found smoothies to be less [[Satiety|satiating]], despite providing the same amount of energy as unblended foods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rogers |first1=Peter J. |last2=Shahrokni |first2=Roya |date=2018-03-30 |title=A Comparison of the Satiety Effects of a Fruit Smoothie, Its Fresh Fruit Equivalent and Other Drinks |journal=Nutrients |volume=10 |issue=4 |page=431 |doi=10.3390/nu10040431 |issn=2072-6643 |pmc=5946216 |pmid=29601488|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Types==

=== Green smoothie ===
A ''green smoothie'' can consist of any combination (including [[green leafy vegetable]]s) or relative quantity of vegetables from which the resulting product is colored green.<ref name="kline">{{cite web|author=Angela Kline|date=23 September   2019|title=Smoothies Offered in Child Nutrition Programs |url=https://www.cacfp.org/assets/pdf/Smoothies+Offered+in+Child+Nutrition+Programs+QandA+cacfp.org/|publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]: National [[Child and Adult Care Food Program]] Association|page=2|quote=2. Can smoothies containing a blend of different vegetables, vegetable juice blends, or fruit and vegetable juice blends}}</ref> Commonly, a green smoothie consists of dark green vegetables, such as [[spinach]], [[kale]], [[Swiss chard]], [[collard greens]], [[celery]], [[parsley]], or [[broccoli]], with the remaining ingredients being mostly or entirely [[fruit]].<ref name=kline/> Most green leafy vegetables have a [[bitter flavor]] when served raw, but this can be ameliorated by choosing certain less-bitter vegetables (e.g. baby spinach) or combining with fruits or other sweet ingredients.<ref name=kline/><ref>{{cite web |title=Drink your fruits and vegetables? |url=https://www.health.harvard.edu/diet-and-weight-loss/drink-your-fruits-and-vegetables |publisher=Harvard Heart Letter, Harvard Medical School |access-date=25 October 2018 |date=May 2018 |archive-date=25 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181025190139/https://www.health.harvard.edu/diet-and-weight-loss/drink-your-fruits-and-vegetables}}</ref>

=== Protein smoothie ===
A ''protein smoothie'' is a combination of water or milk, [[protein powder]], fruits, and vegetables. They can be consumed any part of the day and are used as protein supplement for those who want to increase their protein intake. Protein powder can have a chalky taste when mixed individually by itself with milk or water. The protein smoothie improves the taste of the protein powder through addition of fruits or other sweeteners.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=How to build a better smoothie, according to a nutritionist |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/better/pop-culture/how-build-better-smoothie-according-nutritionist-ncna874006 |access-date=2022-03-01 |website=NBC News |date=29 May 2018 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Yogurt smoothie ===
A yogurt smoothie is a smoothie that includes [[yogurt]] as a protein source and to add a creamy texture to the drink. [[Greek Yogurt|Greek yogurt]], specifically, is included as a thickener (due to its strained consistency) and in order to take advantage of its claimed health benefits.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/better/pop-culture/how-build-better-smoothie-according-nutritionist-ncna874006 |title=How to build a better smoothie, according to a nutritionist |date=2018-05-27 |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=[[NBC]] |last=Cassetty |first=Samantha |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180527131101/https://www.nbcnews.com/better/pop-culture/how-build-better-smoothie-according-nutritionist-ncna874006 |archive-date=2018-05-27 |language=en}}</ref>

==Around the world==
{{More citations needed|date=August 2025}}
India has [[lassi]], a yogurt smoothie composed of [[crushed ice]], yogurt, sugar or salt, and in some cases fruits, like [[mango]].<ref name="etiq">{{cite book |last=Shah |first=Niraalee |url={{Google books|7YdUEAAAQBAJ|page=PT289|plainurl=yes}} |title=Indian Etiquette: A Glimpse Into India's Culture |date=2021 |publisher=Notion Press |pages=289}}</ref>

Fruit [[Sharbat (beverage)|sharbat]] (a popular West and South Asian drink) sometimes include [[yogurt]] and [[honey]]. [[Pineapple]] smoothies made with just crushed ice and sugar are common in Southern India. Lassi or a very similar drink exists by different names in other countries.

Three wise men (cocktail):
{{short description|Cocktail blending three types of whiskey together}}

'''Three wise men''' is a drink consisting of three types of [[Whisky|whiskey]] with brand names that are each named after a man (ordinarily [[Johnnie Walker]], [[Jack Daniel's|Jack Daniel]] and [[Jim Beam]]).<ref name="Spruce">{{cite web |first=Colleen |last=Graham |title=Three Wise Men: The Shot Drink That Mixes 3 Great Whiskies |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/three-wise-men-shot-recipe-761509 |website=The Spruce Eats |date=September 7, 2018 |access-date=September 12, 2018}}</ref> The three named men are the "wise men" in the name of the drink, which is an allusion to the [[Biblical Magi]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Three Wise Men Recipe |url=https://bevvy.co/cocktail/three-wise-men/rcl |website=Bevvy |language=en |date=13 May 2015}}</ref> Several variations exist that include other ingredients or substitute [[tequila]] or [[rum]] for some of the whiskey.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Burnett |first1=Heather |title=Three Wise Men Shot 6 Ways: The Strongest Whiskey Cocktail Ever |url=https://wordtoyourmotherblog.com/three-wise-men-shot/ |website=Word To Your Mother |date=22 April 2019}}</ref>

== Recipe ==
:1 part [[Scotch whisky]] (e.g., [[Johnnie Walker]] Red or Black Label)
:1 part [[Tennessee whiskey]] (e.g., [[Jack Daniel's]])
:1 part [[Bourbon whiskey]] (e.g., [[Jim Beam]] White or Black Label)
:Serve [[Straight up (bartending)|neat]], [[ice cube|on the rocks]], or shaken with ice and strained,<ref name="Spruce" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Three Wise Men Shot |url=https://tipsybartender.com/recipe/three-wise-men-shot/ |website=Tipsy Bartender |language=en |date=10 November 2017}}</ref> according to taste. Or serve the three whiskeys as three separate [[Shooter (drink)|shots]] that are lined up and consumed sequentially.<ref name="Spruce" />

=== Variations ===
By adding an ingredient, a number of variations can be made, such as:
* A '''three wise men go hunting''', or "three wise men on a hunt" consists of the traditional recipe with an additional 1 part [[Wild Turkey bourbon]].<ref name="Spruce" />
* A '''three wise men visit Mexico''' is made with the three aforementioned liquors and 1 part tequila, e.g., [[Jose Cuervo]].<ref name="Spruce" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Three Wise Men Shot Recipe (Quick and Easy) – Tammilee Tips |url=https://www.tammileetips.com/three-wise-men-shot-recipe/ |website=www.tammileetips.com}}</ref>

'''Vodka Cruiser''' is a line of brightly coloured [[vodka]]-based [[alcoholic beverage]]s primarily sold in [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]]. Sometimes described as an [[alcopop]], this premixed drink is available in seventeen flavours, including guava, lemon, lime, passion fruit, pineapple, raspberry, and other flavours depending on location. The product originates from New Zealand, and is produced by [[Asahi Breweries|Asahi Beverages]], formerly known as Independent Liquor.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-09-30 |title=Asahi buys Cruisers and Woodstock |url=https://www.smh.com.au/business/asahi-buys-cruisers-and-woodstock-20110930-1l0xj.html |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}}</ref>

Vodka Cruisers normally come in 275 ml (9.3 oz) bottles, so each bottle contains slightly less alcohol than a standard shot. In 2022, Asahi Australia launched a range of limited-edition 3.1L "Double Magnum" sized bottles, containing the volume of roughly 11 regular cruisers, which could be won in a giveaway to celebrate the brand's 21st birthday.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-14 |title=Vodka Cruiser releases new 'Double Magnum' bottles - here's how to get one |url=https://7news.com.au/lifestyle/food-wine/vodka-cruiser-releases-limited-edition-double-magnum-bottles-heres-how-to-get-one-c-6050909 |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=7NEWS |language=en}}</ref>

== Varieties ==
In late 2003, Independent Liquor introduced a "Cruiser Black" range, containing a higher alcohol volume than standard varieties. In New Zealand, Vodka Cruisers are also available in a 7% alcohol, premium formulation sold in cardboard packages containing 12 cans of 250 ml each. According to the package labelling, each can has an alcohol content equivalent to 1.6 standard drinks, though the New Zealand definition of a standard drink would place one can at 1.75 standard drinks. In 2023, Asahi introduced a second high ABV range with the Vodka Cruiser Double line, which contains the equivalent of 2 standard drinks per beverage and comes packaged in 375ml cans rather than the standard 275ml bottles.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Enerva |first=Kaycee |date=2023-03-06 |title=Vodka Cruiser's new line has twice the alcohol |url=https://insidefmcg.com.au/2023/03/06/vodka-cruisers-new-line-has-twice-the-alcohol/ |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=Inside FMCG |language=en-AU}}</ref>

In 2009, Independent Distillers attempted to expand the Cruiser brand across a larger range of premix alcoholic beverages with the introduction of new female-oriented drinks, including the [[Alcopop|ready-to-drink]] line "Lady Luck", which contained half the sugar of a standard vodka cruiser, a [[Lager|blonde lager]] under the name "Hummingbird", and a cider under the name of "Apparella".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Team |first=The Shout |date=2009-09-09 |title=New Beer, Cider and RTDs from Independent |url=https://theshout.com.au/new-beer-cider-and-rtds-from-independent/ |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=The Shout |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=McIntyre |first=Paul |date=2009-09-09 |title=Alcopop maker hums a new tune |url=https://www.smh.com.au/business/companies/alcopop-maker-hums-a-new-tune-20090909-fhmt.html |access-date=2023-01-17 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}}</ref> Each of these product lines were available for a short period before being discontinued. 

In 2012, Asahi Beverages announced the reformulation of the Vodka Cruiser product line in Australia, introducing six new core flavours to replace the original lineup while reducing the drink's sugar content.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-10-24 |title=New Cruiser flavours, less sugar |url=https://theshout.com.au/new-cruiser-flavours-less-sugar/ |website=The Shout}}</ref>

In 2022, Asahi released 600ml long neck versions of the Guava and Raspberry Vodka Cruiser flavours for a limited time in Australia, following demand from fans on social media.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jackson |first=Stefanie |date=2022-09-21 |title=Vodka Cruiser Long Necks are officially here for a good time not a long time |url=https://www.delicious.com.au/drinks/news/article/vodka-cruiser-releases-limited-edition-long-neck-bottles/z0b8ze79 |website=delicious.}}</ref>

Smoking bishop:
{{short description|Type of mulled wine, punch or wassail}} [[File:A Christmas Carol - Scrooge and Bob Cratchit.jpg|thumb|right|"...we will discuss your affairs this very afternoon, over a Christmas bowl of smoking bishop, Bob!"
— [[Ebenezer Scrooge]]]] '''Smoking bishop''' is a type of [[mulled wine]], [[punch (drink)|punch]], or [[wassail]], especially popular in [[Victorian era|Victorian England]] at Christmas time, and it is mentioned in Dickens' 1843 story ''[[A Christmas Carol]]''.{{citation |page=54|title=Drinking with Dickens |author=Cedric Dickens |publisher=Elevendon Press |year=1983 |isbn=9780882548791|quote=“A Merry Christmas, Bob!” said Scrooge with an earnestness that could not be mistaken, as he clapped him on the back. “A merrier Christmas, Bob, my good fellow, than I have given you for many a year! I’ll raise your salary, and endeavour to assist your struggling family, and we will discuss your affairs this very afternoon over a bowl of smoking bishop, Bob!”}} Smoking bishop was made from [[port wine|port]], [[red wine]], [[lemon]]s or [[Seville orange]]s, sugar, and spices such as [[cloves]]. The citrus fruit was roasted to [[caramelization|caramelise]] it and the ingredients then warmed together. A myth persists{{citation needed|date=December 2016}} that the name comes from the shape of the traditional bowl, shaped like a [[bishop]]'s [[mitre]], and that in this form, it was served in medieval [[guildhall]]s and universities. Other variations of drinks known collectively as "ecclesiastics"{{cite news|publisher=[[NPR]]|last=Bramley|first=Anne|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2015/12/25/460576292/smoking-bishop-a-boozy-christmas-drink-brimming-with-english-history|date=25 December 2015|access-date=26 December 2015|title=Smoking Bishop: A Boozy Christmas Drink Brimming with English History}} included{{citation |title=Food and Cooking in Victorian England |author=Andrea Broomfield |page=154 |publisher=Greenwood |year=2007 |isbn=9780275987084}} the smoking [[archbishop]] (made with [[claret]]), the smoking [[beadle]] (made with [[ginger wine]] and [[raisin]]s), the smoking [[Cardinal (Catholicism)|cardinal]] (made with [[Champagne]] or [[Rhine wine]]) and the smoking [[pope]] (made with [[burgundy wine|burgundy]]). ==Recipe== [[File:Smoking Bishop.png|thumb|upright|The mitre-shaped punchbowl, as illustrated in Eliza Acton's ''Modern Cookery'']] [[Eliza Acton]] published a recipe in her ''Modern Cookery'' in 1845:
Make several incisions in the rind of a lemon, stick cloves in these, and roast the lemon by a slow fire. Put small but equal quantities of [[cinnamon]], [[clove]]s, [[mace (spice)|mace]], and [[allspice]], with a race of [[ginger]], into a saucepan with half a pint of water: let it boil until it is reduced one-half. Boil one bottle of port wine, burn a portion of the spirit out of it by applying a lighted paper to the saucepan; put the roasted lemon and spice into the wine; stir it up well, and let it stand near the fire ten minutes. Rub a few knobs of sugar on the rind of a lemon, put the sugar into a bowl or jug, with the juice of half a lemon (not roasted), pour the wine into it, grate in some [[nutmeg]], sweeten it to the taste, and serve it up with the lemon and spice floating in it. Bishop is frequently made with a Seville orange stuck with cloves and slowly roasted, and its flavour "to many tastes is infinitely finer" than that of the lemon.{{citation |page=175 |chapter=A Glass of Bishop |title=The Book of Christmas |author=Jane Struthers |publisher=Random House |year=2012 |isbn=9781448148936}}

'''''Tsokolate''''' ({{IPA|tl|tʃoko'late|lang}} {{Respell|choh-koh-LAH-teh}}), also spelled '''''chocolate''''' is a native [[Cuisine of the Philippines|Filipino]] thick [[hot chocolate]] drink. It is made from ''tabliya'' or ''tablea'', tablets of pure ground roasted [[Theobroma cacao|cacao]] beans, dissolved in water and milk. Like in Spanish and Mexican versions of hot chocolate, the drink is traditionally made in a ''[[tsokolatera]]'' and briskly mixed with a wooden baton called the ''[[Molinillo (whisk)|molinillo]]'' (also called  ''batidor'' or ''batirol''), causing the drink to be characteristically frothy. ''Tsokolate'' is typically sweetened with a bit of ''[[muscovado]]'' sugar, and has a distinctive grainy texture.<ref name="polistico">{{cite book|author =Polistico, Edgie|title =Philippine Food, Cooking, & Dining Dictionary|publisher =Anvil Publishing, Incorporated|year =2017|isbn =9786214200870|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=STSWDwAAQBAJ}}</ref><ref name="cabrera"/>

While today coffee is far more common, ''tsokolate'' is traditionally consumed at breakfast and/or ''[[merienda]]'' (afternoon snack time) as a substitute for or alongside coffee (which it predated in the country), traditionally paired with traditional ''[[kakanin]]'' delicacies or ''[[pandesal]]'' and other types of traditional [[Filipino pastries]]. It is also popular during [[Christmas in the Philippines|Christmas season]] in the [[Philippines]], particularly among children.<ref name="cabrera">{{cite web |last1=Cabrera |first1=Maryanne |title=sokolate (Filipino Hot Chocolate) |url=https://www.thelittleepicurean.com/2018/01/tsokolate-filipino-hot-chocolate.html |website=The Little Epicurean |date=January 27, 2018 |access-date=December 13, 2018}}</ref><ref name="kp">{{cite web |title=Tsokolate |url=https://www.kawalingpinoy.com/tsokolate/ |website=Kawaling Pinoy |date=December 8, 2014 |access-date=December 13, 2018}}</ref>

==Names==
The word ''tsokolate'' itself is merely the prescribed formal [[Tagalog language]] or [[Filipino language]] spelling of both Spanish ''chocolate'' and English chocolate, with adjusted orthography to reflect a more native construction (''tso'' vs ''cho'', ''k'' vs ''c'') and the latter spelling tends to be more common.

''Tsokolate'' is also known as '''''suklati''''' in [[Kapampangan language|Kapampangan]]; '''''sikulate''''' in [[Maguindanao language|Maguindanao]]; and '''''sikwate''''' or '''''sikuwate''''' in [[Visayan languages]]. All are derived from Spanish ''[[wikt:chocolate|chocolate]]'' ("chocolate"), ultimately from [[Nahuatl language|Nahuatl]] ''[[wikt:chocolatl|xocolātl]]''.<ref name="polistico"/>

''Tsokolate'' and these other terms may refer both to the hot chocolate drink or chocolate in general, but in breakfast and ''[[merienda]]'' contexts, the hot drink is almost always meant.

==Tableya==
[[File:Tablea- The Pinoy Chocolate.jpg|thumb|''Tableya'' balls with [[champorado]] and tsokolate]]
''[[wikt:tableya|Tableya]]'' (also spelled ''tabliya'' or ''tablea'', from Spanish ''[[wikt:tablilla|tablilla]]'', "tablet") are small traditionally home-made tablets of pure ground roasted [[Theobroma cacao|cacao]] beans. ''Tableya'' is made by drying beans of ripe [[Theobroma cacao|cacao]] fruit for two or three days. The dried beans are shelled and roasted. They are ground into a thick [[chocolate liquor]] paste that are then formed into the characteristic little discs or balls and allowed to dry.<ref name="entrep">{{cite news |title=Home-based business idea: How to make 'tablea' |url=https://www.entrepreneur.com.ph/business-ideas/homebased-business-idea-how-to-make-tablea |access-date=December 13, 2018 |work=Entrepreneur Philippines |date=December 12, 2014}}</ref><ref name="nikkei">{{cite news |last1=Sarmiento |first1=Prime |title=Filipinos' love of chocolates helps to revive cacao industry |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Life-Arts/Life/Filipinos-love-of-chocolates-helps-to-revive-cacao-industry2 |access-date=December 13, 2018 |work=Nikkei Asian Review |date=October 14, 2017}}</ref><ref name="perez">{{cite news |last1=Perez |first1=Ace June Rell S. |title=Redefining the taste of tablea |url=https://www.sunstar.com.ph/article/34941 |access-date=December 13, 2018 |work=SunStar Philippines |date=October 4, 2015}}</ref> 
Aside from ''tsokolate'', ''tableya'' is used in a wide variety of other traditional desserts in the Philippines, most prominently in ''[[champorado]]'', a [[glutinous rice]] [[porridge]] flavored with chocolate.<ref name="entrep"/><ref name="batangas">{{cite web |title=Tablea Tsokolate or Cacao Chocolate |url=https://www.batangas-philippines.com/tablea-tsokolate.html |website=Batangas-Philippines.com |access-date=December 13, 2018 |archive-date=September 23, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923171134/http://www.batangas-philippines.com/tablea-tsokolate.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Preparation==
[[File:Dumaguete Sta Monica Beach Club - Suman Mangga Tsokolate 2.jpg|thumb|''Tsokolate'' with ''[[suman (food)|suman]]'' rice cakes and ripe [[carabao mango]]es]]
''Tsokolate'' is traditionally prepared by boiling water and milk in a special high-necked [[Pitcher (container)|pitcher]]-shaped pot known as a ''[[tsokolatera]]'' (also ''tsokolatehan'', ''sikulatihan'', ''sikwatehan'', etc.). It is taken off from the flame once bubbles start to form and a few discs of ''tabliya'' are dropped into the liquid. ''[[Muscovado]]'' sugar and more milk or cream is also added, to taste. A special wooden baton called the ''[[Molinillo (whisk)|molinillo]]'' (also called  ''batidor'' or ''batirol'') is then inserted through the top and briskly twirled using the palms of the hands to bring the liquid to a froth. It is then poured into individual cups.<ref name="b2b">{{cite book|author =Juan, Pacita|author2 =Ramos, Josephine|author3 =Francisco, Maria Regina|title =Cacao: Bean to Bar|publisher =Anvil Publishing, Incorporated|year =2017|isbn =9789712729157|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=l_82DwAAQBAJ}}{{Dead link|date=January 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref name="mm">{{cite web |title=Batidor, Batirol, Molinillo, Chocolatera, atbp. |url=http://www.marketmanila.com/archives/batidor-batirol-molinillo-chocolatera-atbp |website=Market Manila |date=August 18, 2007 |access-date=December 13, 2018}}</ref><ref name="garcia">{{cite web |last1=Garcia |first1=Bianca |title=How to Make Tsokolate (Filipino Hot Chocolate)… and a Giveaway! |url=http://www.confessionsofachocoholic.com/chocolate/how-to-make-tsokolate-filipino-hot-chocolate-and-a-giveaway |website=Confessions of a Chocoholic |date=January 4, 2012 |access-date=December 13, 2018}}</ref>

Modern methods of making ''tsokolate'' can include using regular [[whisk]]s, [[blender]]s, or [[milk frother]]s to achieve the same frothy consistency. Additional ingredients like [[cinnamon]], [[vanilla]], ''[[pinipig]]'' rice flakes, or even [[rum]] or [[tequila]] can also be added. However, using commercial [[cocoa powder]] instead of ''tabliya'' is strongly frowned upon, as it does not give the same texture or taste.<ref name="kp"/><ref name="b2b"/><ref name="garcia"/><ref name="cabrera"/>
[[File:Tsokolate_de_Ylocos_Cacao_Tablea1.jpg|200px|thumbnail|right|Tsokolate de Ylocos Cacao ''tableya'', from [[Salcedo, Ilocos Sur]]]]

[[File:Camiña Balay nga Bato’s tsokolate de batirol.jpg|200px|thumbnail|right|Camiña Balay nga Bato's tsokolate de batirol with Ugoy-ugoy from [[Iloilo]]]]

==Cultural significance==
''Tsokolate'' is commonly consumed at breakfast or ''[[merienda]]'' with traditional ''[[kakanin]]'' or bread. Common pairings with ''tsokolate'' include ''[[pandesal]]'', ''[[puto maya]]'', ''[[puto bumbong]]'', ''[[churro]]s'', ''[[ensaymada]]'', ''[[buñuelo]]s'' (or ''[[cascaron]]''), ''[[suman (food)|suman]]'', ''[[kesong puti]]'', and ''[[bibingka]]''. It is also popular during [[Christmas in the Philippines|Christmas season]] in the [[Philippines]], particularly among children.<ref name="cabrera"/>

In the novel ''[[Noli Me Tángere (novel)|Noli Me Tangere]]'' (1887) by the Philippine national hero, [[José Rizal]], the antagonist character Padre Salvi is alleged by his rival, the ''[[Alferez (rank)|alferez]]'' of the ''[[Civil Guard (Philippines)|Guardia Civil]]'', to calculatingly serve thick ''chocolate'' (''espeso'') for important guests and watered-down ''chocolate'' (''aguado'') for guests he deemed unimportant. According to the alferez, Salvi surreptitiously signals his servant to prepare either by saying "make a cup of ''chocolate'', eh?" or "make a cup of ''chocolate'', ah?" - "eh" and "ah" actually being short for ''espeso'' and ''aguado''. The narrator states he is unsure if this is just slander because the same story has been told about many priests, or it may be a practice of Salvi's [[Franciscan Order]]. Following Rizal, the terms "Chocolate Eh" and "Chocolate Ah" have been adopted by some establishments.<ref name="maranan">{{cite book|author=Santos-Taylor, L. Marcelline|editor =Maranan, Edgar |editor2=Maranan-Goldstein, Len|title =A Taste of Home: Pinoy Expats and Food Memories|chapter =Soul Comforts: Kapeng Barako and Tsokolate|publisher =Anvil Publishing, Incorporated|year =2017|isbn =9789712733031|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=n909DwAAQBAJ}}</ref>

'''Tubho tea''' (sometimes spelled '''tubha'''), is a traditional [[herbal tea]] of the [[Ivatan people]] in the [[Philippines]] made from dried leaves of the [[tubho fern]].<ref name="slow food">{{cite web |title=Tubho |url=https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/tubho-2/ |website=Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity |access-date=19 December 2018}}</ref>

==Tubho fern==
Tubho tea is made from the tubho fern, ''[[Odontosoria biflora]]'', also known as ''Sphenomeris biflora'' and ''Sphenomeris chinensis'' subsp. ''biflora''.<ref name=Barc03/><ref name=CFLW/> It is native to [[:Category:Flora of Southeast China|Southeast China]], Korea, Japan and its offshore islands, [[Taiwan]], and the [[Philippines]].<ref name=POWO_17165070-1/>

==Preparation==
Tubho tea is not made from fresh fronds of the tubho, instead it is made from mature fronds which have already wilted and dried while still on the plant. They are preferred because they are less bitter. The dried fronds are boiled in water until the water turns dark brown. The leaves are then removed and it is served hot. The leaves may be reused, as long as they still turn the water dark brown when boiled. The tea is traditionally sweetened with [[brown sugar]]. However, it can also be consumed similar to other teas, like with cream, honey, or lemon. Some modern versions serve it iced. The taste of the tea is described as slightly bitter and nutty.<ref name="slow food"/><ref name="Lauchengco">{{cite web |last1=Lauchengco |first1=Jess |title=How to brew the Tubho Tea the Ivatan Way |url=http://www.jessiekaaa.com/2015/05/how-to-brew-tubho-tea-ivatan-way.html |website=The Traveling Cupcake |access-date=19 December 2018}}</ref><ref name="lapena">{{cite news |last1=Lapeña |first1=Carmela G. |title=A day on Sabtang island in Batanes |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/lifestyle/travel/227681/a-day-on-sabtang-island-in-batanes/story/ |access-date=19 December 2018 |work=GMA News Online |date=28 July 2011}}</ref>

The [[Department of Science and Technology (Philippines)|Department of Science and Technology]] (DOST) has developed a powdered version of tubho tea which is made available in [[Sabtang, Batanes|Sabtang]] town. The DOST plans to develop a method that would enable wider commercial production of tubho tea.<ref name="eyes">{{cite news |last1=Visaya |first1=Villamor Jr. |title=DOST eyes commercialization of 'tubho tea' industry in Batanes |url=https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1115147 |access-date=20 September 2020 |work=Philippine News Agency |date=11 September 2020}}</ref>

==Ivatan culture==
Local [[Ivatan people]] claim that the tea is the secret to their longevity and has medicinal benefits.<ref name="lapena"/> Tubho tea is not cultivated. It is harvested from wild plants in the [[Batanes Islands]] in small quantities, particularly in the southernmost islands of [[Sabtang, Batanes|Sabtang]]. They are usually locally consumed or sold to tourists, though some restaurants in other parts of the Philippines serve it as part of their menus.<ref name="slow food"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Sabtang Island, Part 1: The Savidug stone houses |url=https://lakwatserang-guro.com/2015/05/31/sabtang-island-part-1-the-sinakan-stone-houses/ |website=Ang Lakwatserang Guro |access-date=19 December 2018}}</ref>

'''''Sagada coffee''', ''also known as ''Sagada arabica'', is a [[Single-origin coffee|single-origin]] [[coffee varietals|coffee varietal]] grown in [[Sagada]] in the [[Cordillera Central (Luzon)|Cordillera]] highlands of the northern [[Philippines]]. It belongs to the species ''[[Coffea arabica]]'', of the [[List of coffee varieties|Typica variety]].

==History==
Arabica coffee was introduced to Sagada in the late 19th century. Relatively later in comparison to lowland [[coffee varietals|coffee varietal]]s which were introduced to the [[Philippines]] earlier during the [[History of the Philippines (1521–1898)|Spanish colonial period]]. This was because Sagada only became recognized as a political unit by the [[Captaincy General of the Philippines|Spanish colonial government]] in 1847 and didn't have much contact with the Spanish prior to that.<ref name="Anacio"/>

There are multiple conflicting accounts of when and how arabica coffee was introduced to [[Sagada]]. Most accounts credit Jaime P. Masferré, a retired [[Spanish people|Spanish]] soldier originally from [[Catalonia]]. He was a former detachment commander of the [[Civil Guard (Philippines)|Guardia Civil]]. He married Mercedes Cunyap Langkew, a Sagada native, and established a plantation in the late 1890s in the town of Batalao after the [[Spanish Empire]] surrendered the Philippines to the [[United States Military Government of the Philippine Islands|United States colonial government]]. He grew citrus trees, [[Diospyros discolor|mabolo persimmon]], [[chayote]], and arabica coffee (probably from [[Benguet coffee|Benguet]]) which supposedly later became part of the crops of the local communities.<ref name="Malanes">{{cite news |last1=Malanes |first1=Maurice |last2=Nakamura |first2=Midori |last3=Tacloy |first3=John |title=History of Coffee in the Cordillera |url=https://kapitako.jimdo.com/2016/10/10/history-of-coffee-in-the-cordillera/ |access-date=December 19, 2018 |work=Kapi Tako |date=October 10, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Anacio">{{cite book|author=Anacio, Danesto B.|editor =Servaes, Jan|title =Sustainable Development Goals in the Asian Context|chapter =Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in Perspective: Lessons from the American Episcopal Missions in Sagada, Northern Philippines|publisher =Springer|year =2016|page=73|isbn =9789811028151|chapter-url =https://books.google.com/books?id=c0txDQAAQBAJ}}</ref> His son, [[Eduardo Masferré]] also became notable in his own right and is regarded as the "father of Philippine photography."<ref name="carino">{{cite journal |last1=Aguilar-Cariño |first1=Maria Luisa B. |title=Eduardo Masferré and the Philippine Cordillera |journal=Philippine Studies |date=1994 |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=336–351 |jstor=42633450 }}</ref><ref name="masferre">{{cite book|author=Masferré, Eduardo |title =A Tribute to the Philippine Cordillera|publisher =Asiatype, Inc.|year =1999|page=2|isbn = 9789719171201|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=UrSHR6OLme8C}}</ref>

The coffee trees were also said to have been spread to the northern areas of Sagada by Okoi, a [[Japanese in the Philippines|Japanese immigrant]] and a carpenter who worked for the American missionaries in the village of Fidelisan. He acquired coffee seedlings through his friendship with Masferré and planted them in Fidelisan.<ref name="Malanes"/>

==Cultivation==
Sagada coffee production is centered in the municipalities of [[Sagada]] and [[Besao, Mountain Province|Besao]] in [[Mountain Province]], northern [[Luzon]]. Like [[Benguet]], the climate of the [[Cordillera Central (Luzon)|Cordillera]] highlands of Sagada is highly suitable for arabica cultivation.<ref name="agri">{{cite news |title=Mt. Province coffee backed |url=http://www.bworldonline.com/content.php?section=&title=Mt.-Province-coffee-backed&id=44883 |access-date=December 20, 2018 |work=BusinessWorld |date=January 12, 2012}}</ref> Production is mostly in backyard and small-scale farms of the Sagada natives since the early 1900s. In Fidelisan, there are century-old coffee trees that still produce beans.<ref name="tayo"/><ref name="Malanes"/>

Most were for local consumption, though they bartered surplus beans to traveling traders from the lowlands. They also used coffee beans to barter for goods from local merchants. Cultivating and harvesting Sagada coffee were traditionally women's activities, often involving the entire community.<ref name="tayo"/><ref name="Malanes"/> Sagada coffee is characterized by its bittersweet taste with fruity or floral overtones.<ref name="tpk">{{cite web |title=Sagada Dark Roast Cold Brew + Figures Of Beans |url=https://www.thepeachkitchen.com/2017/08/sagada-dark-roast-figures-of-beans/ |website=The Peach Kitchen |access-date=December 20, 2018|date=August 2017 }}</ref><ref name="nolisoli">{{cite news |last1=Emocling |first1=Oliver |title=Kris Aquino should drink these on her coffee date |url=http://nolisoli.ph/28251/kris-aquino-just-invited-a-blogger-for-a-coffee-date/ |access-date=December 20, 2018 |work=Nolisoli |date=November 9, 2017}}</ref><ref name="Co">{{cite web |last1=Co |first1=Ailene |title=Seattle's Best Coffee Offers World-Class Beans From Sagada, Benguet, and Matumtum |url=http://www.trend-hotspot.com/food/seattles-best-coffee-offers-world-class-beans-from-sagada-benguet-and-matumtum/ |website=Trend Hotspot |access-date=December 20, 2018|date=March 19, 2018 }}</ref>

Sagada coffee is rare, even in local markets, because there have never been large-scale plantations of Sagada coffee until recently.<ref name="tayo">{{cite news |last1=Verne |first1=La |title=From Bean to Brew |url=http://www.tayoliterarymag.com/la-verne/ |work=Tayo Literary Magazine}}</ref><ref name="Del Mundo">{{cite news |last1=Del Mundo |first1=Ida Anita Q. |title=A brewing revolution |url=https://www.philstar.com/other-sections/starweek-magazine/2008/02/10/43908/brewing-revolution |access-date=December 20, 2018 |work=PhilStar Global |date=February 10, 2008}}</ref> There are increasing government initiatives to encourage its production in recent years, including providing training and equipment. In Sagada, there is a municipal ordinance that requires every household to plant at least five Sagada coffee trees. Before granting a marriage license, the local Sagada government also requires couples to plant the same number of trees.<ref name="agri"/><ref name="tibaldo">{{cite news |last1=Tibaldo |first1=Art |title=Brewing and Understanding Coffee Inside and Out |url=http://agriculture.com.ph/2018/03/18/brewing-and-understanding-coffee-inside-and-out/ |access-date=December 20, 2018 |work=Agriculture Monthly |issue=November |date=2014}}</ref> However the industry still struggles because of lack of awareness and low local demand.<ref name="Co-Calleja">{{cite news |last1=Co-Calleja |first1=Alina R. |title=I've 'bean' to Sagada...via a coffee lab in QC |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/lifestyle/food/597177/i-ve-bean-to-sagada-via-a-coffee-lab-in-qc/story/ |access-date=December 20, 2018 |work=GMA News Online |date=January 26, 2017}}</ref>

Test pilot (cocktail):
{{short description|Type of cocktail}}
The '''test pilot''' cocktail is a vintage [[Tiki culture|tiki drink]] invented by Donn Beach. Beach was known for changing his recipes over time,<ref>{{cite web |title=Jet Pilot soars over its ancestors |url=http://www.slammie.com/atomicgrog/blog/2012/02/07/mai-kai-cocktail-review-jet-pilot-soars-over-its-ancestors-with-flying-colors/ |website=slammie.com |date=7 February 2012 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref> and multiple versions of the test pilot attributed to both him and others make the cocktail one of his more frequently imitated and varied tiki drinks.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose|page=96 }}</ref> Test pilot recipes call for multiple rums and typically include the use of [[falernum]] syrup and lime juice. The more popular also include Pernod ([[pastis]]/[[absinthe]]) and [[bitters]].

==Test pilot versions==
A recipe from a [[Don the Beachcomber]] drink guide calls for 1 oz of Lemon Hart Demerara 151 proof rum and 3/4 oz each of Jamaican dark rum, Puerto Rican dark rum, lime juice, grape juice, and honey. Two dashes each of bitters and grenadine should also be added, then flash blended with cracked ice and served in a double [[old fashioned glass]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bitner |first1=Arnold |title=Hawai'i Tropical Rum Drinks by Don the Beaschcomber |date=2001 |publisher=Mutual Publishing |location=Honolulu|page=47}}</ref> The date of the recipe's origin and when and where it was served is not mentioned.

Another version that Jeff Berry attributes to Donn Beach from circa 1941 while less strong is still very potent and calls for 1 1/2 oz of Jamaican dark rum, 3/4 oz of Puerto Rican light rum, 3 teaspoons of [[Cointreau]], 1/8 a teaspoon of Pernod, a 1/2 oz of both lime juice and falernum syrup, and a dash of bitters.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose|page=96 }}</ref> The use of Pernod and bitters was employed by Beach as one of his signature combinations, and some cocktail enthusiasts feel it is a pivotal part of the recipe.<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=http://www.cocktailchronicles.com/2006/08/01/test-pilot/ |website=cocktailchronicles.com |date=August 2006 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Classic Tiki - The Jet Pilot |url=https://cold-glass.com/2016/06/05/classic-tiki-the-jet-pilot/ |website=cold-glass.com |date=5 June 2016 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot Tiki Drink Recipe |url=https://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2011/04/test-pilot-tiki-drink-recipe.html |website=seriouseats.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref> Several additional cocktail recipe references choose to highlight this version.<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot Cocktail Recipe |url=https://tuxedono2.com/test-pilot-cocktail-recipe |website=tuxedono2.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=https://www.myrecipes.com/recipe/test-pilot |website=myrecipes.com |accessdate=19 February 2019 |archive-date=3 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190303201505/https://www.myrecipes.com/recipe/test-pilot |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot Recipe |url=https://www.supercall.com/recipe/test-pilot-recipe |website=supercall.com |date=9 August 2016 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=https://kindredcocktails.com/cocktail/test-pilot |website=kindredcocktails.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

A [[Trader Vic's|Trader Vic]] test pilot version listed in his 1972 revised drink guide switches the lime juice for lemon and jettisons the Pernod and bitters, calling only for 1 3/4 oz dark Jamaican rum, 3/4 oz light Puerto Rican rum, 1/4 oz of Cointreau, 1/4 oz falernum, and 1/4 oz lemon juice.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vic |first1=Trader |title=Trader Vic's Bartenders Guide, Revised |date=1972 |publisher=[[Doubleday (publisher)|Doubleday]] |location=Garden City, NY |edition=revised|page=186}}</ref>  ''Difford's Guide'' chose to highlight the Trader Vic's version.<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1940/test-pilot |website=diffordsguide.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

==The Jet Pilot==
Some Beachcomber and Trader Vic competitors named their versions as the ''Jet Pilot'', including at [[Joseph Stephen Crane|The Luau]] restaurant and the [[Mai-Kai Restaurant|Mai-Kai]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Pilot Tiki Cocktails |url=https://blog.distiller.com/pilot-tiki-cocktails/ |website=blog.distiller.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Classic Tiki - The Jet Pilot |url=https://cold-glass.com/2016/06/05/classic-tiki-the-jet-pilot/ |website=cold-glass.com |date=5 June 2016 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref> The Jet Pilot was similar to Beach's 1941 version but was slightly spicier with the addition of stronger rum, grapefruit juice, and cinnamon syrup.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tiki Classics Jet Pilot |url=http://cocktailchem.blogspot.com/2011/12/tiki-classics-jet-pilot.html |website=cocktailchem.blogspot.com |date=6 December 2011 |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Jet Pilot Cocktail Recipe |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/jet-pilot-cocktail-recipe-760532 |website=thespruceeats.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

==Impact on tiki culture==
Beyond the Jet Pilot, other aviation themed tiki cocktails include the similarly named ''Ace Pilot'', Don Beach's [[Q.B. Cooler]], and Trader Vic's [[PB2Y (cocktail)|PB2Y]] (named after the Navy's [[Consolidated PB2Y Coronado|Coronado plane]]).

A [[tiki bar]] named ''Test Pilot'' operates in [[Santa Barbara, California]], that serves a test pilot cocktail, described as having a flavor profile of "house rum blend, clove, citrus, bitters, [and] absinthe foam".<ref>{{cite web |title=Test Pilot |url=http://www.testpilotcocktails.com/ |website=testpilotcocktails.com |accessdate=19 February 2019}}</ref>

'''Soda gembira''' (lit. 'happy soda') is an [[Indonesian cuisine|Indonesian]] [[List of Indonesian beverages|drink]]. It is made up of [[cocopandan syrup]], [[condensed milk]], seltzer and [[ice cube|ice]]. A related drink, Soda Susu, uses [[carbonated water]] instead of strawberry-flavored Fanta.

Soda gembira is a popular beverage in Indonesia. It is usually served during [[iftar]] in [[Ramadan]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://anekaresepmasakan.info/es-soda-gembira-spesial-menu-buka-puasa/|title=Resep Es Soda Gembira Spesial Menu Buka Puasa|lang=id|url-status=dead|access-date=2020-06-28|archive-date=2016-06-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160613180344/http://anekaresepmasakan.info/es-soda-gembira-spesial-menu-buka-puasa/}}</ref> and at wedding receptions, alongside foods including [[bakso]], [[nasi goreng]], [[rendang]], and [[Soto (food)|soto]].

==Details==
Soda Gembira is a typical Indonesian drink. It is famous for its combination of sweet and refreshing flavors. This drink is made from a combination of [[Flavored syrup|red syrup]], which is usually [[Cocopandan syrup|cocopandan]] flavored, [[Condensed milk|sweetened condensed milk]], and carbonated soda, such as Sprite or Fanta. The red syrup provides a bright color and distinctive sweet taste, while the sweetened condensed milk adds a creamy texture. The soda provides a refreshing carbonated sensation, making it an ideal drink for hot weather or special occasions.<ref>{{Cite web | last=Schmid |first=Gregor | title = Soda Gembira: Minuman Khas Indonesia yang Menyegarkan | url = https://kaijuphile.com/soda-gembira-minuman-khas-indonesia-menyegarkan/ | access-date = 24 October 2024 | publisher = Kaijuphile | date = 2024-09-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=SODA GEMBIRA |url=https://pdfcoffee.com/resep-minuman-modern-pdf-free.html |access-date=2024-10-24 |website=pdfcoffee.com |language=en}}</ref>

The origins of Soda Gembira do not have a specific history. However, Dutch colonial influence likely played a role in the use of sweetened condensed milk, which was starting to become popular in Indonesia at that time.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Wijaya|first=Yana Gabriella|date=2020-05-31|title=Sejarah Susu di Indonesia, Dulu Dianggap Darah Putih|url=https://travel.kompas.com/read/2020/05/31/161246127/sejarah-susu-di-indonesia-dulu-dianggap-darah-putih|work=[[Kompas.com]]|language=id|access-date=2021-10-22|editor-last=Aisyah|editor-first=Yuharrani}}</ref> On the other hand, the use of sweet syrup was already part of the local beverage tradition in Indonesia, while the introduction of soda drinks to Indonesia in the mid-20th century paved the way for the creation of this drink. The combination of local ingredients, such as cocopandan syrup with carbonated soda, created a new, unique taste that was loved by many people. Soda Gembira is often served in food stalls, especially in Padang restaurants or other traditional eateries. This drink is not only popular because of its pleasant taste but also because of its attractive appearance with a striking red color that symbolizes joy. In some variations, this drink can be served with ice cubes or additions such as basil and [[nata de coco]] to enrich the texture.

In addition to being a favorite choice in restaurants and food stalls, Soda Gembira also often appears at various family events or celebrations as a dessert drink. With a strong sweet taste and refreshing carbonated sensation, Soda Gembira is a symbol of a relaxed and happy atmosphere, in accordance with its name, which reflects joy and pleasure.<ref>{{Cite web | last=Schmid |first=Gregor | title = Soda Gembira: Minuman Khas Indonesia yang Menyegarkan | url = https://kaijuphile.com/soda-gembira-minuman-khas-indonesia-menyegarkan/ | access-date = 24 October 2024 | publisher = Kaijuphile | date = 2024-09-14}}</ref>

'''Seedlip''' is a British company that makes plant-based [[liquor]] substitutes for use in non-alcoholic [[mixed drinks]].

Seedlip describes its products as "the world's first distilled non-alcoholic spirits".<ref>{{Cite web|last=Fleming|first=Molly|date=2020-02-05|title=Seedlip on its mission to prove no-alcohol 'shouldn't be second best'|url=https://www.marketingweek.com/seedlip-no-alcohol-campaign/|access-date=2020-11-02|website=Marketing Week|language=en}}</ref> They are sold in four varieties: "Garden 108" (peas and garden herbs), "Spice 94" (spices, citrus peels and barks), "Grove 42" (citrus and spices), and the newest "Notas de Agave" (prickly pear, lime and agave).<ref>{{Cite web|last=Prikhodko|first=Anastasia|date=24 January 2020|title=Seedlip success: The non-alcoholic spirits selling out in the UK|url=https://www.theceomagazine.com/lifestyle/food-beverage/seedlip/|access-date=2020-11-02|website=The CEO Magazine|language=en-US}}</ref> According to their labels, Seedlip products consist of water, "natural botanical distillates and extracts (15%)", the preservative [[potassium sorbate]], and [[citric acid]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Seedlip Garden 108|url=https://seedlipdrinks.com/uk/shop/seedlip-garden-108|access-date=2020-11-02|website=Seedlip}}</ref> On their own, their taste has been described as "a sort of pleasantly pungent savoury-herby-medicinal water".<ref>{{Cite news|last=Nicholson|first=Rebecca|date=10 September 2017|title='Non-drinkers deserve a great adult cocktail': how alcohol-free spirits became a stealth hit|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2017/sep/10/non-alcoholic-spirits-adult-cocktail-booze-free|access-date=2020-11-02|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Claire Lower of ''[[Lifehacker]]'' was critical of the product, writing that it added little to [[mocktails]] and that its usefulness depended heavily on the [[mixologist]]'s skills and on the other ingredients.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Lower|first=Claire|date=19 February 2020|title=Sober People Deserve Better Than Seedlip|url=https://skillet.lifehacker.com/sober-people-deserve-better-than-seedlip-1841776075|access-date=2020-11-02|website=Lifehacker|language=en-us}}</ref>

Seedlip is one of the best-known<ref>{{Cite web|last=Cope|first=Rebecca|date=1 October 2020|title=Cheers! These are the best alcohol-free brands for Stoptober|url=https://www.tatler.com/article/alcohol-free-wine-spirit-brands|access-date=2020-11-02|website=Tatler|language=en-GB}}</ref> but also most expensive<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Woolfson|first=Daniel|date=21 November 2019|title=Polarising, pricey and non-alcoholic: why Seedlip is booze's biggest success story|url=https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/big-interview/polarising-pricey-and-non-alcoholic-why-seedlip-is-boozes-biggest-success-story/599697.article|access-date=2020-11-02|website=The Grocer|language=en}}</ref> brands in what is, as of 2020, the rapidly growing field of liquor substitutes.<ref name=":0" /> Founded in 2014 by Ben Branson, a former luxury brand designer,<ref name=":0" /> the company has been majority-owned by the multinational alcohol company [[Diageo]] since 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Davies|first=Rob|date=7 August 2019|title=Diageo buys majority stake in non-alcoholic spirit Seedlip|url=http://www.theguardian.com/business/2019/aug/07/diageo-buys-seedlip-to-cash-in-on-trend-for-low-alcohol-lifestyle|access-date=2020-11-02|website=The Guardian|language=en}}</ref> The name derives from the [[:wikt:seedlep|seedlep]] or seedlip, a basket for carrying seeds while sowing.

In December 2020, British company Lockdown Liquor & Co announced its collaboration with Seedlip in making Grove Picante, Lockdown Liquor's first non-alcoholic spirit. Grove Picante is an inspired creation from Lockdown Liquor's Picante spirit and Seedlip's Grove 42 non-alcoholic spirit. '''Sleepy girl mocktail''' is a [[Viral video|viral]] homemade [[Drink|beverage]] that [[TikTok food trends|gained popularity on TikTok]] as a [[Insomnia|sleep aid]].<ref name="Blum 2024 k433">{{cite web | last=Blum | first=Dani | title=Sleepy Girl Mocktail: Can This Tart Cherry Juice Drink Help You Fall Asleep? | website=The New York Times | date=2024-01-17 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/01/17/well/live/sleepy-girl-mocktail-cherry-magnesium.html#:~:text=The%20recipe%20for%20a%20%E2%80%9Csleepy,sleep%2C%20however%2C%20remain%20skeptical. | access-date=2024-01-17}}</ref> The first propagator of the drink is reported to be Calee Shea who posted about it in January 2023, but Gracie Norton, a content creator on TikTok, popularized the drink with her post.<ref name="Heinrich 2023 t067">{{cite web | last=Heinrich | first=Shelby | title=Viral Viral Sleepy Girl Cocktail Recipe And Review | website=BuzzFeed | date=2023-04-21 | url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/shelbyheinrich/tiktok-sleepy-girl-mocktail-review | access-date=2024-01-18}}</ref><ref name="Berryman 2024 p660">{{cite web | last=Berryman | first=Louella | title=Does the sleepy girl mocktail really work? | website=Women's Health | date=2024-01-10 | url=https://www.womenshealthmag.com/uk/food/a46328807/sleepy-girl-mocktail/ | access-date=2024-01-17}}</ref><ref name="Green 2024 s659">{{cite web | last=Green | first=Cassandra | title=Everything You Need To Know About The 'Sleepy Girl Mocktail' | website=ELLE | date=2024-01-15 | url=https://www.elle.com.au/life/sleepy-girl-mocktail-recipe-tiktok-trend-explained/ | access-date=2024-01-17}}</ref> The drink became viral that year.<ref name="Fiedler 2023 i335">{{cite web | last=Fiedler | first=Christina Montoya | title=TikTok's Sleepy Girl Mocktail May Be the Perfect Pre-Bedtime Drink | website=Better Homes & Gardens | date=2023-04-10 | url=https://www.bhg.com/sleepy-girl-mocktail-tiktok-trend-7376377 | access-date=2024-01-17}}</ref> The drink surged in popularity in January 2024, as "[[Dry January]]" prompted numerous individuals to seek mocktail recipes online.<ref name="Werner 2024 f540">{{cite web | last=Werner | first=Kaleigh | title=What is the Sleepy Girl Mocktail? TikTok's newest drink obsession | website=The Independent | date=2024-01-18 | url=https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/sleepy-girl-mocktail-tiktok-b2481091.html | access-date=2024-01-22}}</ref>

== Ingredients ==
The primary ingredients of sleepy girl mocktail include:
* '''Tart [[cherry juice]]:''' Claimed to possess potential sleep-inducing properties due to its relatively high melatonin content.<ref name="Steinhilber 2023 q418" /> Studies on its effectiveness are limited, with melatonin levels lower than typical sleep-inducing supplements.<ref name="Blum 2024 k433" /> Other nutrients in the juice like [[tryptophan]] and [[polyphenol]] [[Antioxidant|antioxidants]] may also play a role in promoting sleep.<ref name="Steinhilber 2023 q418" />
* '''[[Magnesium (medical use)|Magnesium powder]]:''' Touted for sleep benefits, but conclusive evidence supporting its positive impact is lacking.<ref name="Blum 2024 k433" /> Some studies suggest potential benefits for individuals with restless leg syndrome.<ref name="Blum 2024 k433" /> It may be of particular benefit to those with [[magnesium deficiency]], a common condition that is correlated with [[anxiety]] and [[Depression (mood)|depression]].<ref name="Shultz 2024 a699">{{cite web |last=Shultz |first=Cara Lynn |date=2024-01-19 |title=What Is the Magic Ingredient in TikTok's 'Sleepy Girl Mocktail'? |url=https://people.com/sleepy-girl-mocktail-magnesium-anxiety-sleep-8430926 |access-date=2024-01-20 |website=Peoplemag}}</ref> Most magnesium found in retail stores is [[magnesium oxide]], which is not well-absorbed.<ref name="Shultz 2024 a699" /> Thus, [[magnesium glycinate]] is the preferred option.<ref name="Shultz 2024 a699" /> However, there is a risk of [[Hypermagnesemia|magnesium toxicity]] if too much magnesium is ingested.<ref name="Shultz 2024 a699" />
* '''[[Seltzer]] or lemon-lime soda:''' Fizzing agents enhancing the texture and flavor of the mocktail.<ref name="Blum 2024 k433" /> Recipes often call for [[Prebiotic (nutrition)|prebiotic]] soda, such as [[Olipop]].<ref name="Steinhilber 2023 q418">{{cite web |last=Steinhilber |first=Brianna |date=2023-04-28 |title=Can the 'sleepy girl mocktail' really help you fall asleep faster? |url=https://www.today.com/health/diet-fitness/sleepy-girl-mocktail-rcna81975 |access-date=2024-01-19 |website=TODAY.com}}</ref> Drinks with lower sugar content are recommended, as higher blood sugar levels can negatively impact sleep.<ref name="Nast 2023 o228">{{cite web |last=Londong |first=Bianca |date=2023-04-25 |title=The 'sleepy girl mocktail' is trending on TikTok because it's giving people the best night's sleep of their life |url=https://www.glamourmagazine.co.uk/article/sleepy-girl-mocktail |access-date=2024-01-20 |website=Glamour UK}}</ref> However, it is possible that the carbonation may lead to feelings of bloating and abdominal discomfort, negatively impacting sleep.<ref name="Davison 2024 r512">{{cite web | last=Davison | first=Tamara | title=Here's how to make Tiktok's 'sleepy girl mocktail' | website=Evening Standard | date=2024-01-19 | url=https://www.standard.co.uk/going-out/foodanddrink/sleepy-girl-mocktail-recipe-tiktok-trend-recipe-b1133289.html | access-date=2024-01-22}}</ref>

== Preparation ==
First, any glass of one's choice is filled with ice.<ref name="Fiedler 2023 i335" /> Then, the tart cherry juice is then added.<ref name="Fiedler 2023 i335" />  Next, the magnesium powder is dissolved in the juice.<ref name="Fiedler 2023 i335" /> Finally, the soda or seltzer is used to top off the drink.<ref name="Fiedler 2023 i335" /> [[Alcoholic beverage|Alcohol]] is notably excluded from the recipe, even though it is a [[depressant]], because it can lead to worse quality of sleep.<ref name="Fiedler 2023 i335" />

== Scientific evidence ==
Scientific evidence supporting the efficacy of sleepy girl mocktail's ingredients remains inconclusive, with the [[placebo effect]] potentially playing a significant role in any perceived sleep-related benefits.<ref name="Blum 2024 k433" /> The ritual of preparing and consuming the sleepy girl mocktail may contribute to a perceived enhancement in sleep quality.<ref name="Blum 2024 k433" /><ref name="Docherty 2024 t284">{{cite web | last=Docherty | first=Erin | title=Sleepy Girl Mocktail: Does it actually work? | website=Mamamia | date=2024-01-18 | url=https://www.mamamia.com.au/does-sleepy-girl-mocktail-work/ | access-date=2024-01-18}}</ref>

Tart cherry juice, according to a 2011 study in the ''[[European Journal of Nutrition]]'', may boost melatonin production and promote relaxation.<ref name="McCarthy 2024 c153">{{cite web | last=McCarthy | first=Kelly | title=What is a sleepy girl mocktail? How to make the viral tart cherry juice pre-bedtime drink | website=ABC News | date=2024-01-18 | url=https://abcnews.go.com/food/story/sleepy-girl-mocktail-make-viral-tart-cherry-juice/?id=106442503 | access-date=2024-01-18}}</ref><ref name="Howatson Bell Tallent Middleton 2012 pp. 909–916">{{cite journal | last1=Howatson | first1=Glyn | last2=Bell | first2=Phillip G. | last3=Tallent | first3=Jamie | last4=Middleton | first4=Benita | last5=McHugh | first5=Malachy P. | last6=Ellis | first6=Jason | title=Effect of tart cherry juice (Prunus cerasus) on melatonin levels and enhanced sleep quality | journal=European Journal of Nutrition | volume=51 | issue=8 | date=2012 | issn=1436-6207 | doi=10.1007/s00394-011-0263-7 | pages=909–916 | pmid=22038497 }}</ref> A more recent study from July 2023 in ''[[Current Sleep Medicine Reports]]'' suggested potential improvements in total sleep time and efficiency with tart cherry juice, but further research is needed to confirm these findings.<ref name="McCarthy 2024 c153"/><ref name="Stretton Eranki Kovoor Bacchi 2023 pp. 225–233">{{cite journal | last1=Stretton | first1=Brandon | last2=Eranki | first2=Aditya | last3=Kovoor | first3=Joshua | last4=Bacchi | first4=Stephen | last5=Gupta | first5=Aashray | last6=Maddern | first6=Guy | last7=Boyd | first7=Mark | title=Too Sour to be True? Tart Cherries (Prunus cerasus) and Sleep: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis | journal=Current Sleep Medicine Reports | volume=9 | issue=3 | date=2023-07-11 | issn=2198-6401 | doi=10.1007/s40675-023-00261-w | pages=225–233| doi-access=free }}</ref>

The magnesium may promote physical and mental relaxation which may in effect promote sleep.<ref name="Clinic 2023 a041">{{cite web | title=Is the Sleepy Girl Mocktail Your Magic Bullet for Better Sleep? | website=Cleveland Clinic | date=2023-11-08 | url=https://health.clevelandclinic.org/sleepy-girl-mocktail | access-date=2024-01-18}}</ref><ref name="Wienecke Nolden 2016 pp. 12–16">{{cite journal | last1=Wienecke | first1=Elmar | last2=Nolden | first2=Claudia | title=Langzeit-HRV-Analyse zeigt Stressreduktion durch Magnesiumzufuhr | journal=MMW - Fortschritte der Medizin | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=158 | issue=S6 | year=2016 | issn=1438-3276 | doi=10.1007/s15006-016-9054-7 | pages=12–16 | language=de}}</ref>

A '''sour''' is a traditional family of [[mixed drink]]s. ''Sours'' belong to one of the old families of original cocktails and are described by [[Jerry Thomas (bartender)|Jerry Thomas]] in his 1862 book ''How to Mix Drinks''.<ref name="Cocktail Chronicles">Paul Clarke. [http://www.cocktailchronicles.com/2005/09/25/make-yourself-comfortable/ Make Yourself Comfortable]. September 25, 2005. The Cocktail Chronicles. Retrieved on January 1, 2007.</ref> 

Sours are mixed drinks containing a base liquor, [[Lemon juice|lemon]] or [[lime juice]], and a sweetener ([[simple syrup]] or [[orgeat syrup]]).<ref name="Joy 158-159">{{cite book|author=Regan, Gary |title=The Joy of Mixology, The Consummate Guide to the Bartender's Craft |year=2003 |publisher=Clarkson Potter |isbn=0609608843|pages=158–159}}</ref> [[Egg white|Egg whites]] are also included in some sours.

==Types of sours==

===Gin sour===
The '''gin sour''' is a traditional [[mixed cocktail]] that predates [[Prohibition in the United States]]. It is a simple combination of gin, lemon juice, and sugar. Adding carbonated water to this turns it into a [[gin fizz]].

It was popular during the 1940s, and [[Kevin Starr]] includes it in "an array of drinks (the gin sour, the whiskey sour, the [[Rickey (cocktail)#The gin Rickey|gin Rickey]], the [[Tom Collins]], the [[Pink lady (cocktail)|pink lady]], the [[Old fashioned (cocktail)|old fashioned]]) that now seem period pieces, evocative of another era".{{ref|starr}}

===Pisco sour===
{{main|Pisco sour}}
The classic '''pisco sour''' recipe contains [[pisco]] brandy (usually an un-aged grape brandy from Perú), fresh lime juice, fresh lemon juice, simple syrup, egg white, and [[bitters]].<ref name="LA Speakeasy">Navarro, V. [https://www.laspeakeasy.com/pisco-sour/ Classic Pisco Sour] ''LA Speakeasy''</ref> It is [[Cocktail shaker|shaken]], [[Cocktail strainer|strained]], and served [[Straight up (bartending)|straight]] in a cocktail glass then garnished with the bitters (cinnamon can be used). The addition of egg white creates a foamy head when shaken before serving. While pisco sour is flavoured with key lime by default, pisco is combined with other fruit to create mango sour, maracuya ([[passion fruit]]) sour, lucuma sour and so forth.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://peru.com/estilo-de-vida/gastronomia/maracuya-sour-que-necesitas-y-como-se-prepara-este-exquisito-trago-noticia-213918 |title=Maracuya sour: Qué necesitas y cómo se prepara este exquisito trago |first=Redacción |last=Peru.com |date=December 6, 2013 |website=Perú.com}}</ref> Peru has a National Pisco Sour Day (which lasts a weekend) in mid-February,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://elcomercio.pe/noticias/dia-del-pisco-sour |title=Todas las noticias de Día del Pisco Sour |website=El Comercio}}</ref> and Chile has Pisco Day in mid-May.

===Rum sour===

The basic [[Daiquiri]], sometimes called a Daiquiri sour, is made with rum, lime juice and simple syrup.<ref>{{cite web |title=Daiquiri cocktail |website=Difford's |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1083/daiquiri-cocktail}}</ref> One account of the drink's origin is that the general manager of the Spanish-American Iron Core Company, which operated the "Daiquiri" mine, ran out of gin one night when making gin sour for his guests, and switched to rum. This rum sour became known as the Daiquiri. However, earlier printed recipes for rum sour exist such as one from [[Jerry Thomas (bartender)|Jerry Thomas]] from 1887.<ref>{{cite book |last=Broom |first=Dave |title=Rum The Manual |date=2016 |publisher=Octopus Books |isbn=9781784720667 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HfwyDQAAQBAJ}}</ref>

===Whiskey sour===

{{main|Whiskey sour}}

The '''whiskey sour''' is a [[mixed drink]] containing [[bourbon whiskey]] or [[rye whiskey]], lemon juice, sugar, and optionally a dash of egg white to make it a Boston Sour. It is shaken and served either straight or over ice. The traditional garnish is half an orange slice and a [[maraschino cherry]]. If floated with claret red wine it's called a [[New York sour]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Difford |first=Simon |title=New York Sour |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3398/new-york-sour-cocktail |access-date=September 29, 2022 |website=Diffords Guide}}</ref>

A notable variant of the whiskey sour is the [[Ward 8 (cocktail)|Ward 8]], which often is based with either bourbon or rye whiskey, both lemon and orange juices, and grenadine syrup as the sweetener. The egg white sometimes employed in other whiskey sours is generally not included in this variation.

===Other sours===
* '''[[Amaretto sour]]''': [[Amaretto]] liqueur, lemon juice and sometimes egg white, bitters or sugar syrup.<ref>{{cite web|title=Amaretto Sour|url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/53/amaretto-sour|website=Difford's Guide|access-date=21 March 2018}}</ref>
* '''Brandy sour''' or [[brandy daisy]] (Jerry Thomas, 1887): brandy, clear or orange [[curaçao liqueur|curaçao]], sugar, lemon juice, shaken and strained into a wine glass.
* '''[[Caipirinha]]''': [[Cachaça]], sugar, lime, ice in an [[old fashioned glass]].
* '''[[Brandy sour (Cyprus)|Cypriot brandy sour]]''': [[Cyprus brandy]], lemon cordial and bitters, stirred in a tall glass, and topped with soda or lemonade.
* '''[[b:Bartending/Cocktails/Glossary#M|Midori sour]]''': Honeydew melon liquor, grenadine, lemon juice. Poured properly, it resembles a green [[Tequila sunrise (cocktail)|tequila sunrise]] with visible layers.
* '''Santa Cruz sour''' (Jerry Thomas, 1887): Santa Cruz rum, sugar, lemon juice, shaken and strained into a wine glass.
* '''Tequila sour''': Tequila, lemon juice, lime juice, agave nectar, Bittercube Corazon bitters, egg white.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tequila Sour|url=http://recipe.awesomedrinks.com/recipe/tequila-sour/|website=Awesome Drinks}}</ref>
